## Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1840s–1860s)

### Jurisdiction Overview

Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton Counties, with Pottsville as the county seat. During the 1840s–1860s, it was the heart of Pennsylvania's anthracite coal mining region, attracting large waves of Welsh, Irish, English, and German immigrants. The Philadelphia and Reading Railroad reached the area by the 1840s. Key denominations included Lutheran, German Reformed, Welsh Calvinist Methodist, Methodist Episcopal, and Roman Catholic.

---

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)

Pennsylvania had **no effective statewide civil registration** during the 1840s–1860s. Local registration was nominally required but compliance was poor. **Church records are the practical substitute** for births (baptisms), marriages, and deaths (burials) in this period. Other alternatives include family Bibles, newspaper notices, and cemetery inscriptions.

---

### Key Record Types & Online Access

#### Federal Census (Most Accessible)
- **FamilySearch Image Group 007621224** — U.S. Federal Census, Schuylkill County, 1850–1860; 412 images, **96% name-indexed and full-text searchable**. Start here.
- The 1840 census named only the head of household; 1850 and 1860 named every person.
- **Mortality schedules** for 1850 and 1860 recorded deaths in the preceding year — a valuable death-record substitute.
- **Ancestry** also holds the 1850 Schuylkill County census: https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/

#### Church Records
- **FamilySearch Image Group 004288771** — Lutheran Church Records, Schuylkill County, 1840–1875; 198 images. **Browse-only, not name-indexed** — entries are in English and German. Must be read page-by-page.
- A broader "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" collection (covering 1708–1985, ~1.2M records) is on FamilySearch — verify directly at FamilySearch.org.
- Records for Welsh Calvinist Methodist, Roman Catholic, German Reformed, and Methodist Episcopal congregations are largely **physical-only** at individual churches or diocesan archives (Diocese of Allentown for Catholic; Lutheran Archives Center at Philadelphia).

#### Probate Records
- **FamilySearch Image Group 004812990** — Probate Records, Schuylkill County, 1845–1880; 286 images. Only 4% name-indexed, but **full-text searchable** — try a text search before browsing.
- **FamilySearch Collection 1999196** — Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994; 3.2 million images, browse-only (statewide).
- Types include wills, letters of administration, guardianship files, inventories, and estate distributions. Physical originals at the Schuylkill County Courthouse, Orphans' Court Division.

#### Naturalization Records
- Given the massive immigrant mining population, naturalization records are **especially valuable** here. Pre-1906 declarations of intention and petitions were filed at the **Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas** in Pottsville — physical-only, not digitized.
- The **1863 Civil War draft enrollment lists** name every adult male, including recent immigrants not yet naturalized — an excellent census substitute.

#### Military Records
- Mexican-American War (1846–1848) bounty land warrants; Civil War service records and pension files (NARA/Fold3).
- Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) holds state adjutant general records for Civil War service.

#### Land & Tax Records
- Pennsylvania is a **state-land state** — metes-and-bounds descriptions. Deeds are at the Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds (physical only for this period).
- Tax assessment lists (personal property and real estate) can bridge gaps between census years — physical-only at the courthouse.
- **Ancestry**: Pennsylvania Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768–1801 (background/pre-period): https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/

#### Newspapers
- The ***Miners' Journal*** (Pottsville, founded 1825) is a **critical source** — detailed obituaries, marriage notices, estate and legal notices. Microfilm at the Schuylkill County Historical Society and Historical Society of Pennsylvania. Some issues on Chronicling America (Library of Congress) and Newspapers.com.

#### Cemetery Records
- FindAGrave and BillionGraves cover many Schuylkill County cemeteries. Physical sexton and burial registers are held by individual congregations and municipalities.

---

### Repository Guide

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Census (96% indexed), probate (full-text), Lutheran church records (browse-only) | Free |
| **Ancestry** | 1850 census, pre-period tax lists | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Civil War service & pension files | Subscription |
| **Chronicling America (LOC)** | Digitized newspapers | Free |
| **Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville** | Deeds, probate, court records, naturalizations, tax records | In-person or mail |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg** | Land records, Civil War adjutant general records | In-person; some online finding aids at phmc.pa.gov |
| **Schuylkill County Historical Society, Pottsville** | Local history, newspaper microfilm, cemetery records, published histories | In-person |
| **NARA Mid-Atlantic Region, Philadelphia** | Federal records: naturalization, military, census originals | In-person or online request |
| **Diocese of Allentown / Lutheran Archives Center, Philadelphia** | Diocesan Catholic and Lutheran registers not yet microfilmed | Contact directly |

---

### Records NOT Yet Online

- County deed books and mortgage records
- County tax assessment lists for the 1840s–1860s
- Naturalization declarations and petitions (pre-1906)
- Church registers for non-Lutheran denominations (Welsh Calvinist Methodist, Methodist Episcopal, German Reformed, Roman Catholic)
- Mine employment records and company records
- Sexton and burial registers for individual cemeteries

---

### Research Tips

1. **Start with the 1850 and 1860 federal censuses** (FamilySearch image group 007621224, 96% indexed) — these are the most accessible anchor sources and include birthplace data critical for tracing immigrants.
2. **Church records substitute for vital records** — the Lutheran volume (image group 004288771) must be browsed image-by-image in English and German. For other denominations, contact the church or diocesan archive directly.
3. **The *Miners' Journal* is uniquely valuable** for this county — its obituaries and legal notices often named individuals found nowhere else.
4. **German-language records:** Many Lutheran and Reformed church records are in German Kurrent script. Be prepared to read the original or engage a paleography specialist.
5. **Tax records bridge inter-census years** — township-level tax lists for off-years (1841, 1845, 1851, 1855, etc.) can locate an individual between the 1840, 1850, and 1860 censuses.
6. **Search adjoining counties** (Berks, Northumberland, Columbia, Luzerne, Carbon) — miners moved between districts, and families living near county boundaries may appear in neighboring jurisdictions.
7. **Mortality schedules** for 1850 and 1860 record deaths in the preceding year and serve as death-record substitutes when no church burial register survives.
8. **Consult published county histories** (Munsell's *History of Schuylkill County*, 1881) for biographical sketches and transcriptions of records that may since have been lost — available through the FHL catalog, Ancestry, and Google Books.
9. **The probate volume** (image group 004812990) is full-text searchable despite being barely name-indexed — run a text search before committing to a page-by-page browse.
10. **No courthouse fires or major record losses** for this county were confirmed in this survey — contact the Schuylkill County Historical Society to verify whether any specific records were destroyed.

# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1840s–1860s)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** 1811, carved from Berks and Northampton Counties
- **County seat:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place population tool for this query; no figures can be cited.
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated — Schuylkill County was the heart of Pennsylvania's anthracite region. Supporting industries included iron furnaces, railroads (Philadelphia and Reading Railroad reached the area by the 1840s), and agriculture in rural townships.
- **Ethnic composition:** The 1840s–1860s saw large-scale immigration of Welsh, Irish, English, and German miners. Earlier settlers were predominantly German and Scots-Irish.
- **Religious denominations:** Lutheran, Reformed (German Reformed), Welsh Calvinist Methodist, Methodist Episcopal, Roman Catholic, Episcopal, and various Baptist congregations were all present.
- **Key historical events:** The coal boom of the 1840s–1850s brought rapid population growth. The Civil War (1861–1865) produced draft records and pension files. The Molly Maguires conflict was taking shape in the mining communities during this period.

## Boundary changes

- Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 and its boundaries were essentially stable through the 1840s–1860s target period. No boundary changes split records across successor jurisdictions during these decades.
- Records predating 1811 will be found under Berks County (to the southeast) and Northampton County (to the northeast).

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records returned only generic content and did not supply a specific statewide registration date. It is well established that Pennsylvania did not have effective statewide civil registration during the 1840s–1860s. Local (borough/township) registration was nominally required but compliance was poor and survival is inconsistent.
- **What this means for this period:** Do not rely on civil vital records as a primary source for the 1840s–1860s. Church records are the principal substitute for births (baptisms), marriages, and deaths (burials) in this period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers, family Bible entries, newspaper notices, and cemetery inscriptions are the practical primary sources.

### Church records

- **What FamilySearch has digitized:** `volume_search` returned one digitized volume for Schuylkill County church records:
  - **Image group 004288771** — Church Records (Lutheran), covering Schuylkill County, 1840–1875. 198 images. **Languages: English and German** — researchers must be prepared to read German-language entries. `recordSearchablePercent`: 0 (not name-indexed). `fulltextSearchable`: false. **This volume must be browsed image by image with no search capability.** This is a browse-only resource.
- **Collections search** also returned a "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" collection (collection ID SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, date range 1708–1985) with approximately 1.2 million records and 607,000 images — this collection covers the county broadly. Note: this collection's ID prefix ("SYNTH") marks it as a test fixture in the tool data; treat it with caution and verify its contents directly at FamilySearch.org before relying on it.
- **Denominations and repositories:** Welsh Calvinist Methodist, Methodist Episcopal, Roman Catholic, German Reformed, and other denominations each maintained their own registers. Diocesan and denominational archives (Catholic Diocese of Allentown; Lutheran archives at Philadelphia) hold records not necessarily on FamilySearch.
- **Warning:** Church records in this area frequently appear in German for Lutheran and Reformed congregations. Welsh-language records exist for Welsh Calvinist Methodist churches.

### Census records

- **Federal census (county level):** `volume_search` returned one digitized, indexed volume:
  - **Image group 007621224** — U.S. Federal Census, Schuylkill County, covering 1850–1860. 412 images. `recordSearchablePercent`: 96 (highly name-indexed). `fulltextSearchable`: true. **Indexed and searchable by name online.** This is the most accessible digitized source for the period.
- **Available census years in the target window:** 1840, 1850, and 1860 federal censuses all fall within the period. The 1840 census named only the head of household; the 1850 and 1860 censuses named every person in the household.
- **Mortality schedules:** Federal mortality schedules (1850 and 1860) recorded deaths in the year preceding the census and can substitute for missing death records. They would accompany these census years.
- **Ancestry also holds:** "1850 United States Federal Census - Schuylkill County" (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/) — separately accessible on Ancestry with a subscription.
- **State census:** The Pennsylvania Wiki pages returned only generic content and did not confirm a Pennsylvania state census for intercensal years in this period; no state census can be cited from tool results.

### Probate and court records

- **What FamilySearch has digitized:** `volume_search` returned one digitized volume:
  - **Image group 004812990** — Probate Records, Schuylkill County, 1845–1880. 286 images. `recordSearchablePercent`: 4 (almost entirely unindexed). `fulltextSearchable`: true (full-text searchable even though not name-indexed). This volume can be searched by text string but is largely a browse-through resource.
- **Collections search** also returned "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (collection ID 1999196) — 3.2 million images, no indexed records. This is a large browse-only image collection covering Pennsylvania statewide, held at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196.
- **Types:** Wills (testate estates), letters of administration (intestate estates), guardianship files, inventories, and estate distributions. County-level jurisdiction. Held at the Schuylkill County Courthouse, Orphans' Court Division.
- **Naturalization records:** Pre-1906, naturalizations could be filed in any court of record — the Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas holds declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization for this period. Given the large immigrant mining population, these are especially important.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Pennsylvania is a state-land state (not a federal-land state), meaning land was granted by the Penn proprietorship and the Commonwealth, not the Bureau of Land Management. Metes-and-bounds descriptions predominate.
- **Land distribution jurisdiction:** The Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) holds warrant and survey files from the General Land Office records of the Commonwealth. Deeds are recorded at the county level.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, and patent books are held at the Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds office. Tax records (also county-held) can substitute for missing census years.
- **Ancestry also holds:** "Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768–1801" (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/) — this predates the target period but is useful for identifying families present before the 1840s.
- **No digitized deed or land volumes were returned** by `volume_search` for this period — land records for this county in the 1840s–1860s are a digitization gap; the physical records are at the courthouse.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** The Mexican-American War (1846–1848) and the Civil War (1861–1865) both fall within or adjacent to the period.
- **Civil War:** Service records, pension files, and compiled military service records are at NARA (National Archives and Records Administration). Pennsylvania State Archives holds state-level adjutant general records for Civil War service. Draft registration (conscription) records under the 1863 Enrollment Act name every male adult in the county — a valuable census substitute particularly for immigrant men.
- **Bounty land warrants:** Issued for service in the Mexican-American War; these generated land entry files at the federal level.
- **Access:** NARA records are accessible through Fold3 (subscription) and some through FamilySearch. No Schuylkill County-specific military volumes were returned by `volume_search`.

### Cemetery records

- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) and BillionGraves cover many Schuylkill County cemeteries, though coverage depth varies by cemetery. These are not within the FamilySearch-curated external links returned for this period but are the standard resources.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for municipal cemeteries and burial registers for church cemeteries are held by individual congregations and municipalities. Many rural church cemeteries have records only at the local church.
- **Note:** Mining communities often had company-maintained cemeteries, particularly for Catholic and Welsh Nonconformist congregations.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** Pottsville had active newspapers during this period, including the *Miners' Journal* (founded 1825), which ran obituaries, marriage notices, and legal notices through the entire target period.
- **Access:** The *Miners' Journal* is one of the most genealogically valuable sources for this county — obituaries for mining-area residents were often detailed. Paper copies and microfilm are held at the Schuylkill County Historical Society and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania. Some digitized issues may be available through Chronicling America (Library of Congress) and Newspapers.com.
- **Legal notices:** Sheriff's sales, estate notices, and naturalization announcements appeared in local papers and name individuals not recorded elsewhere.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was the primary port of entry for immigrants coming to the Pennsylvania coal region in this period. New York (Castle Garden, not yet Ellis Island in the 1840s–1860s) was also common.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists (Philadelphia and New York), declarations of intention and naturalization petitions (Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas), and — for the Civil War period — alien registration documents.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest when researching a family.
- **Access:** NARA holds the original passenger lists; Ancestry and FamilySearch have indexed versions for Philadelphia and New York arrivals in this period.

### Tax records

- **Types:** County property tax and personal property tax lists, held at county level.
- **Value:** Tax lists from the 1840s–1860s can place an individual in a specific township in years without a census, and can document property holdings and occupational status.
- **Access:** No digitized Schuylkill County tax volumes were returned by `volume_search`. Physical records are at the Schuylkill County Courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Other record types

- **Occupational records (coal mining):** Mine employment records, accident reports, and company records for the Reading Coal and Iron Company and other operators may survive in corporate archives or the Pennsylvania State Archives. These are unique to the anthracite region and can document workers not appearing in other record types.
- **County court records:** County court minute books record a wide range of transactions beyond lawsuits — road maintenance assignments, payments to indigent residents, and other county business that names ordinary people not party to any suit.
- **Published county histories:** Nineteenth-century county histories (such as Munsell's *History of Schuylkill County*, 1881) reprint early records and carry biographical sketches that are sometimes the only surviving transcription of records since lost. The FHL (Family History Library) catalog and WorldCat list these.

---

- **The Miners' Journal (Pottsville, founded 1825)** is a critical source for this county and period. Obituaries, marriage notices, estate notices, and legal notices named individuals who appear in few other records. Search microfilm at the Schuylkill County Historical Society.
- **For German-heritage families:** Many Lutheran and Reformed church records from this county are in German script (Kurrent). Be prepared to either read the original or engage a paleography specialist.
- **Tax records can bridge gaps between censuses.** County personal property and real estate tax lists for 1841, 1845, 1851, 1855, and similar off-years can place an individual in a specific township between the 1840, 1850, and 1860 federal census years. These are physical-only at present.
- **Search adjoining counties.** Neighboring counties — Berks to the southeast, Northumberland to the west, Columbia and Luzerne to the north, Carbon to the east — may hold records for families who lived near county boundaries or whose records predate Schuylkill County's 1811 formation. County boundary is not the same as family boundary, and miners moved between mining districts across county lines.
- **The probate records volume (image group 004812990)** is full-text searchable despite being only 4% name-indexed — try a text search before committing to a page-by-page browse.
- **Consult published county histories** (Munsell 1881 and similar) for biographical sketches and transcriptions of records that may since have been lost. These are available through the FHL catalog and many can be found on Ancestry or Google Books.

---

The FamilySearch wiki tool returned generic fallback content for all Pennsylvania and Schuylkill County pages during this survey, which is a significant gap. The guide above is grounded in what the collections, volume, and external-links tools actually returned. For deeper jurisdiction-specific guidance, visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records directly in a browser to check current page content, as those pages may contain information the wiki tool was unable to retrieve in this session.

---

Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania is a coal-mining county formed in 1811 whose records from the 1840s to 1860s are spread across churches, the county courthouse in Pottsville, and the Pennsylvania State Archives in Harrisburg. Because Pennsylvania had no effective statewide birth, marriage, or death registration during those decades, church registers — particularly Lutheran ones, often in German — stand in for vital records; the 1850 and 1860 federal censuses (highly indexed on FamilySearch) are the most accessible anchor sources. Three digitized FamilySearch volumes cover the county in this period: the census (96% indexed), probate records (largely browse-only but full-text searchable), and Lutheran church records (browse-only, bilingual English/German). A large share of records — deeds, tax lists, naturalizations, non-Lutheran church registers, and court files — remain physical-only at the courthouse or historical society and have not been digitized.

To make the most of this survey, the next step is to build a targeted research plan that sequences these sources in the most efficient order for the specific individuals you are researching.

Here is the locality guide returned by the research agent:

---

## Alabama Region, Pre-Statehood (circa 1800): Archives & Record Repositories

**The key insight:** Around 1800, there was no "Alabama" yet. The entire region was part of the **Mississippi Territory** (formed 1798), and the Mobile coastal area was still under **Spanish** control until 1813. Records follow that jurisdictional history.

---

### Jurisdiction Timeline

| Period | Jurisdiction |
|---|---|
| 1702–1763 | French colonial (Mobile area) |
| 1763–1780 | British colonial (Mobile area) |
| 1780–1813 | Spanish colonial (Mobile District) |
| 1798–1817 | Mississippi Territory, United States |
| 1817–1819 | Alabama Territory |
| 1819– | State of Alabama |

Washington County (formed 1800) was the **only** Alabama-region county in existence at the turn of the century. All other county record series begin later.

---

### Key Archives & Repositories

**Online (FamilySearch — free)**
- *Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950* — earliest indexed vital collection (612,345 records)
- *Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950* (156,789 records)
- *Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985* (438,210 records)
- *Alabama, Compiled Census & Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890*
- *Mississippi, Territorial & State Land Records, 1798–1907* (312,450 records) — covers the Alabama region during the territorial period
- *Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920* (245,670 records)
- *Mississippi, Compiled Census & Census Substitutes, 1792–1890*
- Two **browse-only** digitized volumes (0% name-indexed): territorial court/land records 1808–1819 and Washington County deeds/probate 1803–1820

**Alabama Department of Archives & History (ADAH), Montgomery**
- Territorial censuses for the Alabama region: **1801, 1805, 1808, 1810** — the most important pre-statehood finding tools
- Early county tax lists; microfilm of church records
- Website: archives.alabama.gov

**County Courthouses**
- Washington, Mobile, and Baldwin counties hold original deed books, probate files, and court minutes from their formation dates

**Mobile Municipal Archives**
- Microfilm of French colonial church records and Spanish colonial records

**European Archives (for Mobile-area ancestors before 1813)**
- *Archivo General de Indias*, Seville, Spain — Spanish colonial land grants, census returns, church records for the Mobile District (partially digitized at pares.mcu.es); copies at the Library of Congress
- *Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer*, Aix-en-Provence, France — French colonial records

**National Archives (NARA), Southeast Region (Atlanta)**
- Military pensions (War of 1812), territorial militia rolls, Indian affairs records (Record Group 75), naturalization petitions

**Other Online**
- BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) — free federal land patents
- Fold3 — War of 1812 and militia military records (subscription)
- Ancestry — 1810 federal census (first to cover the Alabama region)

---

### What Does NOT Exist Online
- Territorial censuses 1801–1808 (ADAH only, physical)
- Most Spanish and French colonial records (European archives; partially digitized)
- Washington County early deed/probate originals (digitized but browse-only, no name index)
- Early county tax lists (ADAH and county courthouses only)
- Baptist/Methodist circuit rider records (scattered local church archives)

---

### Top Research Tips

1. **Start with Mississippi Territory collections**, not Alabama — that is what your ancestor belonged to around 1800.
2. **Use the ADAH territorial censuses** (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810) as the primary substitute for a pre-1810 federal census.
3. **If near Mobile**, expect records in Spanish or French in Seville or Aix-en-Provence.
4. **For land**, Alabama is a federal-land state — search BLM GLO for patents first.
5. **Two key FamilySearch volumes** (territorial court/land records and Washington County deeds) are digitized but must be browsed page-by-page — no name search exists.

The critical next step is to determine **where in the Alabama region** your ancestor was — Mobile coastal area (Spanish/French colonial records apply) versus the interior (records only begin with county formation, mostly after 1803).

Here is the complete locality guide.

---

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region, Pre-Statehood (circa 1800)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** The Alabama region was not yet a distinct jurisdiction in 1800. It was then part of the **Mississippi Territory**, created in 1798 from land ceded by Georgia and Spain. The territory expanded in 1804 and again in 1812 to encompass all of present-day Alabama and Mississippi. In 1817 the eastern half became the **Alabama Territory**, and Alabama achieved statehood in **1819**.
- **Administrative center:** Territorial government sat at Natchez, then later St. Stephens (in present-day Washington County, Alabama).
- **Parent jurisdiction in 1800:** Mississippi Territory, United States (1798-1817)
- **Population during period:** No specific population figures were returned by the tools for this territory in 1800. Settlement was sparse and concentrated near the Mobile Bay area and along rivers. Significant in-migration from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia followed the Creek War of 1813-1814.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, early cotton cultivation, fur trade, and maritime trade through Mobile.
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations throughout the interior; French Creole and Spanish Creole communities in the Mobile area; Anglo-American settlers arriving from the East; enslaved African Americans.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic Church (dominant in the Mobile area under French and Spanish rule); Baptist and Methodist circuit riders arriving with Anglo-American settlers in the territorial period.
- **Key historical events:** French founding of Mobile (1702); transfer to Britain (1763); Spanish occupation (1780-1813); U.S. organization of Mississippi Territory (1798); Creek War (1813-1814); organization of Alabama Territory (1817); statehood (1819).

## Boundary changes

The Alabama region passed through multiple sovereign jurisdictions before and during 1800:

| Period | Jurisdiction | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1702-1763 | French colonial (Mobile area) | France claimed the interior |
| 1763-1780 | British colonial (Mobile area) | Britain held the Gulf Coast |
| 1780-1813 | Spanish colonial (Mobile District) | Spain held Mobile until U.S. seizure |
| 1798-1817 | Mississippi Territory, United States | Entire Alabama region |
| 1817-1819 | Alabama Territory, United States | Eastern half of former Miss. Territory |
| 1819- | State of Alabama | Statehood achieved |

**Critical research implication:** An ancestor in the Alabama region around 1800 was under the authority of the Mississippi Territory. Records from that period are Mississippi Territory records, not Alabama state records. The oldest county in the Alabama region — Washington County, formed 1800 — began generating local records from around 1803.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration existed in the Alabama region around 1800. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Alabama Vital Records and the Alabama-specific topic pages did not return content in this survey — verify current start dates and levels at [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Vital_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Vital_Records) directly. FamilySearch's Alabama indexed collections begin with county marriages in 1809, suggesting no earlier civil registration is yet digitized.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch holds **Alabama, County Marriages, 1809-1950** (collection 1598408; 612,345 records, 306,172 images). This is the earliest indexed vital collection. No birth or death registration collection for the territorial period was returned.
- **Where held:** County courthouses (marriages); Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery.
- **Gaps:** No civil birth or death registration at any level during the territorial period around 1800. Vital events in this era must be sought in church registers and other substitute sources.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic church registers in Mobile (Spanish-era and beyond); Baptist and Methodist circuit records; family Bibles; cemetery inscriptions.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dominant in Mobile before 1813); Baptist; Methodist (circuit-riding preachers reaching frontier settlements).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials. Catholic registers from the Spanish period are the richest pre-1800 source.
- **Where held:**
  - FamilySearch: **Alabama, Church Records, 1803-1950** (collection 1986396; 156,789 records, 78,394 images) — indexed and browsable online.
  - Catholic registers from the Mobile Spanish period: Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain); Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (Aix-en-Provence, France); microfilm copies at the Mobile Municipal Archives. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)), the Mobile Municipal Archives holds microfilm of French and Spanish colonial church records.
- **Language:** Spanish and French for Mobile-area Catholic registers predating 1813. Researchers must be able to read or transcribe these originals, or find a published transcript.

### Census records

- **Territorial censuses:** The Mississippi Territory enumerated settlers in the present-day Alabama region in **1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810**. These are held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History** in Montgomery, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)). These fill the gap before federal census coverage.
- **Federal census:** The **1810 federal census** is the first to include the Alabama portion of the Mississippi Territory. The 1800 federal census does not reliably cover the Alabama region.
- **Census substitutes index:** FamilySearch holds **Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810-1890** (collection 2016756; 287,634 records, no images — index only). The Mississippi-side equivalent, **Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792-1890** (collection 1927171; 198,340 records), also covers the territorial period when Alabama was part of the Mississippi Territory.
- **Access:** The index collections are name-searchable online. The ADAH territorial census volumes are physical holdings; some may be microfilmed.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, and territorial court proceedings.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch's Alabama probate collection begins in 1809 (county-level). Territorial court records begin earlier; volume 004512889 on FamilySearch covers **Alabama territorial court and land records, 1808-1819** (214 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable — browse-only).
- **Washington County deed and probate records, 1803-1820** are digitized in FamilySearch volume 004512890 (96 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable — browse-only).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch has both volumes (browse-only). The **Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985** collection (1537764; 438,210 records, 219,105 images) is indexed and browsable for post-1809 material. Original records at county courthouses and ADAH.
- **Mississippi Territory court records** are also relevant: FamilySearch holds **Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799-1920** (collection 1855293; 245,670 records, 122,835 images).

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey (Alabama is a federal-land state). Land patents came from the U.S. federal government through the General Land Office, not from the state or territory.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The U.S. General Land Office administered land grants in the Mississippi Territory / Alabama Territory. The BLM General Land Office website (glorecords.blm.gov) holds federal patent records.
- **Types:** Federal land grants and patents; Spanish and British colonial land grants in the Mobile area (predating U.S. authority); county deed books; tax records.
- **Colonial land grants (Mobile area):** Spanish grants are at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and the Library of Congress (copies). British grants are at The National Archives (Kew, UK). Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)).
- **Territorial period land records:** FamilySearch holds **Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798-1907** (collection 1919694; 312,450 records, 156,225 images) — covering the territorial period when the Alabama region was part of Mississippi Territory.
- **Where held:** BLM GLO online (federal patents); ADAH; county courthouses; FamilySearch (as above). Two digitized but browse-only volumes (004512889, 004512890) cover Alabama territorial court/land and Washington County deeds respectively.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War (1813-1814); War of 1812; earlier militia activity under territorial authority.
- **Record types:** Territorial militia rolls; War of 1812 service and pension records; bounty land warrant applications (some veterans received federal land grants in Alabama).
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), Washington D.C. and Southeast Region (Atlanta); Fold3 (subscription, online); ADAH; FamilySearch (some militia rolls microfilmed).
- **Note:** War of 1812 pension records often name family members and are valuable for establishing relationships in the pre-statehood era.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Early cemeteries in the Mobile area (Catholic); rural burying grounds on settler farmsteads throughout the territory.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) — curated links returned in this survey. Coverage of pre-1820 rural graves is sparse.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records, where they survive, are at local churches or ADAH. Many early graves are unmarked or graves are lost.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The Mobile area had early newspapers under American authority post-1813. Press in the interior was minimal before statehood.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (subscription, returned in this survey); Alabama Virtual Library; Library of Congress Chronicling America (chroniclingamerica.loc.gov — free).
- **Content value:** Obituaries, legal notices, and land sale notices begin appearing in the territorial period. Coverage of rural areas before 1819 is very limited.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Mobile (Gulf Coast); New Orleans (Louisiana, adjacent territory).
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (NARA); naturalization petitions (territorial court records, any court of record pre-1906).
- **Where held:** NARA; FamilySearch; Ancestry (subscription). The territorial court records volumes on FamilySearch may include naturalization proceedings.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents — examine the full manifest when researching a family.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Territorial tax lists; property and poll tax after county formation.
- **Date range:** Territorial tax lists begin with the formation of counties (Washington County, 1800; other counties formed later).
- **Where held:** ADAH; county courthouses. Some territorial and early county tax lists are microfilmed by FamilySearch and/or ADAH.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists from 1801, 1805, and other territorial years can substitute for the absent pre-1810 census.

### Other record types

- **Indian affairs records:** The Creek and Cherokee nations controlled much of the territory around 1800. NARA holds Indian affairs records (Record Group 75) that name both Native residents and settlers who interacted with the agencies.
- **Spanish and French colonial land grants and census returns:** Separate from church records, the Spanish colonial administration in Mobile conducted census returns. Per the FamilySearch Wiki, Spanish records of the Mobile District include census returns, church registers, and land grants, held at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)).
- **Town and county histories:** Published 19th-century county histories for Washington, Baldwin, and Mobile counties may preserve transcriptions of records since lost.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Alabama, County Marriages 1809-1950 (612,345 records); Alabama, Probate Records 1809-1985 (438,210 records); Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index 1810-1890 (287,634 records); Alabama, Church Records 1803-1950 (156,789 records); Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records 1798-1907 (312,450 records); Mississippi, County Court Records 1799-1920 (245,670 records); Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes 1792-1890 (198,340 records); 2 browse-only digitized volumes (territorial court/land records 1808-1819; Washington County deeds/probate 1803-1820) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census collection (1810 census covers Alabama area) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (War of 1812, territorial militia) | Subscription |
| BLM GLO | Federal land patents (glorecords.blm.gov) | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records — military, Indian affairs, naturalization | Free finding aids; some records online |
| Library of Congress | Copies of Spanish colonial records; Chronicling America newspapers | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch's volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes for Alabama, 1780-1820, and that was the complete result set (totalResults: 2). The indexed collections returned 4 Alabama-scope and 4 Mississippi-scope collections. The record counts above come directly from the collections_search tool output — they have not been independently verified as complete totals.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery | Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810); tax lists; early county records; microfilm of church records | In-person; some records via mail request; online catalog at archives.alabama.gov |
| County courthouses (Washington, Mobile, Baldwin counties) | Original deed books, probate files, court minutes from county formation dates | In-person or mail |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | Microfilm of French colonial church records and Spanish colonial records | In-person |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Original Spanish colonial records for the Mobile District (land grants, census, church records) | In-person or digitized portal (pares.mcu.es) |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records for the Mobile area | In-person |
| Library of Congress, Washington D.C. | Copies of Spanish and French colonial records | In-person; some digitized online |
| National Archives (NARA) Southeast Region, Atlanta | Federal territorial and early statehood records; military pensions; Indian affairs | In-person; some records on Ancestry/Fold3 |

---

## Records NOT online

- Territorial censuses for the Alabama region (1801, 1805, 1808) — held physically at ADAH; not yet available in a name-indexed online database.
- Original Spanish colonial census returns and most land grants for the Mobile District — held in Seville and partially in Washington D.C.; only partially digitized.
- French colonial records — held in Aix-en-Provence; not widely digitized.
- Early Washington County deed and probate originals (the FamilySearch volume 004512890 is digitized but browse-only, 0% indexed).
- Territorial court records volume (004512889) — digitized but browse-only, 0% indexed.
- Most early county tax lists — physical only at ADAH and county courthouses.
- Baptist and Methodist circuit rider records — scattered among local church archives and denominational repositories; very limited online presence.

---

## Known record losses

No specific courthouse fire or flood losses for this period were returned by the survey tools. The broader risks for this era are:

- Record-keeping was sparse and inconsistent throughout the territorial period — do not assume a record was created just because a jurisdiction existed.
- Washington County, formed in 1800, is the only county in the Alabama region that existed at the turn of the century. All other county-level record series begin after their county's formation date.
- Some early territorial records may never have been formally filed or may remain unprocessed in archival collections.

---

## Research tips

- **Search the Mississippi Territory first.** Around 1800, your ancestor lived in the Mississippi Territory, not Alabama. Begin with Mississippi Territory land records (FamilySearch collection 1919694), court records (1855293), and census substitutes (1927171) before turning to Alabama state collections. ([FamilySearch Wiki — Alabama Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records))
- **Use territorial census substitutes.** The Mississippi Territory censuses of 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 are the closest equivalent to a census for this area around 1800. These are at ADAH, Montgomery. ([FamilySearch Wiki — Alabama Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records))
- **Know which colonial power was in control.** If your ancestor was in the Mobile area before 1813, records may be in Spanish or French and are held in European archives. The FamilySearch Wiki notes that Spanish records of the Mobile District — including census returns, church registers, and land grants — are held at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress. ([FamilySearch Wiki — Alabama Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **Alabama is a federal-land state.** Land patents were issued by the U.S. General Land Office, not by the state. Search the BLM GLO database (glorecords.blm.gov) for federal patents granted to settlers in the territorial period. County deed books at the courthouse record subsequent private sales.
- **Browse-only FamilySearch volumes require image-by-image review.** The 2 digitized FamilySearch volumes covering 1808-1820 (IDs 004512889 and 004512890) are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. To use them you must browse each image sequentially — there is no name search.
- **Washington County is the anchor.** It is the oldest county in the Alabama region (formed 1800) and the earliest point at which county-level Alabama records were generated. If you do not know your ancestor's precise location, start there for the earliest county records.
- **Check the adjoining jurisdiction: the western (Mississippi) side.** The Mississippi Territory was a single administrative unit. Tax lists, land entries, and court records were sometimes recorded at the territorial level rather than the county level, and those records are filed under Mississippi Territory regardless of which side of the modern state line the ancestor lived on. Search both the Alabama-scope and Mississippi-scope FamilySearch collections.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy page** contains the most current guidance on what records exist and where: [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy). The Alabama-specific topic pages (Vital Records, Church Records, Land and Property, Probate Records, Census) did not return Alabama-specific content during this survey — visit each directly for the most detailed current guidance.

---

The four `wiki_place_page` sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) all returned only a generic fallback page rather than Alabama-specific content; this is recorded in the persisted entry (loc_001). The Alabama-specific wiki topic pages (Vital Records, Church Records, Land and Property, Probate Records, Census, Naming Customs) similarly returned only the generic fallback — the Alabama Genealogy page URL returned by wiki_search ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy)) is the most reliable direct link for current Alabama research guidance.

---

The guide has been saved to the research project as **loc_001**.

---

Researching the Alabama region around 1800 is genuinely complex because there was no "Alabama" yet — the area was part of the Mississippi Territory, and before that, the Mobile area was under Spanish and French control. The oldest county (Washington County, formed in 1800) only began keeping local records around 1803, and most of what survives from before 1810 must be found in territorial-level collections, Spanish colonial archives in Seville, French colonial archives in France, or at the Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery, which holds the territorial census lists from 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810. Two small digitized volumes of territorial court, land, and probate records exist on FamilySearch but must be browsed image by image — there is no name search for them. The most important warning is to search Mississippi Territory record collections first, then Alabama, because that is where the administrative authority sat in 1800.

The next step is to narrow down which part of the Alabama region your ancestor was in — whether near Mobile (where colonial-era records in Spanish and French apply) or in the interior (where records only begin with county formation) — so research can be routed to the right repository.

Here is the locality guide the research agent produced:

---

# Locality Guide: Arkansas Region — Spanish Colonial Period (ca. 1686–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
The Arkansas Post, established in 1686, was the only European administrative center in the region. Under **French rule (1686–1763)** it was part of La Louisiane; under **Spanish rule (1763–1800)** it became part of Spanish Louisiana (Louisiana española), administered from New Orleans. The population was tiny — fewer than 400 residents at Arkansas Post in the 1790 Spanish census — composed of French Creole settlers, Spanish soldiers, enslaved persons, and Quapaw peoples. The area was **exclusively Roman Catholic**.

---

## The Critical Warning: Arkansas Did Not Exist

All civil and administrative authority ran through **New Orleans**, not any Arkansas jurisdiction. The State of Arkansas wasn't organized until 1836 (territory 1819; first U.S. county 1813). **Searching Arkansas county records for this period will find nothing.** Begin at Louisiana and Spanish colonial repositories.

---

## Key Record Types & Where to Find Them

### Church Records *(your primary vital records)*
There was **no civil registration** — baptisms, marriages, and burials were recorded only by the Catholic mission at Arkansas Post.

- **FamilySearch Image Group 008814402** — 64 browse-only images, Arkansas Post sacramental registers, **1763–1800**, in Spanish. This is the only digitized colonial-era volume. It is **0% name-indexed** and must be examined image by image.
- **Physical originals:** Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock Archives; transcriptions at the Arkansas History Commission
- ⚠️ Records are in **18th-century Spanish colonial script** (letra procesal) — a paleographer may be needed

### Spanish Colonial Administrative Records
- **Papeles Procedentes de Cuba** at the **Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain)** — commandant's correspondence, muster rolls, padrones. These name ordinary residents not found anywhere else.
- **Library of Congress** holds microfilm of portions of this series
- Not publicly name-searchable online

### Census / Padrones
- **1790 Arkansas Post padrón** — held at the **Arkansas History Commission**; not digitized online
- The earliest U.S. federal census for Arkansas is 1830

### Land Records
- Spanish land **concession files** → Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) and Archivo General de Indias
- After 1805, Spanish grant holders had to file U.S. land claims with the Board of Land Commissioners — these restate the original grant and effectively index colonial-era landholders. Searchable at **[glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)** and through **NARA**

### Military Records
- Garrison muster rolls and officer personnel files in the **Papeles Procedentes de Cuba** (Seville); Library of Congress microfilm

### Notarial Records
- Arkansas Post residents who traveled to New Orleans for legal business appear in the **New Orleans Notarial Archives** — wills, sales, manumissions, estate settlements

---

## Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Arkansas History Commission**, Little Rock, AR | Transcripts, microfilm, 1790 padrón, church register transcriptions |
| **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock Archives** | Original/microfilm sacramental registers |
| **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville, Spain | Papeles Procedentes de Cuba: all Spanish Louisiana admin, military, land, census records |
| **Library of Congress**, Washington, D.C. | Microfilm of portions of Papeles Procedentes de Cuba |
| **Louisiana State Archives**, Baton Rouge, LA | Spanish-era land concessions; New Orleans administrative records |
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives** | Colonial-era notarial records involving Arkansas Post residents |
| **NARA** | U.S. Board of Land Commissioners files (post-1805, validating Spanish claims) |

---

## Research Tips

1. **Search New Orleans records in parallel** — any Arkansas Post resident may have executed legal documents in New Orleans.

# Locality Guide: Arkansas Region — Spanish Colonial Period (ca. 1686–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Arkansas Post established by the French in 1686 as the first European settlement in the lower Mississippi Valley
- **County seat / administrative center:** Arkansas Post (Post of the Arkansas, or Poste des Arkansas) — the only European administrative center in the region
- **Parent jurisdiction (French era, 1686–1763):** French Louisiana (La Louisiane), administered from New Orleans
- **Parent jurisdiction (Spanish era, 1763–1800):** Spanish Louisiana (Louisiana española), administered from New Orleans by the Governor-General
- **Population during period:** Very sparse. The 1790 Spanish padrón (census) of Arkansas Post recorded fewer than 400 residents, mostly French-speaking Creole settlers, soldiers, traders, and their enslaved workers; a small number of Native American converts appear in church registers
- **Economy:** Fur trade, subsistence agriculture, military garrison provisioning
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole settlers (dominant), Spanish colonial officials and soldiers, enslaved Africans and African-descended persons, Quapaw and other Native American peoples
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic exclusively — served by the Arkansas Post mission parish, under the Diocese of Louisiana and the Floridas (New Orleans)
- **Key historical events:** Treaty of Paris (1763) transferred French Louisiana to Spain; Spain secretly ceded the territory back to France in 1800 by the Treaty of San Ildefonso; the Louisiana Purchase (1803) brought the region under U.S. control

## Boundary changes
- **Pre-1763:** The Arkansas region was part of French Louisiana, a vast, poorly-defined colonial territory administered from New Orleans
- **1763–1800:** By the Treaty of Paris (1763) the territory passed to Spain as Spanish Louisiana; the Arkansas district was governed as a sub-district of the Province of Louisiana, headquartered at New Orleans
- **1800:** Spain ceded the territory to France; French administration was nominal and brief
- **1803:** The Louisiana Purchase transferred the region to the United States
- **1806/1812:** The District of Louisiana (later Missouri Territory) initially governed the area; Arkansas County was organized in 1813 under Missouri Territory; Arkansas Territory was established separately in 1819; Arkansas became a state in 1836
- **Critical implication:** The State of Arkansas and its county structure did not exist before 1813. All records from the colonial period (before 1800) were created under French or Spanish Louisiana, not under any Arkansas jurisdiction. Searching Arkansas county records will return nothing for this period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** There was no civil registration of vital events in the colonial Arkansas region. The Catholic Church held exclusive responsibility for recording baptisms, marriages, and burials
- **What exists:** Church sacramental registers only (see Church Records below)
- **Where held:** Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock; Arkansas History Commission; FamilySearch microfilm
- **Gaps:** Coverage is fragmentary; not all registers survive intact
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers ARE the primary vital record source for this entire period

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic only. The Arkansas Post mission was the sole organized congregation in the region during the colonial period
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including adult converts, enslaved persons, and Native Americans), marriages, burials; occasional confirmation records
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Image group **008814402** — 64 images of Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial), Arkansas Post, Arkansas County, Arkansas, covering **1763–1800**. This is the only digitized colonial-era volume returned by the survey. It is **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) and must be examined image by image
- **Access (digitized):** FamilySearch.org — browse image group 008814402 directly
- **Where physical originals are held:** Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock Archives; transcribed copies also held at the Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock, AR
- **Language:** Records are in **Spanish** (and sometimes French); 18th-century colonial handwriting (letra procesal or itálica script). A researcher must be able to read period Spanish script or engage a paleographer
- **Earlier French-era registers (pre-1763):** French-era registers from Arkansas Post are mentioned in the FamilySearch Wiki's Arkansas Genealogy page ([Colonial Records section](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)) as also held by the Diocese of Little Rock and the Arkansas History Commission, but no separate digitized volume for the French period was returned by this survey — treat them as physical-only until confirmed otherwise

### Census records
- **Spanish colonial padrones (censuses):** Spain conducted population censuses called padrones of its Louisiana settlements. The **1790 padrón of Arkansas Post** survives and is held at the Arkansas History Commission. It is not indexed on FamilySearch and was not returned as a digitized volume — treat as physical/microfilm
- **Federal census coverage begins:** 1830 (first census after Arkansas Territory was created); Arkansas was not included in the 1810 or 1820 federal census
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** "Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819–1870" (collection ID 2085124, 178,345 records) begins at 1819 — entirely post-colonial, but may help bridge descendants into the American period
- **Other enumerations:** Garrison muster rolls at Arkansas Post, held at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and possibly microfilmed at the Library of Congress, serve as a substitute census for military personnel

### Probate and court records
- **Colonial era:** No formal probate court existed at Arkansas Post. Estate matters were handled by the Spanish commandant as part of his administrative and judicial duties. Surviving records of this type, if any, would be in the commandant's correspondence files at the Archivo General de Indias or the Arkansas History Commission
- **Post-colonial:** Arkansas County (organized 1813) began keeping probate records under U.S. territorial law. Those records are at the Arkansas County courthouse in DeWitt and at the Arkansas History Commission
- **Digitization:** No probate records for the colonial period were returned by this survey; treat as physical-only

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds under French and Spanish colonial concession systems; the U.S. rectangular survey system was imposed after 1803
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Under Spanish rule, land concessions were granted by the Governor-General of Louisiana in New Orleans, with local grants approved by the commandant at Arkansas Post. Original concession files are held at the **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville) and the **Louisiana State Archives** (Baton Rouge)
- **Types:** Spanish land concessions (land grants/patents); post-1803 U.S. land claims validated by the Board of Land Commissioners; BLM General Land Office (GLO) patents
- **Critical trail:** Spanish land grants were not automatically honored under U.S. law; claimants had to file before the U.S. Board of Land Commissioners (after 1805). The claims files from this process — which restate and document the original Spanish grants — are held at NARA and are available through the BLM GLO website (glorecords.blm.gov). These validated-claim files often name original colonial-era settlers and their heirs
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias (Seville); Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge); BLM GLO archives; NARA; Arkansas History Commission
- **Digitization:** BLM GLO patent records are searchable online at glorecords.blm.gov; original Spanish-era concession files are not digitized for public name-search

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The American Revolutionary War (Spain was an ally of France against Britain; the Arkansas garrison saw related activity 1779–1781, including the Battle of Arkansas Post, 1783); general frontier garrison duty throughout the Spanish period
- **Record types:** Garrison muster rolls (hojas de servicio), officer personnel records, post correspondence — all generated at the Arkansas Post garrison
- **Where held:** **Archivo General de Indias**, Papeles Procedentes de Cuba series (the main repository for Spanish Louisiana military and administrative records); Library of Congress has microfilm of portions of this collection; the Arkansas History Commission holds some transcripts and finding aids
- **Access:** The Papeles Procedentes de Cuba series is not digitized for public online search; contact the Archivo General de Indias or use the Library of Congress microfilm

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** The Catholic mission cemetery at Arkansas Post is the only organized colonial burial ground; surviving headstones and sexton-type records are minimal
- **Online coverage:** No colonial-era cemetery records were returned by this survey from FindAGrave or BillionGraves
- **Physical records:** Burials are recorded in the sacramental burial registers (see Church Records above)

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No newspapers existed in the Arkansas region during the colonial period; the nearest press was in New Orleans
- **New Orleans newspapers** from the Spanish period (e.g., the Moniteur de la Louisiane, founded 1794) occasionally reported on events at Arkansas Post and may contain mentions of individuals; held at the Louisiana State Library and Tulane University

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was the sole port of entry for the Arkansas region; all European settlers arriving by sea passed through New Orleans
- **Record types:** Spanish colonial passport records (passports required to travel within Louisiana); ship manifests arriving at New Orleans; emigration records from France, Spain, and the Canary Islands
- **Where held:** Papeles Procedentes de Cuba, Archivo General de Indias (Seville); Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge); New Orleans Notarial Archives
- **Content note:** Spanish colonial-era passenger/travel records are not digitized and indexed in the same way as later U.S. passenger lists; access typically requires archival correspondence or an on-site visit

### Tax records
- **Colonial era:** Tax assessment records were not a standard feature of small frontier posts like Arkansas Post; some tithe or tribute records may exist in church or administrative files
- **Post-1803:** U.S. territorial tax lists begin after 1803; the earliest Arkansas tax records at the county level date to 1813

### Other record types
- **Commandant's correspondence:** The commandant at Arkansas Post was required to report regularly to the Governor-General in New Orleans. These letters and reports — held in the Papeles Procedentes de Cuba at the Archivo General de Indias — name residents, describe events, and document economic and social conditions. They are among the most informative sources for ordinary residents who appear in no other record
- **Notarial records:** Spanish colonial notarial records from New Orleans (held at the New Orleans Notarial Archives) document contracts, sales, manumissions, and estate settlements that may involve Arkansas Post residents who traveled to New Orleans for legal business
- **Published transcriptions and compilations:** Morris S. Arnold's published work on colonial Arkansas (including *Unequal Laws unto a Savage Race: European Legal Traditions in Arkansas, 1686–1836*) transcribes and analyzes many surviving colonial-era records and is an essential secondary source

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Image group 008814402: 64 browse-only images, Arkansas Post sacramental registers, 1763–1800 (Spanish, 0% indexed) | Free |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | U.S.-era land patents only; Spanish-era concession files not in GLO | Free |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | U.S. military records post-1803; no colonial-era Spanish records | Subscription |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. census collection starts 1830 for Arkansas; no colonial-era coverage returned | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` returned 1 digitized volume matching this place and period. The `collections_search` returned 3 collections for Arkansas, none covering the colonial period. The external links search returned 6 general-purpose links (NARA, Ancestry, FindAGrave, Newspapers.com, Fold3, FamilySearch Wiki categories) with no Arkansas-specific colonial content.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission, 1 Capitol Mall, Little Rock, AR 72201 | Transcripts and microfilm of colonial records; 1790 padrón; Arkansas Post church register transcriptions; Arkansas county records from 1813 | In-person or written request; some finding aids online at arkansashistory.com |
| Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock Archives, 2500 N. Tyler St., Little Rock, AR 72207 | Original or microfilm sacramental registers from Arkansas Post mission | Contact the archives for access |
| Archivo General de Indias, Avenida de la Constitución 3, Seville, Spain | Papeles Procedentes de Cuba series: Spanish Louisiana administrative, military, land, and census records 1763–1800 | In-person; finding aids available through the Spanish Ministry of Culture online portal (pares.mcu.es); Library of Congress holds microfilm of portions |
| Library of Congress, Washington, D.C. | Microfilm of portions of the Papeles Procedentes de Cuba (Archivo General de Indias) | In-person at the Manuscript Division; some digitized finding aids |
| Louisiana State Archives, 3851 Essen Lane, Baton Rouge, LA 70809 | Spanish-era land concession records; New Orleans administrative records that concern Arkansas Post | In-person or written request |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives, 1340 Poydras St., New Orleans, LA 70112 | Spanish colonial notarial records involving New Orleans-area and Arkansas Post residents | In-person research |
| NARA, Southwest Region / Washington D.C. | U.S. Board of Land Commissioners files (post-1805, validating Spanish land claims); territorial-era records from 1803 | In-person or NARA online catalog (catalog.archives.gov) |

## Records NOT online

The following record types are known to exist but were not found in any online database during this survey:

- **Spanish colonial administrative records (Papeles Procedentes de Cuba):** Commandant's correspondence, muster rolls, padrones — held at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville; not publicly searchable online
- **1790 Arkansas Post padrón (census):** Held at the Arkansas History Commission; not in any digitized online collection
- **Original French-era church registers (pre-1763):** Diocese of Little Rock and Arkansas History Commission; no digitized volume returned
- **Spanish colonial land concession originals:** Louisiana State Archives and Archivo General de Indias; not name-searchable online
- **New Orleans notarial records involving Arkansas Post residents:** New Orleans Notarial Archives; partially digitized for later periods but colonial-era access requires in-person or archival correspondence

## Known record losses

- Arkansas Post itself was relocated multiple times along the Arkansas River; records moved with the garrison and some were lost in transit or during the turbulent transfer of sovereignty (Spain to France, 1800; France to U.S., 1803)
- Many colonial administrative records that were never sent to New Orleans or Seville simply did not survive the frontier conditions of Arkansas Post
- The Arkansas History Commission reports that surviving colonial records are fragmentary; gaps in the sacramental registers are expected
- No courthouse fires are at issue for the colonial period (no courthouse existed), but records held in private or military hands at Arkansas Post were vulnerable to flood, fire, and neglect

## Research tips

- **The jurisdiction that matters is Spanish Louisiana, not Arkansas.** All civil and administrative authority during 1763–1800 ran through New Orleans. Begin any search at the Louisiana State Archives and the Archivo General de Indias before looking for Arkansas-specific repositories. (Source: [Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **The FamilySearch Wiki confirms three primary repositories** for surviving colonial records: the Arkansas History Commission, the Archivo General de Indias, and the Library of Congress microfilm holdings. (Source: [Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **Church records are your vital records.** There was no civil registration; baptism, marriage, and burial entries in the mission register are the only vital record source for the colonial period. (Source: [Arkansas Genealogy — Church Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records))
- **Browse FamilySearch image group 008814402 directly.** This is the only digitized colonial-era volume identified in this survey. It covers 1763–1800, contains 64 images, is 0% name-indexed, and is in Spanish — you must scroll through it manually
- **Learn to read Spanish colonial script** or find a collaborator who can. Letra procesal and related 18th-century Spanish handwriting styles are difficult; the Paleografía Hispánica resources at the Archivo General de Indias website are a starting point
- **Spanish land claims become U.S. records.** After 1803, holders of Spanish land grants had to file U.S. land claims. These filings — searchable at glorecords.blm.gov and through NARA — restate the original grant and name the settler, effectively creating a 19th-century index to colonial-era landholders
- **Search both sides of the Louisiana–Arkansas administrative boundary.** A resident of Arkansas Post in 1790 may have traveled to New Orleans to execute a will, free an enslaved person, or register a marriage; New Orleans notarial and church records are therefore a parallel search track
- **Published transcriptions save significant time.** Morris S. Arnold and several Arkansas Historical Quarterly articles have transcribed and published key colonial records. Check WorldCat and the Arkansas History Commission's publication list before attempting an archival visit to Seville

- **Spanish colonial administrative records (Papeles Procedentes de Cuba):** Commandant's correspondence, muster rolls, padrones — Archivo General de Indias, Seville; not publicly searchable online
- **1790 Arkansas Post padrón:** Held at the Arkansas History Commission; not in any digitized online collection
- **Original French-era church registers (pre-1763):** Diocese of Little Rock and Arkansas History Commission; no digitized volume returned
- **Spanish colonial land concession originals:** Louisiana State Archives and Archivo General de Indias; not name-searchable online
- **New Orleans notarial records involving Arkansas Post residents:** New Orleans Notarial Archives; colonial-era access requires in-person visit or archival correspondence

- Arkansas Post was relocated multiple times along the Arkansas River; records moved with the garrison and some were lost in transit or during the turbulent transfers of sovereignty (Spain to France, 1800; France to U.S., 1803)

- **The FamilySearch Wiki confirms three primary repositories** for surviving colonial records: the Arkansas History Commission, the Archivo General de Indias, and the Library of Congress microfilm holdings. (Source: [Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **Church records are your vital records.** There was no civil registration in this period; baptism, marriage, and burial entries in the mission sacramental register are the only vital record source. (Source: [Arkansas Genealogy — Church Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records))
- **Browse FamilySearch image group 008814402 directly.** This is the only digitized colonial-era volume identified in this survey: 64 browse-only images, Arkansas Post sacramental registers 1763–1800, in Spanish, 0% name-indexed. You must scroll through it manually.
- **Learn 18th-century Spanish colonial script** or engage a collaborator. Letra procesal and related styles are difficult; the Paleografía Hispánica resources on the Archivo General de Indias website (pares.mcu.es) are a starting point.
- **Spanish land claims become U.S. records after 1805.** Holders of Spanish grants had to file U.S. land claims. These filings restate the original grant and name the settler — effectively creating a 19th-century index to colonial-era landholders. Searchable at glorecords.blm.gov and through NARA.

---

This guide covers the Arkansas region for the period ca. 1686–1800, when it was part of first French and then Spanish Louisiana. The region had virtually no civil record-keeping infrastructure of its own: the only formal records were created by the Catholic Church at Arkansas Post (one browse-only digitized volume survives on FamilySearch, in Spanish), by the Spanish military garrison (muster rolls and correspondence held in Seville), and by colonial administrators who reported upward to New Orleans. The single most important warning is that searching Arkansas county records for this period will find nothing — the State of Arkansas did not exist, and all administrative authority ran through New Orleans.

The next step is to identify which specific individuals or family lines you are tracing in this region, so that a targeted research plan can be built around the repositories and record types identified here.

quirks: The Arkansas region did not exist as a civil jurisdiction before 1800 — records were generated under French and then Spanish Louisiana; search those colonial frameworks, not Arkansas county records.

Civil registration (births, marriages, deaths) did not exist in the colonial period; the Catholic Church at Arkansas Post was the sole vital-records keeper — search sacramental registers, not civil records.

The principal digitized colonial holding is FamilySearch image group 008814402: 64 browse-only images of Spanish colonial sacramental registers from Arkansas Post, 1763–1800, in Spanish — 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image.
Spanish-language records require the researcher to read 18th-century Spanish script (letra procesal or later itálica); consider a professional paleographer or transcription service.

Records may be scattered across three repositories: the Arkansas History Commission (Little Rock), the Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain), and microfilm at the Library of Congress — no single repository holds everything.

Land concessions made under Spanish authority were later validated (or contested) in U.S. territorial-era land claim proceedings; the U.S. Board of Land Commissioners records and the BLM GLO archives are therefore a continuation of the Spanish land record trail.
Catholic sacramental registers from Arkansas Post also record baptisms and marriages of Native Americans and enslaved persons — do not overlook these populations.
The 1790 Spanish colonial census (padrón) of Arkansas Post is a key substitute for any census coverage; it survives and is held at the Arkansas History Commission.

After Spain secretly ceded the region back to France in 1800 and France sold it via the Louisiana Purchase in 1803, record custody shifted; some post-1800 records that bridge the colonial era are held at the Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge and the New Orleans Notarial Archives.
