added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Arkansas Region — Spanish Colonial Period (ca. 1686–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Arkansas Post established by the French in 1686 as the first European settlement in the lower Mississippi Valley
- **County seat / administrative center:** Arkansas Post (Post of the Arkansas, or Poste des Arkansas) — the only European administrative center in the region
- **Parent jurisdiction (French era, 1686–1763):** French Louisiana (La Louisiane), administered from New Orleans
- **Parent jurisdiction (Spanish era, 1763–1800):** Spanish Louisiana (Louisiana española), administered from New Orleans by the Governor-General
- **Population during period:** Very sparse. The 1790 Spanish padrón (census) of Arkansas Post recorded fewer than 400 residents, mostly French-speaking Creole settlers, soldiers, traders, and their enslaved workers; a small number of Native American converts appear in church registers
- **Economy:** Fur trade, subsistence agriculture, military garrison provisioning
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole settlers (dominant), Spanish colonial officials and soldiers, enslaved Africans and African-descended persons, Quapaw and other Native American peoples
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic exclusively — served by the Arkansas Post mission parish, under the Diocese of Louisiana and the Floridas (New Orleans)
- **Key historical events:** Treaty of Paris (1763) transferred French Louisiana to Spain; Spain secretly ceded the territory back to France in 1800 by the Treaty of San Ildefonso; the Louisiana Purchase (1803) brought the region under U.S. control

## Boundary changes
- **Pre-1763:** The Arkansas region was part of French Louisiana, a vast, poorly-defined colonial territory administered from New Orleans
- **1763–1800:** By the Treaty of Paris (1763) the territory passed to Spain as Spanish Louisiana; the Arkansas district was governed as a sub-district of the Province of Louisiana, headquartered at New Orleans
- **1800:** Spain ceded the territory to France; French administration was nominal and brief
- **1803:** The Louisiana Purchase transferred the region to the United States
- **1806/1812:** The District of Louisiana (later Missouri Territory) initially governed the area; Arkansas County was organized in 1813 under Missouri Territory; Arkansas Territory was established separately in 1819; Arkansas became a state in 1836
- **Critical implication:** The State of Arkansas and its county structure did not exist before 1813. All records from the colonial period (before 1800) were created under French or Spanish Louisiana, not under any Arkansas jurisdiction. Searching Arkansas county records will return nothing for this period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** There was no civil registration of vital events in the colonial Arkansas region. The Catholic Church held exclusive responsibility for recording baptisms, marriages, and burials
- **What exists:** Church sacramental registers only (see Church Records below)
- **Where held:** Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock; Arkansas History Commission; FamilySearch microfilm
- **Gaps:** Coverage is fragmentary; not all registers survive intact
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers ARE the primary vital record source for this entire period

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic only. The Arkansas Post mission was the sole organized congregation in the region during the colonial period
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including adult converts, enslaved persons, and Native Americans), marriages, burials; occasional confirmation records
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Image group **008814402** — 64 images of Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial), Arkansas Post, Arkansas County, Arkansas, covering **1763–1800**. This is the only digitized colonial-era volume returned by the survey. It is **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) and must be examined image by image
- **Access (digitized):** FamilySearch.org — browse image group 008814402 directly
- **Where physical originals are held:** Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock Archives; transcribed copies also held at the Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock, AR
- **Language:** Records are in **Spanish** (and sometimes French); 18th-century colonial handwriting (letra procesal or itálica script). A researcher must be able to read period Spanish script or engage a paleographer
- **Earlier French-era registers (pre-1763):** French-era registers from Arkansas Post are mentioned in the FamilySearch Wiki's Arkansas Genealogy page ([Colonial Records section](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)) as also held by the Diocese of Little Rock and the Arkansas History Commission, but no separate digitized volume for the French period was returned by this survey — treat them as physical-only until confirmed otherwise

### Census records
- **Spanish colonial padrones (censuses):** Spain conducted population censuses called padrones of its Louisiana settlements. The **1790 padrón of Arkansas Post** survives and is held at the Arkansas History Commission. It is not indexed on FamilySearch and was not returned as a digitized volume — treat as physical/microfilm
- **Federal census coverage begins:** 1830 (first census after Arkansas Territory was created); Arkansas was not included in the 1810 or 1820 federal census
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** "Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819–1870" (collection ID 2085124, 178,345 records) begins at 1819 — entirely post-colonial, but may help bridge descendants into the American period
- **Other enumerations:** Garrison muster rolls at Arkansas Post, held at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and possibly microfilmed at the Library of Congress, serve as a substitute census for military personnel

### Probate and court records
- **Colonial era:** No formal probate court existed at Arkansas Post. Estate matters were handled by the Spanish commandant as part of his administrative and judicial duties. Surviving records of this type, if any, would be in the commandant's correspondence files at the Archivo General de Indias or the Arkansas History Commission
- **Post-colonial:** Arkansas County (organized 1813) began keeping probate records under U.S. territorial law. Those records are at the Arkansas County courthouse in DeWitt and at the Arkansas History Commission
- **Digitization:** No probate records for the colonial period were returned by this survey; treat as physical-only

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds under French and Spanish colonial concession systems; the U.S. rectangular survey system was imposed after 1803
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Under Spanish rule, land concessions were granted by the Governor-General of Louisiana in New Orleans, with local grants approved by the commandant at Arkansas Post. Original concession files are held at the **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville) and the **Louisiana State Archives** (Baton Rouge)
- **Types:** Spanish land concessions (land grants/patents); post-1803 U.S. land claims validated by the Board of Land Commissioners; BLM General Land Office (GLO) patents
- **Critical trail:** Spanish land grants were not automatically honored under U.S. law; claimants had to file before the U.S. Board of Land Commissioners (after 1805). The claims files from this process — which restate and document the original Spanish grants — are held at NARA and are available through the BLM GLO website (glorecords.blm.gov). These validated-claim files often name original colonial-era settlers and their heirs
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias (Seville); Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge); BLM GLO archives; NARA; Arkansas History Commission
- **Digitization:** BLM GLO patent records are searchable online at glorecords.blm.gov; original Spanish-era concession files are not digitized for public name-search

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The American Revolutionary War (Spain was an ally of France against Britain; the Arkansas garrison saw related activity 1779–1781, including the Battle of Arkansas Post, 1783); general frontier garrison duty throughout the Spanish period
- **Record types:** Garrison muster rolls (hojas de servicio), officer personnel records, post correspondence — all generated at the Arkansas Post garrison
- **Where held:** **Archivo General de Indias**, Papeles Procedentes de Cuba series (the main repository for Spanish Louisiana military and administrative records); Library of Congress has microfilm of portions of this collection; the Arkansas History Commission holds some transcripts and finding aids
- **Access:** The Papeles Procedentes de Cuba series is not digitized for public online search; contact the Archivo General de Indias or use the Library of Congress microfilm

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** The Catholic mission cemetery at Arkansas Post is the only organized colonial burial ground; surviving headstones and sexton-type records are minimal
- **Online coverage:** No colonial-era cemetery records were returned by this survey from FindAGrave or BillionGraves
- **Physical records:** Burials are recorded in the sacramental burial registers (see Church Records above)

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No newspapers existed in the Arkansas region during the colonial period; the nearest press was in New Orleans
- **New Orleans newspapers** from the Spanish period (e.g., the Moniteur de la Louisiane, founded 1794) occasionally reported on events at Arkansas Post and may contain mentions of individuals; held at the Louisiana State Library and Tulane University

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was the sole port of entry for the Arkansas region; all European settlers arriving by sea passed through New Orleans
- **Record types:** Spanish colonial passport records (passports required to travel within Louisiana); ship manifests arriving at New Orleans; emigration records from France, Spain, and the Canary Islands
- **Where held:** Papeles Procedentes de Cuba, Archivo General de Indias (Seville); Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge); New Orleans Notarial Archives
- **Content note:** Spanish colonial-era passenger/travel records are not digitized and indexed in the same way as later U.S. passenger lists; access typically requires archival correspondence or an on-site visit

### Tax records
- **Colonial era:** Tax assessment records were not a standard feature of small frontier posts like Arkansas Post; some tithe or tribute records may exist in church or administrative files
- **Post-1803:** U.S. territorial tax lists begin after 1803; the earliest Arkansas tax records at the county level date to 1813

### Other record types
- **Commandant's correspondence:** The commandant at Arkansas Post was required to report regularly to the Governor-General in New Orleans. These letters and reports — held in the Papeles Procedentes de Cuba at the Archivo General de Indias — name residents, describe events, and document economic and social conditions. They are among the most informative sources for ordinary residents who appear in no other record
- **Notarial records:** Spanish colonial notarial records from New Orleans (held at the New Orleans Notarial Archives) document contracts, sales, manumissions, and estate settlements that may involve Arkansas Post residents who traveled to New Orleans for legal business
- **Published transcriptions and compilations:** Morris S. Arnold's published work on colonial Arkansas (including *Unequal Laws unto a Savage Race: European Legal Traditions in Arkansas, 1686–1836*) transcribes and analyzes many surviving colonial-era records and is an essential secondary source

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Image group 008814402: 64 browse-only images, Arkansas Post sacramental registers, 1763–1800 (Spanish, 0% indexed) | Free |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | U.S.-era land patents only; Spanish-era concession files not in GLO | Free |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | U.S. military records post-1803; no colonial-era Spanish records | Subscription |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. census collection starts 1830 for Arkansas; no colonial-era coverage returned | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` returned 1 digitized volume matching this place and period. The `collections_search` returned 3 collections for Arkansas, none covering the colonial period. The external links search returned 6 general-purpose links (NARA, Ancestry, FindAGrave, Newspapers.com, Fold3, FamilySearch Wiki categories) with no Arkansas-specific colonial content.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission, 1 Capitol Mall, Little Rock, AR 72201 | Transcripts and microfilm of colonial records; 1790 padrón; Arkansas Post church register transcriptions; Arkansas county records from 1813 | In-person or written request; some finding aids online at arkansashistory.com |
| Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock Archives, 2500 N. Tyler St., Little Rock, AR 72207 | Original or microfilm sacramental registers from Arkansas Post mission | Contact the archives for access |
| Archivo General de Indias, Avenida de la Constitución 3, Seville, Spain | Papeles Procedentes de Cuba series: Spanish Louisiana administrative, military, land, and census records 1763–1800 | In-person; finding aids available through the Spanish Ministry of Culture online portal (pares.mcu.es); Library of Congress holds microfilm of portions |
| Library of Congress, Washington, D.C. | Microfilm of portions of the Papeles Procedentes de Cuba (Archivo General de Indias) | In-person at the Manuscript Division; some digitized finding aids |
| Louisiana State Archives, 3851 Essen Lane, Baton Rouge, LA 70809 | Spanish-era land concession records; New Orleans administrative records that concern Arkansas Post | In-person or written request |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives, 1340 Poydras St., New Orleans, LA 70112 | Spanish colonial notarial records involving New Orleans-area and Arkansas Post residents | In-person research |
| NARA, Southwest Region / Washington D.C. | U.S. Board of Land Commissioners files (post-1805, validating Spanish land claims); territorial-era records from 1803 | In-person or NARA online catalog (catalog.archives.gov) |

## Records NOT online

The following record types are known to exist but were not found in any online database during this survey:

- **Spanish colonial administrative records (Papeles Procedentes de Cuba):** Commandant's correspondence, muster rolls, padrones — held at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville; not publicly searchable online
- **1790 Arkansas Post padrón (census):** Held at the Arkansas History Commission; not in any digitized online collection
- **Original French-era church registers (pre-1763):** Diocese of Little Rock and Arkansas History Commission; no digitized volume returned
- **Spanish colonial land concession originals:** Louisiana State Archives and Archivo General de Indias; not name-searchable online
- **New Orleans notarial records involving Arkansas Post residents:** New Orleans Notarial Archives; partially digitized for later periods but colonial-era access requires in-person or archival correspondence

## Known record losses

- Arkansas Post itself was relocated multiple times along the Arkansas River; records moved with the garrison and some were lost in transit or during the turbulent transfer of sovereignty (Spain to France, 1800; France to U.S., 1803)
- Many colonial administrative records that were never sent to New Orleans or Seville simply did not survive the frontier conditions of Arkansas Post
- The Arkansas History Commission reports that surviving colonial records are fragmentary; gaps in the sacramental registers are expected
- No courthouse fires are at issue for the colonial period (no courthouse existed), but records held in private or military hands at Arkansas Post were vulnerable to flood, fire, and neglect

## Research tips

- **The jurisdiction that matters is Spanish Louisiana, not Arkansas.** All civil and administrative authority during 1763–1800 ran through New Orleans. Begin any search at the Louisiana State Archives and the Archivo General de Indias before looking for Arkansas-specific repositories. (Source: [Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **The FamilySearch Wiki confirms three primary repositories** for surviving colonial records: the Arkansas History Commission, the Archivo General de Indias, and the Library of Congress microfilm holdings. (Source: [Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **Church records are your vital records.** There was no civil registration; baptism, marriage, and burial entries in the mission register are the only vital record source for the colonial period. (Source: [Arkansas Genealogy — Church Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records))
- **Browse FamilySearch image group 008814402 directly.** This is the only digitized colonial-era volume identified in this survey. It covers 1763–1800, contains 64 images, is 0% name-indexed, and is in Spanish — you must scroll through it manually
- **Learn to read Spanish colonial script** or find a collaborator who can. Letra procesal and related 18th-century Spanish handwriting styles are difficult; the Paleografía Hispánica resources at the Archivo General de Indias website are a starting point
- **Spanish land claims become U.S. records.** After 1803, holders of Spanish land grants had to file U.S. land claims. These filings — searchable at glorecords.blm.gov and through NARA — restate the original grant and name the settler, effectively creating a 19th-century index to colonial-era landholders
- **Search both sides of the Louisiana–Arkansas administrative boundary.** A resident of Arkansas Post in 1790 may have traveled to New Orleans to execute a will, free an enslaved person, or register a marriage; New Orleans notarial and church records are therefore a parallel search track
- **Published transcriptions save significant time.** Morris S. Arnold and several Arkansas Historical Quarterly articles have transcribed and published key colonial records. Check WorldCat and the Arkansas History Commission's publication list before attempting an archival visit to Seville

Here is the full locality guide returned by the agent:

---

# Locality Guide: Ohio / Northwest Territory (c. 1785–1810)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** The Northwest Territory was established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. Ohio became a state on 1 March 1803 — the first state carved from the Northwest Territory.
- **Administrative center:** Marietta (founded 1788, first American settlement); Cincinnati emerged as a secondary center.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory, United States (1787–1803).
- **Population:** ~45,000 in the 1800 census; ~231,000 in 1810.
- **Economy:** Frontier subsistence farming, flatboat trade along the Ohio River, fur trade, military provisioning.
- **Key historical events:** Northwest Ordinance (1787); Marietta settlement (1788); Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794) and Treaty of Greenville (1795) opened most of present Ohio to settlement; Ohio statehood (1803).

---

## Boundary Changes

This is the **single most important jurisdictional issue** for 1790 Ohio research.

- **1787:** The Northwest Ordinance creates the Northwest Territory — a single undivided jurisdiction with no county subdivisions.
- **1788:** **Washington County, Northwest Territory** is organized — the first county, covering essentially all of present-day Ohio east of the Scioto River.
- **1790:** **Hamilton County, Northwest Territory** is organized from the western portion of Washington County, covering southwestern Ohio.

**Key implication:** In 1790, a person in Ohio fell under *one of exactly two counties* — Washington or Hamilton. Any courthouse record from that year is in one of those two sets. Searching by any *later* Ohio county name for events occurring in 1790 will fail.

Post-statehood county formation was rapid — Ross, Adams, Jefferson Counties and many others were quickly carved from the two originals. As counties divided, records did not always transfer cleanly. You must determine which county held the specific territory at the **date of the event**, not which county covers that territory today.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **No civil birth or death registration existed** in territorial Ohio (1787–1803). These records were simply never created — it is not destruction, but absence.
- **Marriage recording** from county level from 1789 onward (Washington County 1788, Hamilton County 1790).
- FamilySearch collection 1803785 — "Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013" (1,523,678 records, indexed).

### Church Records
- The *only* source for baptisms and burials in this period.
- FamilySearch collection 2246917 — "Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950" (678,234 records).
- Denominations present: Methodist circuit riders, Presbyterian, Quaker, Baptist, German Lutheran/Reformed.
- Other repositories: Quaker records at Earlham College; Presbyterian Historical Society (Philadelphia); Methodist denominational archives.

### Census Records
- **The 1790 federal census did not enumerate the Northwest Territory.**
- The **1800 census** is the first with meaningful Ohio coverage; the 1810 census covers Ohio as a state. Both are indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- Work backward from 1800 — a person enumerated there in Washington or Hamilton County was almost certainly in the same territory in 1790.

### Probate and Court Records
- Territorial court records from Washington County (1788) and Hamilton County (1790).
- Held at county courthouses and the **Ohio History Connection** (Columbus).
- No dedicated online collection found for this period — **physical only**.

### Land Records — The Anchor Source
Ohio is a federal-land state but with **multiple distinct survey systems operating simultaneously**:

| District | Area | System | Repository |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Seven Ranges** | Eastern Ohio | Federal rectangular | BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) |
| **Ohio Company Purchase** | SE Ohio (Marietta area) | Ohio Company | Ohio History Connection |
| **Virginia Military District** | Between Scioto & Little Miami rivers | Virginia metes-and-bounds | Library of Virginia |
| **Connecticut Western Reserve** | NE Ohio | Connecticut Land Company | Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland |
| **U.S. Military District** | North-central Ohio | Federal bounty land | BLM GLO |

**Critical tip:** If your ancestor held land in the Virginia Military District, his warrant originated in Virginia — it is at the **Library of Virginia**, not any Ohio repository. Searching only Ohio collections will miss this entire series.

FamilySearch collection 1542187 — "Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840" (234,567 records, indexed).

### Military Records
- Northwest Indian War (1785–1795) service records; Revolutionary War pension files.
- **Revolutionary War pension declarations** filed in Ohio courts are particularly rich — they often name wife, children, ages, and county of residence.
- NARA; Fold3.com for digitized pension and service records.

### Tax Records
- FamilySearch collection 1987542 — "Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850" — begins at 1800, leaving a full gap for the pre-statehood decade.
- Territorial tax lists (1788–1800) are at the Ohio History Connection; online availability unconfirmed.

### Newspapers
- **No Ohio newspaper existed in 1790.** The *Centinel of the North-Western Territory* (Cincinnati) was founded in 1793 — the first newspaper in the Northwest Territory.
- Available via Chronicling America and Newspapers.com from 1793 onward.

---

## Digitized Volumes on FamilySearch (1780–1810)

| Volume | Coverage | Record type | Indexed | Full-text |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 005112233 | Northwest Territory, 1788–1799 | Territorial Land Records | 0% | No |
| 005112240 | Washington County, Ohio, 1799–1803 | County Tax Records | 12% | No |

Both volumes must be **browsed image-by-image** — neither is full-text searchable, and indexing is minimal. This is a very thin digitization footprint for the pre-statehood decade.

---

## Records NOT Online / Known Gaps

- Territorial court minutes (1788–1803) — physical only at county courthouses and Ohio History Connection.
- Territorial tax lists (1788–1800) — online availability unconfirmed.
- Early church records (1787–1800) — collection exists on FamilySearch but indexing depth for this frontier period is unconfirmed; many circuit-rider registers were never microfilmed.
- **No civil birth or death records were ever created** for the territorial period.

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Determine the 1790 county first.** Only Washington County and Hamilton County existed in 1790. Do not search by any later Ohio county name.
2. **Land records are your anchor.** With no civil vital registration and sparse church records, land entry records (patents, deeds, survey plats) are often the first and most reliable documentation placing an ancestor in territorial Ohio. Start with [BLM GLO](https://glorecords.blm.gov) for federal tracts, then county deed books.
3. **Virginia Military District requires a Virginia search.** Go to the Library of Virginia, not any Ohio repository, for VMD land warrants.
4. **Connecticut Western Reserve records are in Cleveland.** Western Reserve Historical Society, not Columbus.
5. **Revolutionary War pension declarations are rich substitutes for missing vital records.** They often name wife, children, ages, and county of residence.
6. **Work backward from the 1800 census** — the first federal census with Ohio coverage — to identify an ancestor in the territory around 1790.
7. **Search migration-origin counties.** Settlers in 1790 Ohio typically arrived from Pennsylvania (via the Ohio River), Virginia (Zane's Trace or the VMD), or Kentucky. Records from those years of migration may survive in Allegheny County, PA; Augusta or Rockbridge County, VA; or Mason/Campbell County, KY.

# Locality Guide: Ohio / Northwest Territory (c. 1785–1810)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Northwest Territory established by Northwest Ordinance of 1787. Ohio statehood: 1 March 1803.
- **Administrative center:** Marietta (first settlement, 1788); Cincinnati secondary center.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory, United States (1787–1803).
- **Population during period:** ~45,000 in 1800 census; ~231,000 in 1810 census.
- **Economy:** Frontier subsistence farming, flatboat trade, fur trade, military provisioning.
- **Ethnic composition:** Anglo-American settlers from Virginia, Pennsylvania, and New England; some German-speaking settlers; French Canadians near trading posts. Indigenous nations (Shawnee, Delaware, Wyandot, Miami) dominant through 1790s.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist circuit riders, Presbyterian missionaries, Quakers, Baptists, small Lutheran/German Reformed congregations.
- **Key historical events:** Northwest Ordinance (1787); Marietta settled (1788); Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794); Treaty of Greenville (1795) opened most of Ohio to settlement; Ohio statehood (1803).

## Boundary changes
1787: Northwest Territory created — no county subdivisions.
1788: Washington County organized (eastern/central Ohio).
1790: Hamilton County organized from western Washington County (southwestern Ohio).
In 1790 only these two counties existed. Records must be searched under Washington or Hamilton County, not any later county name.
1803: Ohio statehood transfers authority from territorial to state courts.

## Available record types

### Vital records
- No civil registration of births or deaths in territorial Ohio. County marriage recording from 1789 (FamilySearch collection 1803785). Church registers are the only source for baptisms/burials.

### Church records
- FamilySearch collection 2246917 (Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950, 678,234 records). Also denominational archives: Quaker (Earlham College), Presbyterian (Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia), Methodist (Drew University).

### Census records
- 1790 census did not enumerate the Northwest Territory. 1800 and 1810 federal censuses cover Ohio. No territorial census confirmed.

### Probate and court records
- Washington County records from 1788; Hamilton County from 1790. Physical: county courthouses and Ohio History Connection. Not in FamilySearch collections search results for this period.

### Land records
- Multiple survey systems: Seven Ranges (BLM GLO), Ohio Company Purchase (Ohio History Connection), Virginia Military District (Library of Virginia), Connecticut Western Reserve (Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland), U.S. Military District (federal bounty land). FamilySearch collection 1542187 (Ohio, Land Records, 1787-1840, 234,567 records).

### Military records
- Northwest Indian War (1785-1795); Revolutionary War pension declarations filed in Ohio courts. NARA, Fold3.com.

### Cemetery records
- Pioneer cemeteries at Marietta and Cincinnati. FindAGrave (sparse for frontier period). No sexton records confirmed for 1790.

### Newspaper records
- Centinel of the North-Western Territory (Cincinnati, from 1793). Ohio History Connection; Chronicling America; Newspapers.com.

### Immigration/emigration
- No Ohio ports. Atlantic passenger lists at NARA/Ancestry for earlier crossings; land records and pension declarations note origin.

### Tax records
- FamilySearch collection 1987542 (Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1850) — begins at 1800. Territorial tax lists (1788-1800) at Ohio History Connection; online availability unconfirmed.

## Repository guide

### Online
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | County Marriages 1789+ (1,523,678); Church Records 1787+ (678,234); Land Records 1787+ (234,567); Tax Records 1800+ (345,890); 2 browse-only volumes | Free |
| BLM GLO | Federal land patents | Free |
| Fold3 | Military pension/service records | Subscription |
| Ancestry | Federal census 1800, 1810 | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |
| NARA | Federal records finding aids | Free/some digital |

### Physical
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Ohio History Connection, Columbus | Territorial court records, land office records, county histories | In-person; ohiohistory.org |
| Washington County Courthouse, Marietta | County records from 1788 | In-person |
| Hamilton County Courthouse, Cincinnati | County records from 1790 | In-person |
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Virginia Military District warrants | In-person; lva.virginia.gov |
| Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland | Connecticut Western Reserve land records | In-person |
| NARA, Washington D.C. | Military pensions, census originals | In-person; Ancestry/Fold3 |

## Records NOT online
- Territorial court minutes (1788-1803)
- Territorial tax lists (1788-1800)
- Early frontier church records (1787-1800, sparse)
- Ohio Company purchase records
- Virginia Military District survey plats (not all searchable by name)

## Known record losses
- No civil birth/death registration ever existed for the territorial period — not destroyed, simply never created.
- Some early county records poorly preserved in frontier courthouses.
- County subdivision transfers after 1803 resulted in some gaps.

## Research tips
- Determine which 1790 county (Washington or Hamilton) holds the record before searching.
- Virginia Military District requires a separate Virginia search at Library of Virginia.
- Connecticut Western Reserve records are in Cleveland at the Western Reserve Historical Society.
- Land records are the anchor source for this period — start with BLM GLO.
- Revolutionary War pension declarations often name family members and county of residence.
- Work backward from the 1800 census, which is the first with Ohio coverage.
- Search migration-origin counties in Pennsylvania, Virginia, and Kentucky for earlier records.

# Locality Guide: Ohio / Northwest Territory (c. 1785–1810)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** The Northwest Territory was established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. Ohio became a state on 1 March 1803 — the first state carved from the Northwest Territory.
- **Administrative center:** Marietta (founded 1788, first American settlement); Cincinnati emerged as a secondary center.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory, United States (1787–1803).
- **Population during period:** The place_population tool returned no data for this period. Based on federal census results: approximately 45,000 in the 1800 census; approximately 231,000 in 1810.
- **Economy:** Frontier subsistence farming, flatboat trade along the Ohio River, fur trade, military provisioning.
- **Ethnic composition:** Anglo-American settlers from Virginia, Pennsylvania, and New England; some German-speaking settlers; small numbers of French Canadians near early trading posts. Indigenous nations (Shawnee, Delaware, Wyandot, Miami) were dominant through the 1790s and well into the early 1800s.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist circuit riders, Presbyterian missionaries, Quakers (especially in the Virginia Military District), Baptists, small Lutheran/German Reformed congregations among German settlers.
- **Key historical events:** Northwest Ordinance (1787); settlement of Marietta (1788); Fort Washington at Cincinnati (1789); Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794) and Treaty of Greenville (1795) opened most of present Ohio to settlement; Ohio statehood (1803).

## Boundary changes

This is the single most important jurisdictional issue for 1790 Ohio research.

**1787:** The Northwest Ordinance creates the Northwest Territory, encompassing what is now Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, and part of Minnesota. The territory was a single undivided jurisdiction with no county subdivisions.

**1788:** Washington County, Northwest Territory is organized — the first county, covering essentially all of present-day Ohio east of the Scioto River. Records from this year onward were created under Washington County authority.

**1790:** Hamilton County, Northwest Territory is organized from the western portion of Washington County, covering the area south and west of the Great Miami River. Records for events in southwestern Ohio from 1790 onward belong to Hamilton County.

**Key implication:** In 1790, a person in Ohio fell under one of exactly two counties — Washington or Hamilton. Any courthouse record from that year is in one of those two sets. Searching by any later Ohio county name for events occurring in 1790 will fail.

**Post-statehood county formation:** Ross County (1798), Adams and Jefferson Counties (1797), and many others were quickly carved from the two original counties. As counties divided, records did not always transfer cleanly. The researcher must determine which county held the specific territory at the date of the event, not which county covers that territory today. Source: wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory.

**Statehood (1803):** Transferred authority from territorial courts to newly chartered state courts. Early county court records created under territorial authority are generally held today at the county courthouse or the Ohio History Connection.

## Available record types

**Note on registration level:** The FamilySearch Wiki Ohio-specific pages (Ohio_Vital_Records, Ohio_Genealogy, Ohio_Land_and_Property, Ohio_Church_Records, Ohio_Probate_Records, Ohio_Census, Ohio_Naming_Customs) and all four wiki_place_page sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) all returned a generic redirect page rather than Ohio-specific content during this survey. Claims below are grounded in the collections_search results, volume_search results, and the wiki_search return (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory and #Land_Records). Consult the FamilySearch Research Wiki directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy for additional specifics.

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** No civil registration of births or deaths existed in territorial Ohio (1787–1803) and no civil birth or death registration at any level is confirmed for this period by the tools. The FamilySearch collections search returned marriages from 1789 at the county level (collection 1803785). The Ohio Vital Records wiki page returned a generic redirect — no Ohio-specific registration date was provided.
- **What exists for 1790:** County-level marriage recording from 1789 onward; no civil birth or death records.
- **Where held:** County deed/record books (Washington County from 1788, Hamilton County from 1790); FamilySearch collection 1803785 (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1803785), 1,523,678 records, indexed.
- **Gaps:** No civil birth or death registration for the entire territorial period. Marriage records exist only for the two counties then organized.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers are the only source for baptisms and burials in this period.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Methodist (circuit riders), Presbyterian, Quaker, Baptist; small German Lutheran and Reformed congregations.
- **Record types:** Baptisms/christenings, marriages, burials, membership rolls, disciplinary proceedings, Quaker Monthly Meeting minutes.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 2246917 "Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950" (678,234 records, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917). Denominational archives: Quaker records at Earlham College (Indiana) and the Ohio Valley Yearly Meeting; Presbyterian at the Presbyterian Historical Society (Philadelphia); Methodist at Drew University or denominational conference archives.
- **Access level:** Indexed collection on FamilySearch; however, indexing depth for the frontier period (1787–1800) specifically is not confirmed by the tool data — expect sparse coverage.
- **Language:** English.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The 1790 federal census did not enumerate the Northwest Territory. The 1800 census is the first with meaningful Ohio coverage; the 1810 census covers Ohio as a state. Both are fully indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Territorial/state census:** The Ohio Census wiki page returned a generic redirect — no Ohio-specific census schedule information was returned. Consult the Ohio History Connection for any territorial enumerations.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, territorial court minutes.
- **Date range:** Washington County records from 1788; Hamilton County from 1790. These are territorial court records predating the county probate court system established after statehood.
- **Where held:** County courthouses; early territorial court records at the Ohio History Connection, Columbus. The Ohio Probate Records wiki page returned a generic redirect.
- **Online:** No dedicated probate collection for this period appeared in either collections_search or volume_search. These records are physical-only.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Ohio is a federal-land state but with multiple distinct systems operating simultaneously — this is the most important land research fact for this period:
  - **Seven Ranges** (eastern Ohio): first federal rectangular survey, 1785–1787.
  - **Ohio Company Purchase** (southeastern Ohio, around Marietta): Ohio Company of Associates, 1787–1788.
  - **Virginia Military District** (between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers): reserved for Virginia Revolutionary War veterans; used Virginia's metes-and-bounds system. Warrants issued in Virginia; records at the Library of Virginia, not Ohio repositories.
  - **Connecticut Western Reserve** (northeastern Ohio): sold to the Connecticut Land Company (1795); records at the Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland, not Columbus.
  - **U.S. Military District** (north-central Ohio): federal bounty land for U.S. veterans; BLM GLO.
  - **Symmes Purchase, Refugee Tract, Donation Tract:** additional smaller districts with their own grant records.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** General Land Office (now BLM) for federal tracts (https://glorecords.blm.gov); Virginia government for VMD (Library of Virginia); Connecticut Land Company for Western Reserve (Western Reserve Historical Society).
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840" (collection 1542187, 234,567 records, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187), indexed.
- **Source:** wiki_search return at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Northwest Indian War (1785–1795); War of 1812 (later).
- **Record types:** Service records for U.S. Army campaigns; pension files and bounty land warrants for Revolutionary War veterans who settled in Ohio.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C. and St. Louis); Fold3.com (https://www.fold3.com/) has digitized pension and service records. Revolutionary War pension declarations filed in Ohio courts are particularly rich — they often name wife, children, ages, and county of residence.
- **Bounty land connection:** U.S. Military District (north-central Ohio) was reserved for U.S. veterans; VMD for Virginia veterans. A soldier ancestor receiving a warrant in either district will appear in federal land records.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Pioneer-era cemeteries associated with Marietta (1788) and Cincinnati (1788). Many early burials were in farm or family plots.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has some Ohio pioneer coverage but early frontier burials are sparsely represented.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for this period rarely survive. The Ohio Genealogical Society holds some county cemetery compilations.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** Centinel of the North-Western Territory (Cincinnati, founded 1793) — the earliest newspaper in the Northwest Territory. No Marietta paper until after statehood.
- **Where held:** Ohio History Connection; Chronicling America (https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/); Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/).
- **Content value:** Obituaries and marriage notices from 1793 onward. Very sparse for 1790 specifically; no newspaper existed in Ohio that year.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant routes:** Settlers arrived overland via Zane's Trace (southeastern Ohio, 1796), by flatboat down the Ohio River from Pittsburgh, and through the Virginia Military District from Virginia. Ohio had no seaports.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists for earlier Atlantic crossings (NARA and Ancestry); land entry records noting place of origin; pension declarations sometimes stating birthplace and prior state of residence.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax records

- **FamilySearch collection:** "Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850" (collection 1987542, 345,890 records, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987542) — begins at 1800, leaving a full gap for the pre-statehood decade.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists from 1800 onward substitute for missing census years. For the 1788–1800 territorial period, territorial tax lists are at the Ohio History Connection; their online availability was not confirmed by the tools.
- **Holding level:** County.

### Other record types

- **Town and county histories:** 19th-century published local histories for Washington and Hamilton Counties frequently reprint early territorial court records, list founding families, and transcribe records since lost. Ohio History Connection; Ohio Genealogical Society library; WorldCat.
- **Territorial legislative/council records:** Northwest Territory legislative council records naming landowners, taxpayers, and officeholders are at the Ohio History Connection and have been partially published.

## Digitized volumes on FamilySearch (1780–1810)

### Online repositories

The collections_search returned 5 indexed collections, of which 2 (marriages from 1789 and land records from 1787) directly overlap the 1785–1810 window. | Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Ohio History Connection (Columbus, OH) | Territorial court records, early county records, Ohio land office records, Ohio Company purchase records, published county histories, newspaper microfilm | In-person; finding aids at ohiohistory.org |
| Washington County Courthouse (Marietta, OH) | County deeds, marriages, probate from 1788 | In-person; some records microfilmed |
| Hamilton County Courthouse (Cincinnati, OH) | County deeds, marriages, probate from 1790 | In-person; some records microfilmed |
| Library of Virginia (Richmond, VA) | Virginia Military District land warrants and surveys; Virginia-issued Revolutionary War bounty land records | In-person and online at lva.virginia.gov |
| Western Reserve Historical Society (Cleveland, OH) | Connecticut Land Company and Connecticut Western Reserve land records | In-person |
| NARA (Washington, D.C.) | Federal land patents, military pension files, Revolutionary War service records, 1800 and 1810 census originals | In-person; digitized on Ancestry and Fold3 |

The following records exist or likely exist but were not found in any online database by this survey:

- Territorial court minutes (1788–1803) for Washington and Hamilton Counties — physical only at county courthouses and Ohio History Connection.
- Territorial tax lists (1788–1800) — online availability unconfirmed; at Ohio History Connection.
- Early frontier church records (1787–1800) — FamilySearch collection 2246917 covers the date range but indexing depth for this frontier period is unconfirmed; many circuit-rider registers were never microfilmed.
- Ohio Company purchase records (1787–1800) — Ohio History Connection.
- Virginia Military District survey plats — Library of Virginia; not all searchable by name online.

## Known record losses

- **No civil birth or death registration was ever created** for the territorial period. This is not destruction — these records simply do not exist. Church registers and family bibles are the only documentation.
- **Frontier courthouse preservation gaps:** Many early county records from 1788–1803 were stored in poorly built frontier courthouses and some have gaps.
- **County subdivision transfer gaps:** As new counties were created rapidly after 1803, records did not always transfer cleanly from parent county offices. A territorial-era record may remain under Washington or Hamilton County even if the location falls in a later county today.

## Research tips

- **Determine the 1790 county first.** Only Washington County (1788, eastern/central Ohio) and Hamilton County (1790, southwestern Ohio) existed in 1790. All courthouse records from that year are in one of these two. Do not search by any later Ohio county name. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory.
- **Virginia Military District requires a separate Virginia search.** If your ancestor held land between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers, his warrant originated in Virginia and is at the Library of Virginia — not at any Ohio repository. Searching only Ohio collections will miss this series. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records.
- **Connecticut Western Reserve records are in Cleveland, not Columbus.** For northeastern Ohio, go to the Western Reserve Historical Society. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records.
- **Land records are the anchor source for 1790.** With no civil vital registration and sparse church records, land entry records (patents, deeds, survey plats) are often the first and most reliable documentation placing an ancestor in territorial Ohio. Start with the BLM GLO website (https://glorecords.blm.gov) for federal tracts, then county deed books.
- **Revolutionary War pension declarations are rich substitutes.** A veteran who settled in Ohio would have appeared before the local court to make his pension declaration. These declarations on Fold3 and Ancestry often name wife, children, ages, and county of residence.
- **The 1800 federal census is the first with Ohio coverage.** Work backward from 1800 — a person in the 1800 census in Washington or Hamilton County was almost certainly in the same territory in 1790.
- **Search migration-origin counties.** Settlers in 1790 Ohio typically arrived from Pennsylvania (via the Ohio River), Virginia (via Zane's Trace or the VMD), or Kentucky (across the Ohio River). Records from the years of migration may survive in Allegheny County, Pennsylvania; Augusta or Rockbridge County, Virginia; or Mason or Campbell County, Kentucky. The FamilySearch Wiki neighboring county table was not available (all Ohio wiki pages returned generic redirects), so consult the Ohio History Connection's county formation maps to identify specific bordering jurisdictions for the township of interest.
- **FamilySearch Wiki Ohio-specific pages were unavailable.** All wiki_place_page sections and all Ohio-specific wiki_read URLs returned a generic redirect during this survey. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy directly for additional detail.

---

This guide covers Ohio during the pre-statehood period around 1790, when the land was the Northwest Territory and only two counties existed. The most important thing to understand is that no government ever recorded births or deaths in this era — those records simply were not created — so land records, church registers, and military pension files carry the research. Land records are the most abundant surviving source and are spread across multiple distinct grant systems (federal, Virginia, and Connecticut), each held in a different repository in a different state.

# Locality Guide: Ohio / Northwest Territory (c. 1785–1810)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Northwest Territory established by Northwest Ordinance of 1787. Ohio statehood: 1 March 1803.
- **Administrative center:** Marietta (first settlement, 1788); Cincinnati secondary center.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory, United States (1787–1803).
- **Population during period:** ~45,000 in 1800 census; ~231,000 in 1810 census.
- **Economy:** Frontier subsistence farming, flatboat trade, fur trade, military provisioning.
- **Ethnic composition:** Anglo-American settlers from Virginia, Pennsylvania, and New England; some German-speaking settlers; French Canadians near trading posts. Indigenous nations (Shawnee, Delaware, Wyandot, Miami) dominant through 1790s.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist circuit riders, Presbyterian missionaries, Quakers, Baptists, small Lutheran/German Reformed congregations.
- **Key historical events:** Northwest Ordinance (1787); Marietta settled (1788); Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794); Treaty of Greenville (1795) opened most of Ohio to settlement; Ohio statehood (1803).

## Boundary changes
1787: Northwest Territory created — no county subdivisions.
1788: Washington County organized (eastern/central Ohio).
1790: Hamilton County organized from western Washington County (southwestern Ohio).
In 1790 only these two counties existed. Records must be searched under Washington or Hamilton County, not any later county name.
1803: Ohio statehood transfers authority from territorial to state courts.

## Available record types

### Vital records
- No civil registration of births or deaths in territorial Ohio. County marriage recording from 1789 (FamilySearch collection 1803785). Church registers are the only source for baptisms/burials.

### Church records
- FamilySearch collection 2246917 (Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950, 678,234 records). Also denominational archives: Quaker (Earlham College), Presbyterian (Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia), Methodist (Drew University).

### Census records
- 1790 census did not enumerate the Northwest Territory. 1800 and 1810 federal censuses cover Ohio. No territorial census confirmed.

### Probate and court records
- Washington County records from 1788; Hamilton County from 1790. Physical: county courthouses and Ohio History Connection. Not in FamilySearch collections search results for this period.

### Land records
- Multiple survey systems: Seven Ranges (BLM GLO), Ohio Company Purchase (Ohio History Connection), Virginia Military District (Library of Virginia), Connecticut Western Reserve (Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland), U.S. Military District (federal bounty land). FamilySearch collection 1542187 (Ohio, Land Records, 1787-1840, 234,567 records).

### Military records
- Northwest Indian War (1785-1795); Revolutionary War pension declarations filed in Ohio courts. NARA, Fold3.com.

### Cemetery records
- Pioneer cemeteries at Marietta and Cincinnati. FindAGrave (sparse for frontier period). No sexton records confirmed for 1790.

### Newspaper records
- Centinel of the North-Western Territory (Cincinnati, from 1793). Ohio History Connection; Chronicling America; Newspapers.com.

### Immigration/emigration
- No Ohio ports. Atlantic passenger lists at NARA/Ancestry for earlier crossings; land records and pension declarations note origin.

### Tax records
- FamilySearch collection 1987542 (Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1850) — begins at 1800. Territorial tax lists (1788-1800) at Ohio History Connection; online availability unconfirmed.

## Repository guide

### Online
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | County Marriages 1789+ (1,523,678); Church Records 1787+ (678,234); Land Records 1787+ (234,567); Tax Records 1800+ (345,890); 2 browse-only volumes | Free |
| BLM GLO | Federal land patents | Free |
| Fold3 | Military pension/service records | Subscription |
| Ancestry | Federal census 1800, 1810 | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |
| NARA | Federal records finding aids | Free/some digital |

### Physical
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Ohio History Connection, Columbus | Territorial court records, land office records, county histories | In-person; ohiohistory.org |
| Washington County Courthouse, Marietta | County records from 1788 | In-person |
| Hamilton County Courthouse, Cincinnati | County records from 1790 | In-person |
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Virginia Military District warrants | In-person; lva.virginia.gov |
| Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland | Connecticut Western Reserve land records | In-person |
| NARA, Washington D.C. | Military pensions, census originals | In-person; Ancestry/Fold3 |

## Records NOT online
- Territorial court minutes (1788-1803)
- Territorial tax lists (1788-1800)
- Early frontier church records (1787-1800, sparse)
- Ohio Company purchase records
- Virginia Military District survey plats (not all searchable by name)

## Known record losses
- No civil birth/death registration ever existed for the territorial period — not destroyed, simply never created.
- Some early county records poorly preserved in frontier courthouses.
- County subdivision transfers after 1803 resulted in some gaps.

## Research tips
- Determine which 1790 county (Washington or Hamilton) holds the record before searching.
- Virginia Military District requires a separate Virginia search at Library of Virginia.
- Connecticut Western Reserve records are in Cleveland at the Western Reserve Historical Society.
- Land records are the anchor source for this period — start with BLM GLO.
- Revolutionary War pension declarations often name family members and county of residence.
- Work backward from the 1800 census, which is the first with Ohio coverage.
- Search migration-origin counties in Pennsylvania, Virginia, and Kentucky for earlier records.

# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1870)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **California statehood:** September 9, 1850 — bypassed territorial status entirely, so there are no territorial-era civil records
- **Pre-statehood:** Ceded from Mexico by the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, February 1848
- **Key hubs:** Sacramento (state capital); San Francisco (commercial and port hub)
- **Population:** ~300,000 arrived during the Gold Rush (1848–1855); the 1850 federal census was **partially destroyed**
- **Ethnic diversity:** Arrivals from the eastern U.S., Mexico, Chile, China, Australia, Hawaii, and Europe; existing Californio population; numerous Native nations

---

## Available Record Types

### Census Records ⭐ (Start Here)
- **1852 California State Census** — *your most important substitute for the damaged 1850 returns*. FamilySearch imageGroup 006601001; 88% name-indexed + full-text searchable. Search this **before** the 1850 federal census.
- **1850 federal census** — partially destroyed; some county returns are entirely missing
- **1860 and 1870 federal censuses** — complete and fully indexed (FamilySearch & Ancestry)
- **Mortality schedules** — available for 1850, 1860, 1870; records deaths in the year preceding each census, capturing miners who died without other records

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- County-level birth and marriage registration began **1850**; statewide registration came much later
- FamilySearch collections:
  - County Births 1850–1919 — collection **2017276** (~789K records)
  - County Marriages 1850–1952 — collection **1452832** (~568K records)
- Death registration was **inconsistent** in mining camps; many camp deaths went unregistered
- *Pre-registration alternatives:* church records, newspaper death notices, cemetery records, probate files

### Immigration & Arrival Records
- **Two primary routes:**
  1. **By sea** to San Francisco (around Cape Horn or via Panama)
  2. **Overland** via the California Trail (no formal customs; use trail diaries, letters, newspapers)
- **Ship passenger manifests** — San Francisco sea arrivals; held at NARA San Francisco (San Bruno, CA); many digitized on Ancestry and FamilySearch
- **Sacramento Port Arrival Registers 1849–1858** — FamilySearch imageGroup 006601003 (298 images); covers the inland steamboat leg after arriving in San Francisco — *browse-only, 0% indexed, must be browsed image-by-image*
- **Overland arrivals:** No customs records; the Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley) holds the largest collection of overland trail diaries in North America

### Mining Records
- **Mining Claim Registers, San Francisco 1849–1855** — FamilySearch imageGroup 006601002 (340 images); *browse-only, organized by district and date — not alphabetically*
- **County deed books** at county recorder offices record mining claim transfers
- **Federal land patents** — searchable free at glorecords.blm.gov (California is a federal land state)

### Probate & Court Records
- **High value for mining research:** Estate files for deceased miners frequently name heirs (parents, siblings, wife) still in the state of origin — often the only link back to the pre-California family
- Naturalization records (pre-1906): declarations of intention could be filed in *any* court — search district, county, and circuit court series separately; they are not duplicates
- Held at county courthouses; FamilySearch has microfilmed some series

### Great Registers (Voter Registration)
- **1866–1910** — FamilySearch collection **1923340** (~1.3M records)
- Content: name, age, **birthplace**, occupation, physical description, residence — a biographical snapshot
- Starts after the Gold Rush decade, but men registered in 1867 almost certainly arrived during the Rush
- Extremely useful for locating men who settled and stayed

### Church Records
- **Mission Records 1769–1850** — FamilySearch collection 1804372 (~99K records, Spanish/Latin) — relevant for families with deep California roots, not forty-niner arrivals
- Protestant denominations (Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, Presbyterian) established in mining towns in the early 1850s
- Catholic diocesan archives in San Francisco, Sacramento, and Los Angeles hold parish registers

### Land Records
- Federal land patents: glorecords.blm.gov (free)
- County deed books: county recorder offices
- Spanish/Mexican rancho grants: Bancroft Library

### Military Records
- Mexican-American War veterans who subsequently settled in California may have pension files giving biographical detail and state of origin
- Civil War: California raised volunteer regiments; service records at NARA; Fold3.com has many digitized
- Pension files often give birthplace and enlistment location — linking a California veteran back to his origin

### Tax Records
- County property and personal property assessment rolls from county formation (most 1850–1852)
- **Critical substitute** for the missing 1850 census — places a miner in a specific county and year
- Held at county archives and assessor offices; most not yet online

### Newspaper Records
- San Francisco's *Alta California* and other papers began by 1849; mining county papers followed quickly
- **Free online:** California Digital Newspaper Collection (cdnc.ucr.edu)
- **Subscription:** Newspapers.com, GenealogyBank
- Content: obituaries, mining partnership notices, ship arrival columns, probate legal notices

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 1852 State Census, County Births/Marriages, Great Registers, Mission Records, Mining Claim Registers (browse), Sacramento Port Registers (browse) | Free |
| Ancestry | Federal Census 1850/1860/1870; ship passenger manifests | Subscription |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents | Free |
| California Digital Newspaper Collection (cdnc.ucr.edu) | California newspapers | Free |
| Fold3 | Civil War service records, pension files | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records statewide | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Ship manifests, military records | Free/in-person |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Key Holdings |
|---|---|
| **NARA San Francisco** (San Bruno, CA) | San Francisco ship passenger manifests; federal court naturalization records |
| **California State Archives** (Sacramento) | State government and transferred county records |
| **California State Library** (Sacramento) | City directories, newspaper microfilm, county histories |
| **Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley** | Largest Gold Rush-era manuscript collection in North America: trail diaries, mine-camp journals, personal papers. Finding aids at oac.cdlib.org |
| **County courthouses** | Probate files, deeds, naturalization, tax rolls — specific to each county |
| **Catholic diocesan archives** | Parish registers (San Francisco, Sacramento, Los Angeles dioceses) |

---

## Known Record Losses
- **1850 federal census** — partial destruction; use the 1852 state census as the primary substitute
- **San Francisco 1906 earthquake and fire** — heavily damaged San Francisco County vital, courthouse, and probate records (affects all events recorded there, regardless of date)
- **Mining camp ephemeral records** — many early camp registers never survived transfer to county custody

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Start with the 1852 state census** (FamilySearch imageGroup 006601001, 88% indexed + full-text) before the 1850 federal census.
2. **Use probate files to reach the state of origin** — estate files for deceased miners frequently name heirs still in Ohio, Missouri, New York, etc.
3. **Search both the ship manifests AND the Sacramento port arrival registers** for sea arrivals — two separate legs of the journey.
4. **Mining claim registers are geographic, not alphabetical** — approach imageGroup 006601002 by district and approximate year.
5. **Pre-1906 naturalizations: search all courts** — district, county, and circuit series are separate, not duplicates.
6. **Identify the specific county before writing to a courthouse** — Gold Rush county lines shifted repeatedly in the 1850s; verify the county of jurisdiction at the specific event date.
7. **Check the BLM GLO website for land patents** (glorecords.blm.gov) — places a person at a specific location on a specific date.
8. **Search Bancroft Library finding aids online first** at oac.cdlib.org before visiting or requesting reproductions.
9. **Check neighboring states' records for the overland journey** — Missouri, Kansas/Nebraska Territory, Utah Territory, and Nevada Territory along the route may document the migration itself.

---

The state was brand new, county lines shifted constantly, and the first federal census was partially destroyed — but an impressive range of records survives: a nearly fully-indexed 1852 state census, county birth and marriage registers from 1850, Gold Rush-era ship passenger manifests at NARA San Bruno, and the Bancroft Library's unparalleled collection of trail diaries and mine-camp papers. The Great Registers from 1866 onward give rich biographical snapshots of men who settled and stayed.
