entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1870)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** California achieved statehood on September 9, 1850, bypassing territorial status entirely
- **Administrative center:** Sacramento (state capital); San Francisco (commercial hub)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Prior to statehood, California was ceded from Mexico to the United States by the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (February 1848)
- **Population during period:** Approximately 300,000 people arrived during the Gold Rush (1848–1855) according to Wikipedia; the 1850 federal census was partially destroyed so exact figures are uncertain
- **Economy:** Placer and hard-rock gold mining; port trade through San Francisco; agriculture; supply and service industries supporting mining camps
- **Ethnic composition:** Highly diverse — arrivals from the eastern United States, Mexico, Chile, China, Australia, Hawaii, and throughout Europe; significant existing Spanish-speaking Californio population and numerous Native American nations
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (the dominant pre-statehood church via the Franciscan missions); Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, and other Protestant denominations established in mining camps; Jewish congregations in San Francisco by the early 1850s
- **Key historical events:** Gold discovered at Sutter's Mill, Coloma, January 24, 1848; mass migration of the forty-niners beginning 1849; California statehood September 9, 1850; decline of placer mining and transition to hard-rock and hydraulic mining through the 1850s–1860s

## Boundary changes
- California entered the Union with its current general boundaries in 1850 — no major internal reorganization of county lines occurred at statehood, though county boundaries shifted repeatedly as new counties were carved from existing ones during the 1850s and 1860s.
- **Important consequence:** A mining camp or settlement may have been in a different county at different points in the 1850s as county lines were redrawn. Always identify which county held jurisdiction at the specific date of interest, not just the modern county.
- There were no territorial records — the earliest government civil records date from 1850.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** County-level registration of births and marriages began in 1850 at the county level. Statewide vital registration did not begin until the early 1900s. The FamilySearch wiki pages specific to California vital records did not load in this survey session — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Vital_Records directly for the precise county start dates.
- **What exists:** County births, 1850–1919 (FamilySearch collection 2017276, ~789,456 records); county marriages, 1850–1952 (FamilySearch collection 1452832, ~567,890 records with ~1,135,780 persons indexed)
- **Where held:** County clerk offices hold the original volumes; FamilySearch has digitized and indexed a substantial portion
- **Gaps:** Death registration at the county level during the 1850s was inconsistent; many mining camp deaths were never registered. Statewide death registration came much later.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (see below); newspaper death notices; cemetery sexton records; probate records naming deceased persons

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (pre-existing mission network and new parishes); Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, Presbyterian congregations founded in mining towns and San Francisco in the early 1850s
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials — and for Catholic parishes, confirmations (a separate dated event)
- **Mission records (pre-1850):** FamilySearch collection 1804372 covers California Mission Records, 1769–1850 (~98,765 records). These document the Spanish colonial and Mexican-era period and are relevant as background for Californio families, not for Gold Rush arrivals.
- **Where held:** The Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley) and the California State Library hold many manuscript church records. Diocesan archives in San Francisco, Los Angeles, and Sacramento hold Catholic records. FamilySearch has microfilmed portions.
- **Language:** Catholic mission records are primarily in Spanish and Latin.

### Census records
- **1850 federal census:** The first federal census taken in California after statehood. **Partially destroyed** — some county returns are missing entirely. This is the single most important caveat for 1850s California research.
- **1852 California state census:** The primary substitute for the missing 1850 returns. FamilySearch has digitized this census (imageGroupNumber 006601001; 522 images; 88% name-indexed; full-text searchable). This is the strongest digitized census source for the Gold Rush period.
- **1860 and 1870 federal censuses:** Complete; fully indexed online at FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Mortality schedules:** Available for 1850, 1860, and 1870 — record deaths in the year preceding the census and can document miners who died without other records.
- **Access:** The 1852 state census is 88% name-indexed and full-text searchable on FamilySearch — search by name directly. Federal census years are fully indexed on both FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration (intestate estates), guardianships, inventories, estate distributions; naturalizations; civil and criminal cases
- **Where held:** County courthouses and county archives; some have been microfilmed by FamilySearch
- **Naturalization note:** Before 1906, declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization could be filed in any court of record — district, county, and circuit courts each have separate series. Search all court types in the county where the person lived.
- **Value for miners:** Probate files for deceased miners frequently name heirs (parents, siblings, wives) back in the state of origin, providing critical links to pre-California families.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** California is a federal (public domain) land state — the rectangular survey system (townships, ranges, sections)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The federal General Land Office (GLO) administered land patents. Searchable at glorecords.blm.gov
- **Types:** Federal land patents and grants; county deed books; Spanish and Mexican land grants (Ranchos); mining claims
- **Mining claims specifically:** County recorder offices registered mining claims. FamilySearch has digitized Mining Claim Registers for San Francisco, 1849–1855 (imageGroupNumber 006601002; 340 images). **Browse-only — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.** Must be browsed image by image.
- **Where held:** County recorder offices hold deed books; BLM GLO website for federal patents; the Bancroft Library holds a major collection of rancho grant documents

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848, just prior to the Gold Rush); Civil War (1861–1865)
- **California volunteers:** California raised several infantry and cavalry regiments for Civil War service, primarily stationed in the West rather than fighting in eastern theaters. Their service records are at NARA.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, draft registrations (Civil War–era enrollment records)
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C., and Atlanta for pension files); Fold3.com has many digitized service records
- **Pre-statehood:** Soldiers in the Mexican-American War who subsequently settled in California may have pension files that provide biographical detail, including origin state.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Gold Rush-era cemeteries exist in mining counties (El Dorado, Placer, Nevada, Calaveras, Tuolumne, Amador) as well as San Francisco and Sacramento. Many early mine-camp graveyards were abandoned or relocated.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) covers many California cemeteries; BillionGraves has additional coverage
- **Physical records:** Sexton records, where they survive, are held by individual cemeteries, county archives, or local historical societies. Coverage is incomplete for 1850s mining camps.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** San Francisco had multiple papers by 1849 (Alta California, the most prominent). Sacramento, Stockton, and mining county towns established papers in the early 1850s.
- **Where held:** The California Digital Newspaper Collection (cdnc.ucr.edu) provides online access to many titles. Newspapers.com and GenealogyBank have additional holdings. The California State Library holds microfilm for many runs.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, mining partnership notices, legal notices (estate probate, land sales), ship arrival columns listing prominent passengers — all are valuable for 1850s research.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Arrival routes:** Two primary routes — by sea to San Francisco (around Cape Horn or via Panama); overland by the California Trail
- **Ship passenger manifests:** Arrivals at San Francisco are the core sea-migration record. These are held at the National Archives at San Francisco (NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno, CA). Many have been digitized and are searchable on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **Port arrival registers (Sacramento):** FamilySearch has digitized Port Arrival Registers for Sacramento, 1849–1858 (imageGroupNumber 006601003; 298 images). **Browse-only — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.** Must be browsed image by image.
- **Overland arrivals:** Overland emigrants did not pass through a formal customs process; trail diaries, letters, and county arrival notices in newspapers are the primary evidence. The Bancroft Library holds a major collection of overland trail diaries.
- **Naturalization:** See court records above — pre-1906 naturalizations are scattered across all courts of record.
- **Content note:** Ship passenger manifests (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax and personal property assessment rolls
- **Date range:** From county formation (most Gold Rush counties formed 1850–1852)
- **Where held:** County archives and county assessor offices; some have been microfilmed
- **Substitute value:** Tax rolls are especially important for 1851–1859, filling the gap caused by the partial destruction of the 1850 federal census. A miner assessed for tools, a mule, and a claim stake is placed in a county and year with specificity census records cannot provide.

### Great Registers (voter registration)
- **Date range:** 1866–1910 (FamilySearch collection 1923340, ~1,345,678 records)
- **Content:** Name, age, birthplace, occupation, physical description, and residence — effectively a biographical snapshot. This is one of the richest sources for locating men who remained in California after the Gold Rush.
- **Limitation:** The Great Registers begin in 1866, after the core Gold Rush period. They are not a primary source for events of the 1850s but are invaluable for tracing what happened to men who stayed.
- **Access:** Indexed at FamilySearch (collection 1923340)

### Other record types
- **Overland trail diaries and manuscripts:** The Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley) holds the largest North American collection of Gold Rush–era personal papers, mine-camp journals, and overland trail diaries. Not available online — in-person or duplication request required.
- **City directories:** San Francisco city directories began in the early 1850s and place residents at specific addresses in intercensal years. The California State Library and the San Francisco Public Library hold major runs.
- **County and local histories:** Many 19th-century California county histories include biographical sketches of early settlers and founding families, sometimes transcribing records since lost. The FamilySearch Catalog and WorldCat list holdings.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | California County Births 1850–1919 (collection 2017276, ~789K records); California Great Registers 1866–1910 (collection 1923340, ~1.3M records); California County Marriages 1850–1952 (collection 1452832, ~568K records); California Mission Records 1769–1850 (collection 1804372, ~99K records); 1852 State Census (imageGroup 006601001, 88% indexed); Mining Claim Registers San Francisco 1849–1855 (imageGroup 006601002, browse-only); Port Arrival Registers Sacramento 1849–1858 (imageGroup 006601003, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census collection (1850, 1860, 1870 California); ship passenger manifests | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Civil War–era military service records and pension files | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records statewide | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical California newspapers | Subscription |
| BLM GLO Records (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents for California | Free |
| California Digital Newspaper Collection (cdnc.ucr.edu) | Digitized California newspapers | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Ship passenger manifests (San Francisco); military records | Free/in-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch volume_search returned 14 total digitized volumes matching California, 1848–1870; the first page of 3 volumes is detailed above. A second page of results exists (nextPageToken was returned). The researcher should request additional pages of volume results for a complete picture of digitized holdings.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) | San Francisco ship passenger manifests; federal court records including naturalizations | In-person; written requests; some digitized on Ancestry/FamilySearch |
| California State Archives (Sacramento) | State government records; county records transferred to state custody | In-person; online catalog at archives.ca.gov |
| California State Library (Sacramento) | City directories; newspaper microfilm; county histories; manuscript collections | In-person; some digitized |
| Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley | Largest Gold Rush–era manuscript collection in North America: trail diaries, mine-camp journals, rancho grant documents, personal papers | In-person; duplication requests; some finding aids online |
| County courthouses | Probate files, deed books, naturalization records, court minutes, tax rolls — held by the county of interest | In-person; written requests vary by county |
| Local historical societies | County histories, photographs, local newspapers, surname files | Varies — contact each society |
| Catholic diocesan archives (San Francisco, Sacramento, Los Angeles) | Parish baptism, marriage, and burial registers | Written request to each diocese |

## Records NOT online
- Most county tax assessment rolls, 1850s
- Overland trail diaries and Gold Rush personal papers at the Bancroft Library
- Many Catholic parish registers (pre-digitization)
- County court minute books and equity case files
- Sexton records for mining camp cemeteries
- San Francisco city directory runs prior to the mid-1850s (partial digitization only)

## Known record losses
- **1850 federal census, partial destruction:** Some California county returns from the first federal census were destroyed. The exact counties affected are not specified in the tool results — consult the FamilySearch wiki or Ancestry's census landing pages for a list. The 1852 state census is the primary substitute.
- **San Francisco fire and earthquake records:** San Francisco suffered multiple major fires in the early 1850s and the catastrophic 1906 earthquake and fire. County vital records and courthouse records for San Francisco were heavily damaged or destroyed in 1906; this affects death, marriage, and probate records for San Francisco County.
- **Mining camp ephemeral records:** Many early mining camps kept informal registers that were never transferred to county custody and did not survive.

## Research tips
- **Start with the 1852 California state census before the 1850 federal census.** The state census is 88% name-indexed and full-text searchable on FamilySearch (imageGroup 006601001), and it substitutes for the missing 1850 county returns. The FamilySearch wiki noted the 1850 returns were partially destroyed. [Source: wiki_search result citing https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records]
- **Use probate files to reach back to states of origin.** When a miner died, his estate file often names heirs — parents, siblings, a wife — still living in Ohio, Missouri, New York, or wherever he came from. This is frequently the only record linking a California death to the family of origin.
- **Search ship passenger manifests AND Sacramento port registers for sea arrivals.** Two routes brought ships into the interior: around the Horn or via Panama to San Francisco, then upriver by steamboat to Sacramento. The Sacramento port registers (imageGroup 006601003) cover 1849–1858 and document the inland leg — but they are browse-only, with no name index.
- **Mining claim registers are browse-only and organized geographically.** The San Francisco mining claim registers (imageGroup 006601002) are not indexed. Approach them by mining district and approximate date, not by surname search.
- **The Great Registers begin in 1866 — use them to find men who stayed.** California Great Registers (collection 1923340) give name, age, birthplace, occupation, and physical description. They do not document the 1850s directly, but a man registered in 1867 as a 35-year-old miner born in Ohio is likely the same forty-niner who arrived in 1852.
- **Identify the specific county before searching courthouse records.** County lines in the Gold Rush counties shifted repeatedly in the 1850s. A mine that was in El Dorado County in 1850 might have been reassigned to Amador County by 1854. Verify the county of jurisdiction at the specific event date before requesting courthouse records.
- **California is a federal land state — use the BLM GLO website.** Land patents are searchable free at glorecords.blm.gov. A land entry places a person at a specific location on a specific date with their full legal name as recorded.
- **For pre-1850 Californio families, begin with Mission Records.** FamilySearch collection 1804372 covers California Mission Records, 1769–1850 in Spanish and Latin. These are relevant only for families with roots in the Spanish colonial or Mexican-era California — not for Gold Rush migrants.
- **Bancroft Library first for manuscript sources.** The Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley holds the largest collection of Gold Rush–era personal papers, mine-camp journals, and overland trail diaries in North America. [Source: wiki_search result citing https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records] Their online finding aids at oac.cdlib.org can be searched before visiting.
- **Pre-1906 naturalizations: search all courts.** Before 1906, a man could file a declaration of intention in any court of record. Search district court, county court, and circuit court records separately for the county — they are different series, not duplicates.

- **1850 federal census:** The first taken in California after statehood. Partially destroyed — some county returns are missing entirely. This is the most important caveat for 1850s California research.
- **1852 California state census:** The primary substitute for the missing 1850 returns. FamilySearch imageGroupNumber 006601001; 522 images; 88% name-indexed; full-text searchable. This is the strongest digitized census source for the Gold Rush period and should be searched before the 1850 federal census.
- **1860 and 1870 federal censuses:** Complete and fully indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Mortality schedules:** Available for 1850, 1860, and 1870. These record deaths in the year preceding the census and can document miners who died without other records.
- **Access:** The 1852 state census is 88% name-indexed and full-text searchable — search by name directly on FamilySearch. Federal census years are fully indexed on both FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills (testate estates), letters of administration (intestate estates), guardianships, inventories, estate distributions; naturalizations; civil and criminal cases
- **Where held:** County courthouses; some series have been microfilmed by FamilySearch
- **Naturalization note:** Before 1906, declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization could be filed in any court of record — district, county, and circuit courts each have separate series. Search all court types in the county where the person lived; they are not duplicates.
- **Value for miners:** Probate files for deceased miners frequently name heirs (parents, siblings, wives) still living in the state of origin, providing the critical documentary link to the pre-California family.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** California is a federal (public domain) land state — rectangular survey (townships, ranges, sections)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The federal General Land Office (GLO) administered land patents, searchable free at glorecords.blm.gov
- **Types:** Federal land patents and grants; county deed books; Spanish and Mexican land grants (Ranchos); mining claims registered at county recorders' offices
- **Mining claims specifically:** FamilySearch has digitized Mining Claim Registers for San Francisco, 1849–1855 (imageGroupNumber 006601002; 340 images). Browse-only — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Must be browsed image by image, organized by mining district and approximate date.
- **Where held:** County recorder offices hold deed books. The BLM GLO website holds federal patents. The Bancroft Library holds a major collection of rancho grant documents.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848, immediately prior to the Gold Rush); Civil War (1861–1865)
- **California volunteers:** California raised infantry and cavalry regiments for Civil War service, primarily stationed in the West. Service records are at NARA.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files (pension files frequently give state of birth and place of enlistment, linking a California veteran back to his origin); Civil War draft enrollment records
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C., and Atlanta for pension files); Fold3.com has many digitized service records
- **Pre-statehood note:** Soldiers who served in the Mexican-American War and subsequently settled in California may have pension files providing biographical detail, including state of origin.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Gold Rush-era cemeteries exist across the mining counties — El Dorado, Placer, Nevada, Calaveras, Tuolumne, Amador — as well as San Francisco and Sacramento. Many early mine-camp graveyards were abandoned or relocated.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) and BillionGraves cover many California cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Sexton records, where they survive, are held by individual cemeteries, county archives, or local historical societies. Coverage for 1850s mining camps is incomplete.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** San Francisco had multiple papers by 1849 (the Alta California being the most prominent). Sacramento, Stockton, and mining county towns established papers in the early 1850s.
- **Where held:** The California Digital Newspaper Collection (cdnc.ucr.edu) provides free online access to many California titles. Newspapers.com and GenealogyBank have additional holdings. The California State Library holds microfilm for many runs.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, mining partnership notices, legal notices (estate probate, land sales), ship arrival columns listing prominent passengers — all are high-value sources for 1850s research.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Arrival routes:** Two primary routes — by sea to San Francisco (around Cape Horn or via the Panama crossing); overland by the California Trail
- **Ship passenger manifests:** Sea arrivals at San Francisco are the core sea-migration record. Held at the National Archives at San Francisco (NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno, CA). Many have been digitized and are searchable on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **Port arrival registers (Sacramento):** FamilySearch imageGroupNumber 006601003; 298 images covering Sacramento, 1849–1858. Browse-only — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Must be browsed image by image. These document the inland steamboat leg after arrival at San Francisco.
- **Overland arrivals:** Overland emigrants did not pass through formal customs. Trail diaries, letters, and county arrival notices in newspapers are the primary evidence. The Bancroft Library holds the largest North American collection of overland trail diaries. [Source: FamilySearch wiki_search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records]
- **Naturalization:** See court records above — pre-1906 naturalizations are scattered across all courts of record in whichever county the person lived.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax and personal property assessment rolls
- **Date range:** From county formation — most Gold Rush counties formed 1850–1852
- **Where held:** County archives and county assessor offices; some have been microfilmed
- **Substitute value:** Tax rolls are especially important for 1851–1859, filling the gap created by the partial destruction of the 1850 federal census. A miner assessed for tools, a mule, and a mining claim is placed in a county and year with specificity census records cannot provide.

### Great Registers (voter registration)
- **Date range:** 1866–1910 — FamilySearch collection 1923340, approximately 1,345,678 records
- **Content:** Name, age, birthplace, occupation, physical description, and residence — a biographical snapshot. One of the richest sources for locating men who remained in California after the Gold Rush.
- **Limitation:** The Great Registers begin in 1866, after the core Gold Rush decade. They do not document 1850s events directly, but a man registered in 1867 as a 40-year-old farmer born in Ohio almost certainly arrived during the Rush.
- **Access:** Indexed on FamilySearch (collection 1923340)

### Other record types
- **Overland trail diaries and manuscripts:** The Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley) holds the largest North American collection of Gold Rush-era personal papers, mine-camp journals, and overland trail diaries. Not available online — in-person visit or duplication request required.
- **City directories:** San Francisco city directories began in the early 1850s. They place residents at specific addresses in intercensal years. The California State Library and the San Francisco Public Library hold major runs.
- **County and local histories:** Many 19th-century California county histories include biographical sketches of early settlers and founding families, sometimes transcribing records since lost. Search the FamilySearch Catalog and WorldCat for holdings.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | County Births 1850–1919 (collection 2017276, ~789K records); Great Registers 1866–1910 (collection 1923340, ~1.3M records); County Marriages 1850–1952 (collection 1452832, ~568K records); Mission Records 1769–1850 (collection 1804372, ~99K records); 1852 State Census (imageGroup 006601001, 88% indexed + full-text); Mining Claim Registers San Francisco 1849–1855 (imageGroup 006601002, browse-only); Port Arrival Registers Sacramento 1849–1858 (imageGroup 006601003, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census (1850, 1860, 1870 California); ship passenger manifests | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Civil War military service records and pension files | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records statewide | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical California newspapers | Subscription |
| BLM GLO Records (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents for California | Free |
| California Digital Newspaper Collection (cdnc.ucr.edu) | Digitized California newspapers | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Ship passenger manifests (San Francisco); military records | Free/in-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch volume_search returned 14 total digitized volumes matching California for 1848–1870. Only the first page of 3 volumes is detailed above. A second page of results exists (the tool returned a nextPageToken). Request additional pages to see the complete digitized holdings picture.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) | San Francisco ship passenger manifests; federal court naturalization records | In-person; written requests; many digitized on Ancestry/FamilySearch |
| California State Archives (Sacramento) | State government records; county records transferred to state custody | In-person; online catalog at archives.ca.gov |
| California State Library (Sacramento) | City directories; newspaper microfilm; county histories; manuscript collections | In-person; some digitized |
| Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley | Largest Gold Rush-era manuscript collection in North America: trail diaries, mine-camp journals, rancho documents, personal papers | In-person; duplication requests; finding aids at oac.cdlib.org |
| County courthouses | Probate files, deed books, naturalization records, court minutes, tax rolls — held by the specific county | In-person; written requests vary by county |
| Local and county historical societies | County histories, photographs, local newspapers, surname files | Contact each society individually |
| Catholic diocesan archives (San Francisco, Sacramento, Los Angeles) | Parish baptism, marriage, and burial registers | Written request to each diocese |

## Records NOT online
- Most county tax assessment rolls for the 1850s
- Overland trail diaries and Gold Rush personal papers at the Bancroft Library
- Most Catholic parish registers from mining county churches
- County court minute books and equity case files
- Sexton records for mining camp cemeteries
- San Francisco city directory runs before the mid-1850s (partial digitization only)

## Known record losses
- **1850 federal census, partial destruction:** Some California county returns from the first federal census were destroyed. The 1852 state census is the primary substitute. Consult the FamilySearch wiki or Ancestry's census landing page for the list of missing counties.
- **San Francisco 1906 earthquake and fire:** San Francisco County vital records, courthouse records, and probate files were heavily damaged or destroyed in April 1906. This primarily affects events recorded in San Francisco County, regardless of when they occurred.
- **Mining camp ephemeral records:** Many early mine-camp registers and informal records were never transferred to county custody and did not survive.

## Research tips
- **Start with the 1852 California state census before the 1850 federal census.** The state census (FamilySearch imageGroup 006601001) is 88% name-indexed and full-text searchable, and it substitutes for the missing 1850 county returns. The 1850 federal census was partially destroyed. [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records]
- **Use probate files to reach back to the state of origin.** When a miner died, his estate file often names heirs — parents, siblings, a wife — still living in Ohio, Missouri, New York, or wherever he emigrated from. This is frequently the only record linking a California death to the family of origin.
- **Search ship manifests AND the Sacramento port arrival registers for sea arrivals.** Two legs: ocean voyage to San Francisco, then steamboat upriver to Sacramento. The Sacramento port registers (imageGroup 006601003) cover 1849–1858 and document the inland leg — but they are browse-only, with no name index.
- **Mining claim registers are browse-only and organized geographically, not alphabetically.** Approach imageGroup 006601002 by mining district and approximate year, not by surname search.
- **The Great Registers begin in 1866 — use them to find men who stayed.** A man in collection 1923340 registered in 1867 as a 38-year-old miner born in Pennsylvania is very likely the same person who arrived in 1850. The register's physical description also helps confirm identity across multiple records.
- **Identify the specific county before requesting courthouse records.** County lines in the Gold Rush counties shifted repeatedly in the 1850s. Verify the county of jurisdiction at the specific event date before writing to a courthouse.
- **California is a federal land state — use the BLM GLO website.** Land patents are searchable free at glorecords.blm.gov. An entry places a person at a specific location on a specific date with their full legal name.
- **Pre-1906 naturalizations: search all courts.** Before 1906, declarations of intention could be filed in any court of record. Search district court, county court, and circuit court records separately — they are different series, not duplicates.
- **Bancroft Library finding aids are searchable online before you visit.** The Online Archive of California (oac.cdlib.org) indexes Bancroft collections by subject, geographic area, and personal name. Search there first to identify relevant manuscript collections before traveling or requesting reproductions. [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records]
- **Check neighboring states' records for the journey west.** Overland emigrants passed through Missouri, Kansas/Nebraska Territory, Utah Territory, and Nevada Territory before entering California. Letters, diaries, and county records along the route may document the migration itself.

---

California in the 1850s is a challenging research environment: the state was brand new, county lines shifted constantly, and the first federal census was partially destroyed. Despite those challenges, an impressive range of records survives — a 1852 state census that is nearly fully indexed, county birth and marriage registers going back to 1850, Gold Rush-era ship passenger manifests at a regional National Archives facility in San Bruno, and the Bancroft Library's unparalleled collection of trail diaries and mine-camp papers. The Great Registers, beginning in 1866, give detailed snapshots of men who settled and stayed. The two biggest practical warnings are that many mining camp deaths were never registered anywhere and that most 1850s tax rolls, court minutes, and church registers for the mining counties are not yet online — they require a courthouse visit or a written request.

If you tell me which county or mining district your ancestor was in, the next step is to narrow the search to specific county collections and identify which records have survived for that jurisdiction.

# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1870)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** California achieved statehood on September 9, 1850, bypassing territorial status entirely
- **Administrative center:** Sacramento (state capital); San Francisco (commercial hub)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Prior to statehood, California was ceded from Mexico to the United States by the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (February 1848)
- **Population during period:** Approximately 300,000 people arrived during the Gold Rush (1848–1855) according to Wikipedia; the 1850 federal census was partially destroyed so exact figures are uncertain
- **Economy:** Placer and hard-rock gold mining; port trade through San Francisco; agriculture; supply and service industries supporting mining camps
- **Ethnic composition:** Highly diverse — arrivals from the eastern United States, Mexico, Chile, China, Australia, Hawaii, and throughout Europe; significant existing Spanish-speaking Californio population and numerous Native American nations
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (the dominant pre-statehood church via the Franciscan missions); Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, and other Protestant denominations established in mining camps; Jewish congregations in San Francisco by the early 1850s
- **Key historical events:** Gold discovered at Sutter's Mill, Coloma, January 24, 1848; mass migration of the forty-niners beginning 1849; California statehood September 9, 1850; decline of placer mining and transition to hard-rock and hydraulic mining through the 1850s–1860s

## Boundary changes
- California entered the Union with its current general boundaries in 1850 — no major internal reorganization of county lines occurred at statehood, though county boundaries shifted repeatedly as new counties were carved from existing ones during the 1850s and 1860s.
- **Important consequence:** A mining camp or settlement may have been in a different county at different points in the 1850s as county lines were redrawn. Always identify which county held jurisdiction at the specific date of interest, not just the modern county.
- There were no territorial records — the earliest government civil records date from 1850.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** County-level registration of births and marriages began in 1850 at the county level. Statewide vital registration did not begin until the early 1900s. The FamilySearch wiki pages specific to California vital records did not load in this survey session — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Vital_Records directly for the precise county start dates.
- **What exists:** County births, 1850–1919 (FamilySearch collection 2017276, ~789,456 records); county marriages, 1850–1952 (FamilySearch collection 1452832, ~567,890 records with ~1,135,780 persons indexed)
- **Where held:** County clerk offices hold the original volumes; FamilySearch has digitized and indexed a substantial portion
- **Gaps:** Death registration at the county level during the 1850s was inconsistent; many mining camp deaths were never registered. Statewide death registration came much later.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (see below); newspaper death notices; cemetery sexton records; probate records naming deceased persons

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (pre-existing mission network and new parishes); Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, Presbyterian congregations founded in mining towns and San Francisco in the early 1850s
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials — and for Catholic parishes, confirmations (a separate dated event)
- **Mission records (pre-1850):** FamilySearch collection 1804372 covers California Mission Records, 1769–1850 (~98,765 records). These document the Spanish colonial and Mexican-era period and are relevant as background for Californio families, not for Gold Rush arrivals.
- **Where held:** The Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley) and the California State Library hold many manuscript church records. Diocesan archives in San Francisco, Los Angeles, and Sacramento hold Catholic records. FamilySearch has microfilmed portions.
- **Language:** Catholic mission records are primarily in Spanish and Latin.

### Census records
- **1850 federal census:** The first federal census taken in California after statehood. **Partially destroyed** — some county returns are missing entirely. This is the single most important caveat for 1850s California research.
- **1852 California state census:** The primary substitute for the missing 1850 returns. FamilySearch has digitized this census (imageGroupNumber 006601001; 522 images; 88% name-indexed; full-text searchable). This is the strongest digitized census source for the Gold Rush period.
- **1860 and 1870 federal censuses:** Complete; fully indexed online at FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Mortality schedules:** Available for 1850, 1860, and 1870 — record deaths in the year preceding the census and can document miners who died without other records.
- **Access:** The 1852 state census is 88% name-indexed and full-text searchable on FamilySearch — search by name directly. Federal census years are fully indexed on both FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration (intestate estates), guardianships, inventories, estate distributions; naturalizations; civil and criminal cases
- **Where held:** County courthouses and county archives; some have been microfilmed by FamilySearch
- **Naturalization note:** Before 1906, declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization could be filed in any court of record — district, county, and circuit courts each have separate series. Search all court types in the county where the person lived.
- **Value for miners:** Probate files for deceased miners frequently name heirs (parents, siblings, wives) back in the state of origin, providing critical links to pre-California families.

- **Mining claim registers are browse-only and organized geographically.** The San Francisco mining claim registers (imageGroup 006601002) are not indexed. Approach them by mining district and approximate date, not by surname search.
- **The Great Registers begin in 1866 — use them to find men who stayed.** California Great Registers (collection 1923340) give name, age, birthplace, occupation, and physical description. They do not document the 1850s directly, but a man registered in 1867 as a 35-year-old miner born in Ohio is likely the same forty-niner who arrived in 1852.
- **Identify the specific county before searching courthouse records.** County lines in the Gold Rush counties shifted repeatedly in the 1850s. A mine that was in El Dorado County in 1850 might have been reassigned to Amador County by 1854. Verify the county of jurisdiction at the specific event date before requesting courthouse records.
- **California is a federal land state — use the BLM GLO website.** Land patents are searchable free at glorecords.blm.gov. A land entry places a person at a specific location on a specific date with their full legal name as recorded.
- **For pre-1850 Californio families, begin with Mission Records.** FamilySearch collection 1804372 covers California Mission Records, 1769–1850 in Spanish and Latin. These are relevant only for families with roots in the Spanish colonial or Mexican-era California — not for Gold Rush migrants.
- **Bancroft Library first for manuscript sources.** The Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley holds the largest collection of Gold Rush–era personal papers, mine-camp journals, and overland trail diaries in North America. [Source: wiki_search result citing https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records] Their online finding aids at oac.cdlib.org can be searched before visiting.
- **Pre-1906 naturalizations: search all courts.** Before 1906, a man could file a declaration of intention in any court of record. Search district court, county court, and circuit court records separately for the county — they are different series, not duplicates.

## Colonial New York City (1700s) — Locality Research Guide

Here is a summary of what the locality-guide agent found and recorded (saved as **loc_001** in your research.json):

---

### Key Takeaway
There were **no civil registration records** in colonial New York — no government-mandated birth, marriage, or death certificates. **Church registers are the primary vital records source** for the entire 1700s.

---

### Church Records (Most Important)
- **Dutch Reformed** — the dominant colonial church; FamilySearch has a digitized 211-image register covering **1700–1776**, though it must be browsed image by image and read in Dutch.
- **Anglican (Trinity Church)** — significant for English settlers; registers survive for much of the century.
- **Presbyterian, Huguenot, Lutheran, Jewish** congregations also kept registers; survival varies.

---

### Probate Records
- Colonial-era probate ran through the **Provincial Prerogative Court** (not a county surrogate). The published ***Abstracts of Wills*** series is the essential finding aid for this era.

---

### Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **New York State Archives (Albany)** | Colonial government, land, court records |
| **New-York Historical Society** | Manuscripts, church records, city records |
| **New York Public Library** | Published vital record abstracts |
| **FamilySearch** | Digitized church registers, some colonial records |

---

### Watch Out For
- **British occupation (1776–1783)** caused gaps and disruptions in municipal records.
- Many records require reading **17th–18th century Dutch or English secretary hand**.

---

### Suggested Next Steps
A good next step would be to identify the specific family lines and religious affiliation (if known) to target the right church registers. Would you like to build a research plan or dive into a specific record type or repository?

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New York City (New York County), New York — 1700s Colonial Period

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Amsterdam founded 1626 as a Dutch colony; seized by the English in 1664 and renamed New York. New York County established under English rule.
- **County seat / administrative center:** New York City (lower Manhattan), also the seat of New York Province
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New York Province (British Crown colony) until 1783; thereafter the State of New York
- **Population during period:** No population data returned by tool. Wikipedia notes estimated growth from ~5,000 in 1700 to ~33,000 by 1790.
- **Economy:** Major commercial port, maritime trade, merchant activity, artisan crafts
- **Ethnic composition:** Dutch, English, Scots-Irish, French Huguenot, German, Jewish (Sephardic and Ashkenazi), enslaved African populations
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed, Anglican (Trinity Church), Presbyterian, French Huguenot, Lutheran, Quaker, Shearith Israel (Jewish)
- **Key historical events:** English takeover from Dutch (1664); Leisler's Rebellion (1689-1691); French and Indian War (1754-1763); Revolutionary War British occupation (1776-1783)

## Boundary changes
- Before 1664: Dutch authority (New Netherland). Records at New York State Archives and State Library.
- 1664-1783: British colonial period. New York County = Manhattan under New York Province.
- 1783-1800: State of New York. Prerogative Court probate function transferred to Surrogate's Court system.
- Neighboring counties: Kings, Queens, Richmond (Staten Island), Westchester — families near county edges may appear in those records.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- No civil registration existed in colonial New York. No statewide system until 1880.
- Church registers are the sole substitute for the entire 1700s.

### Church records
- Denominations: Dutch Reformed (from 1639), Anglican/Trinity Church (from 1697), Presbyterian, Huguenot, Lutheran, Quaker, Shearith Israel
- FamilySearch digitized volume: 007733180 — Dutch Reformed Church Registers 1700-1776, 211 images, browse-only (0% indexed), in Dutch
- FamilySearch collection: New York, Church Records, 1640-1940 (ID 1469062)
- Repositories: Trinity Church Archives; Reformed Church in America Archives (NJ); NYGBS; New-York Historical Society
- Language warning: Dutch Reformed registers in Dutch through mid-century; Huguenot registers in French

### Census records
- First federal census: 1790 (after the colonial period)
- Colonial enumerations and ward tax assessments are the census substitutes
- Generally physical or microfilm only — not indexed online

### Probate and court records
- Colonial probate: Prerogative Court of New York (provincial level, not county)
- Published index: Abstracts of Wills, 1665-1801 (New-York Historical Society)
- FamilySearch collection: New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971 (ID 1542780)
- Mayor's Court records: New York City Municipal Archives and New-York Historical Society

### Land records
- Survey system: Metes and bounds
- Colonial land patents issued by royal governor — held at New York State Archives
- FamilySearch collection: New York, Land Records, 1630-1975 (ID 2078654)
- Also: NYC Register's Office (deed books); New York State Library (Dutch-era grants)

### Military records
- Conflicts: Queen Anne's War, King George's War, French and Indian War, Revolutionary War
- Colonial militia rolls at New York State Archives
- Revolutionary War records at NARA and Fold3
- Loyalist records at The National Archives (Kew, UK)

### Cemetery records
- Trinity Churchyard (from 1697); Dutch Reformed churchyard; Shearith Israel cemeteries
- FindAGrave coverage of Trinity and some other historic Manhattan cemeteries
- Trinity Church burial registers at Trinity Church Archives

### Newspaper records
- New-York Gazette (founded 1725); New-York Weekly Journal (founded 1733)
- Held at New York State Library and New-York Historical Society
- Chronicling America (loc.gov) has some colonial-era issues; Newspapers.com limited for 1700s

### Immigration and emigration records
- New York Harbor was primary colonial port
- Pre-1906 naturalizations in Mayor's Court and Supreme Court of Judicature
- NARA for federal-era records; NYGBS for published colonial passenger indexes

### Tax records
- Ward-by-ward tax assessment rolls — primary census substitute
- FamilySearch collection: Tax Assessment Rolls, 1799-1804 (ID 1678432)
- Earlier colonial tax lists: New York City Municipal Archives and New York State Archives — physical/microfilm only

### Other record types
- New York Colonial Manuscripts (New York State Archives): council minutes, governor's correspondence, chancery records
- Freeman/guild admission records (NYGBS)
- Documentary History of the State of New York (O'Callaghan, 1849-1851) — reprints many colonial records
- Slave records in probate inventories, wills, deeds, and church baptism registers

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church Records 1640-1940 (1469062); Land Records 1630-1975 (2078654); Probate Records 1629-1971 (1542780); Tax Rolls 1799-1804 (1678432); Dutch Reformed Registers 1700-1776 vol. 007733180 (browse-only, Dutch) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | US Federal Census (earliest 1790); additional collections | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War service and pension records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records including Trinity Churchyard | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records and finding aids | Free/partial |
| Chronicling America (loc.gov) | Colonial-era New York newspapers | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers — limited 18th-century NYC coverage | Subscription |

**Coverage note:** volume_search returned 1 total digitized volume at the NYC level for 1700-1800. Much colonial material is indexed at the state scope in collections_search. The single volume confirmed at city level is the Dutch Reformed Church Registers (007733180).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| New York State Archives (Albany) | Colonial Manuscripts; Prerogative Court probate; land patents; militia rolls | In-person; some microfilm via FamilySearch |
| New York City Municipal Archives | Mayor's Court records; ward tax rolls; city administrative records | In-person |
| New-York Historical Society | Church transcriptions; Abstracts of Wills; colonial manuscripts; newspaper runs | In-person; some digitized |
| NYGBS | Published colonial indexes; NY Genealogical and Biographical Record | Membership; in-person library |
| Trinity Church Archives | Anglican burial registers and vestry minutes from 1697 | In-person by appointment |
| Reformed Church in America Archives (NJ) | Dutch Reformed congregational records | In-person; some on FamilySearch microfilm |
| New York State Library (Albany) | Dutch-era records; colonial imprints and newspapers | In-person |
| NARA | Revolutionary War service/pension; post-1789 naturalization | In-person or via Fold3/Ancestry |

## Records NOT online
- Colonial ward tax rolls (pre-1799)
- Mayor's Court civil case files and minute books
- Provincial Supreme Court of Judicature minutes
- Colonial militia muster rolls
- New York Colonial Manuscripts (many volumes not digitized)
- Huguenot congregation registers (partial transcriptions at NYGBS; originals at New-York Historical Society)
- Lutheran and Quaker registers
- Shearith Israel records
- Freeman/guild admission records

## Known record losses
- Revolutionary War occupation (1776-1783) caused disruption; some municipal records are missing for these years
- Dutch-period records are incomplete due to 1664 transition
- Some Prerogative Court estate files are missing
- Colonial parchment records have suffered from damp storage and handling

## Research tips
- Church registers are the vital records for this period — identify every denomination and search each separately
- Probate is filed at the provincial level (Prerogative Court), not county — use the published Abstracts of Wills first
- Colonial militia rolls are a census substitute, organized by ward
- Dutch families: the digitized FamilySearch volume (007733180) is browse-only and in Dutch — plan for translation
- Ward identification narrows tax rolls, court records, and church membership significantly
- Search the New York Genealogical and Biographical Record (NYGBS journal) for colonial transcriptions
- Check Kings, Queens, Richmond, and Westchester counties for families with connections outside lower Manhattan
- The Documentary History of the State of New York (O'Callaghan) reprints many colonial records; partially available via HathiTrust

- 1664-1783: British colonial period. New York County = Manhattan under New York Province.
- 1783-1800: State of New York. Prerogative Court probate function transferred to Surrogate's Court system.
- Neighboring counties: Kings, Queens, Richmond (Staten Island), Westchester — families near county edges may appear in those records.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- No civil registration existed in colonial New York. No statewide system until 1880.
- Church registers are the sole substitute for the entire 1700s.

### Church records
- Denominations: Dutch Reformed (from 1639), Anglican/Trinity Church (from 1697), Presbyterian, Huguenot, Lutheran, Quaker, Shearith Israel
- FamilySearch digitized volume: 007733180 — Dutch Reformed Church Registers 1700-1776, 211 images, browse-only (0% indexed), in Dutch
- FamilySearch collection: New York, Church Records, 1640-1940 (ID 1469062)
- Repositories: Trinity Church Archives; Reformed Church in America Archives (NJ); NYGBS; New-York Historical Society
- Language warning: Dutch Reformed registers in Dutch through mid-century; Huguenot registers in French

### Census records
- First federal census: 1790 (after the colonial period)
- Colonial enumerations and ward tax assessments are the census substitutes
- Generally physical or microfilm only — not indexed online

### Probate and court records
- Colonial probate: Prerogative Court of New York (provincial level, not county)
- Published index: Abstracts of Wills, 1665-1801 (New-York Historical Society)
- FamilySearch collection: New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971 (ID 1542780)
- Mayor's Court records: New York City Municipal Archives and New-York Historical Society

### Land records
- Survey system: Metes and bounds
- Colonial land patents issued by royal governor — held at New York State Archives
- FamilySearch collection: New York, Land Records, 1630-1975 (ID 2078654)
- Also: NYC Register's Office (deed books); New York State Library (Dutch-era grants)

### Military records
- Conflicts: Queen Anne's War, King George's War, French and Indian War, Revolutionary War
- Colonial militia rolls at New York State Archives
- Revolutionary War records at NARA and Fold3
- Loyalist records at The National Archives (Kew, UK)

### Cemetery records
- Trinity Churchyard (from 1697); Dutch Reformed churchyard; Shearith Israel cemeteries
- FindAGrave coverage of Trinity and some other historic Manhattan cemeteries
- Trinity Church burial registers at Trinity Church Archives

### Newspaper records
- New-York Gazette (founded 1725); New-York Weekly Journal (founded 1733)
- Held at New York State Library and New-York Historical Society
- Chronicling America (loc.gov) has some colonial-era issues; Newspapers.com limited for 1700s

### Immigration and emigration records
- New York Harbor was primary colonial port
- Pre-1906 naturalizations in Mayor's Court and Supreme Court of Judicature
- NARA for federal-era records; NYGBS for published colonial passenger indexes

### Tax records
- Ward-by-ward tax assessment rolls — primary census substitute
- FamilySearch collection: Tax Assessment Rolls, 1799-1804 (ID 1678432)
- Earlier colonial tax lists: New York City Municipal Archives and New York State Archives — physical/microfilm only

### Other record types
- New York Colonial Manuscripts (New York State Archives): council minutes, governor's correspondence, chancery records
- Freeman/guild admission records (NYGBS)
- Documentary History of the State of New York (O'Callaghan, 1849-1851) — reprints many colonial records
- Slave records in probate inventories, wills, deeds, and church baptism registers

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church Records 1640-1940 (1469062); Land Records 1630-1975 (2078654); Probate Records 1629-1971 (1542780); Tax Rolls 1799-1804 (1678432); Dutch Reformed Registers 1700-1776 vol. 007733180 (browse-only, Dutch) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | US Federal Census (earliest 1790); additional collections | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War service and pension records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records including Trinity Churchyard | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records and finding aids | Free/partial |
| Chronicling America (loc.gov) | Colonial-era New York newspapers | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers — limited 18th-century NYC coverage | Subscription |

**Coverage note:** volume_search returned 1 total digitized volume at the NYC level for 1700-1800. Much colonial material is indexed at the state scope in collections_search. The single volume confirmed at city level is the Dutch Reformed Church Registers (007733180).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| New York State Archives (Albany) | Colonial Manuscripts; Prerogative Court probate; land patents; militia rolls | In-person; some microfilm via FamilySearch |
| New York City Municipal Archives | Mayor's Court records; ward tax rolls; city administrative records | In-person |
| New-York Historical Society | Church transcriptions; Abstracts of Wills; colonial manuscripts; newspaper runs | In-person; some digitized |
| NYGBS | Published colonial indexes; NY Genealogical and Biographical Record | Membership; in-person library |
| Trinity Church Archives | Anglican burial registers and vestry minutes from 1697 | In-person by appointment |
| Reformed Church in America Archives (NJ) | Dutch Reformed congregational records | In-person; some on FamilySearch microfilm |
| New York State Library (Albany) | Dutch-era records; colonial imprints and newspapers | In-person |
| NARA | Revolutionary War service/pension; post-1789 naturalization | In-person or via Fold3/Ancestry |

## Records NOT online
- Colonial ward tax rolls (pre-1799)
- Mayor's Court civil case files and minute books
- Provincial Supreme Court of Judicature minutes
- Colonial militia muster rolls
- New York Colonial Manuscripts (many volumes not digitized)
- Huguenot congregation registers (partial transcriptions at NYGBS; originals at New-York Historical Society)
- Lutheran and Quaker registers
- Shearith Israel records
- Freeman/guild admission records

## Known record losses
- Revolutionary War occupation (1776-1783) caused disruption; some municipal records are missing for these years
- Dutch-period records are incomplete due to 1664 transition
- Some Prerogative Court estate files are missing
- Colonial parchment records have suffered from damp storage and handling

## Research tips
- Church registers are the vital records for this period — identify every denomination and search each separately
- Probate is filed at the provincial level (Prerogative Court), not county — use the published Abstracts of Wills first
- Colonial militia rolls are a census substitute, organized by ward
- Dutch families: the digitized FamilySearch volume (007733180) is browse-only and in Dutch — plan for translation
- Ward identification narrows tax rolls, court records, and church membership significantly
- Search the New York Genealogical and Biographical Record (NYGBS journal) for colonial transcriptions
- Check Kings, Queens, Richmond, and Westchester counties for families with connections outside lower Manhattan
- The Documentary History of the State of New York (O'Callaghan) reprints many colonial records; partially available via HathiTrust

output.text_response:
Here is the locality guide returned by the research agent:

---

# Virginia, USA — Revolutionary War Research Guide (1775–1783)

## Jurisdiction Overview

Virginia was a Colony of Great Britain until 1776, then the independent Commonwealth of Virginia. Its capital shifted from Williamsburg to Richmond in 1780. At this time, Virginia included present-day **West Virginia** (a separate state only from 1863) and the **Kentucky District** (separate state from 1792). County boundaries were actively changing throughout this period — always verify which county a locality belonged to in a given year.

---

## Key Military Record Sets

**Start here for any suspected soldier:**

- **Pension and Bounty-Land Warrant Application Files** (NARA, Record Group 15) — Available on Fold3 (subscription). These are the richest genealogical sources of the era: sworn narratives written by veterans in old age often name family members, neighbors, commanding officers, and fellow soldiers. Filed under the pension acts of 1818–1820 and 1832–1833.
- **Compiled Military Service Records (CMSRs) — Continental Line** (NARA, Record Group 93) — Muster rolls and service abstracts. Available on Fold3; partially on Ancestry.
- **Virginia Militia Records** — Held at the **Library of Virginia** (Richmond), NOT at NARA. These are separate from the Continental Line and require a separate search. Many are only partially digitized.
- **FamilySearch Collection:** "Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783" (collection 1945678) — 345,678 records, 172,839 images.
- **Virginia Bounty-Land Warrants, 1779–1800** — FamilySearch digitized volume 005301447 (341 images). ⚠️ 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image.
- **Virginia Military District of Ohio** — Post-war bounty lands set aside in south-central Ohio for Virginia veterans. Warrant and survey records at the Library of Virginia link Virginia service to Ohio land claims. If an ancestor vanished from Virginia records after the war, check here.

---

## The Most Important Substitute for the Missing Census

Virginia's **1790 federal census was largely destroyed** when the British burned Washington in 1814. The essential substitute is:

- **1782 Virginia Personal Property Tax List** — FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850" (collection 1456723, 456,789 records, 228,394 images). Digitized volume 005301449 (1782–1799) is **full-text searchable but not name-indexed** — use the full-text search interface. This is the primary tool for placing a family geographically during and immediately after the war.

---

## County-Level Records (Courts, Land, Probate)

- **FamilySearch Collections:**
  - "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900" (collection 1734285) — 2,567,890 records with images
  - "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920" (collection 2134567) — 1,789,012 records with images
- County **court order books** recorded all county business during the war — land sales, estate administration for killed soldiers, guardianship appointments for orphaned children, and naturalization.
- **Marriage bonds** (not civil registration — Virginia had no statewide birth/marriage/death registration in this era) are the primary marriage source.
- **Virginia Auditor's Public Claims Records** — Civilians who supplied food, equipment, or transport to the war effort submitted claims afterward. These records name thousands of non-soldiers. Held at the Library of Virginia; not comprehensively digitized.

---

## Church Records

- **FamilySearch Collection:** "Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929" (collection 1598230) — 1,234,567 records with images.
- Anglican **vestry books** are especially valuable: they recorded poor relief, orphan bindings, and payments — naming families of men killed or disabled in the war who appear nowhere else.
- **Denominations:** Anglican/Episcopal (most complete pre-war registers), Baptist, Presbyterian (Valley counties), Quaker (northern Virginia and Valley), Lutheran and German Reformed (Augusta, Rockingham, Shenandoah, Frederick counties — records often in **German**).
- ⚠️ Some vestry records were lost during Anglican disestablishment (1776–1786).

---

## Newspapers

- **Virginia Gazette** (Williamsburg) — The paper of record for 1775–1783; multiple competing editions. Contains military notices, runaway advertisements (naming family members), estate notices, and official proclamations. Available on **Newspapers.com** (subscription) and through university library databases.

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What's There | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Library of Virginia** (Richmond) | Virginia militia records; land office & bounty-land warrant records; confiscation/Loyalist records; Auditor's public claims; county microfilm | In-person; catalog at lva.virginia.gov; some microfilm via interlibrary loan |
| **NARA** (Washington DC / College Park) | RG 93 (Continental Line service records); RG 15 (pension & bounty-land files) | In-person or Fold3 (subscription) |
| **Virginia Museum of History and Culture** (Richmond) | Officers' orderly books; regimental records; manuscript collections | In-person |
| **FamilySearch** | Military, land, marriage, will, church, tax, court collections (all free) | Free online |
| **Fold3** | CMSRs, pension files, some militia | Subscription |

---

## Known Record Losses

- **1790 Virginia Federal Census** — largely destroyed in 1814; use 1782 tax list instead.
- **County courthouse fires** — numerous 19th–20th century losses; check each county's specific loss history before concluding a record never existed.
- **Anglican vestry records** — some lost during disestablishment of the church (1776–1786).

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with pension files** (Fold3, NARA RG 15) — the highest-priority source for any suspected soldier.
2. **Search Continental Line AND militia separately** — they are in different repositories (NARA vs. Library of Virginia).
3. **Use the 1782 tax list as your census substitute** — full-text searchable on FamilySearch (volume 005301449).
4. **Follow the bounty-land trail to Ohio** — Virginia veterans may have relocated to the Virginia Military District in south-central Ohio after the war.
5. **Check for Loyalist connections** — confiscation records at the Library of Virginia name Loyalists and their community networks.
6. **Watch county formation dates** — pre-formation records will be under the parent county.
7. **Valley German families**: Lutheran and German Reformed church registers are often in 18th-century German script — plan for translation assistance.
8. **No statewide civil registration exists for this period** — vital events are in church registers and county marriage bonds only.

---

Virginia is one of the best-documented states for early American genealogy, but records are split across the National Archives (federal military), the Library of Virginia (state militia and land), county courthouses/FamilySearch (local records), and church repositories. The single most time-saving first step for any suspected soldier is pulling his **pension application file on Fold3** — that one document frequently contains more family information than any other source of this era.
