# Locality Guide: Louisiana (French Colonial Period, 1699–1803)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1699 (French settlement); New Orleans founded 1718
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New France (France), then the Spanish Crown (1762/1769–1800/1803)
- **Population during period:** Sparse; colonial censuses recorded in the hundreds to low thousands of free settlers; enslaved population grew substantially through the 18th century
- **Economy:** Plantation agriculture (indigo, tobacco, sugar), fur trade, river commerce
- **Ethnic composition:** French colonists, Acadian exiles (arriving 1755–1785 after the Grand Derangement), Spanish administrators and settlers, German Coast settlers, enslaved Africans, and Indigenous peoples
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic exclusively under French and Spanish rule (the Code Noir prohibited other public worship)
- **Key historical events:** Founding of New Orleans (1718); Natchez massacre (1729); cession to Spain (Treaty of Fontainebleau, 1762); Spanish effective control begins (1769); arrival of Acadian exiles (1755–1785); Louisiana Purchase (1803)

## Boundary changes
- **1699–1762:** French Louisiana encompassed the entire Mississippi River basin
- **1762:** France secretly ceded Louisiana west of the Mississippi to Spain (Treaty of Fontainebleau); the eastern portion east of the river went to Britain
- **1769:** Spain takes effective administrative control; French records continue in transitional years 1762–1769
- **1800:** Spain secretly retrocedes Louisiana to France (Treaty of San Ildefonso)
- **1803:** Louisiana Purchase transfers the territory to the United States
- **Critical research implication:** Records from the same territory fall under French record-keeping (pre-1769), Spanish record-keeping (1769–1803), and then U.S. systems (post-1803). Researchers must search all three series for families spanning these transitions.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Civil registration did not exist during the French or Spanish colonial period. The FamilySearch Wiki Louisiana Vital Records page returned only generic content and does not state a specific start date for Louisiana statewide civil registration. The Catholic sacramental registers are the sole vital record series for the 1700s.
- **What exists:** No civil birth, marriage, or death certificates for the colonial period
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) — the primary and essential source for all vital events during this period

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (exclusively; other denominations were legally prohibited under French and Spanish rule)
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including of enslaved persons under the Code Noir), marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Earliest records:** St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans — registers from 1720 (FamilySearch image group 004330991, 264 images, covering 1720–1803)
- **Where held:**
  - Archdiocesan Archives of New Orleans (local parishes and New Orleans registers)
  - FamilySearch has 1 digitized volume of Archdiocese of New Orleans sacramental registers (image group 004330991, 1720–1803): **browse-only, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable, in French and Spanish**
  - FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905) covers the broader period
- **Language:** French (1720–1769); Spanish and French (1769–1803)
- **Critical note:** This is the single most important record type for the colonial period. Every free and enslaved person was expected to have a Catholic baptismal record. Researchers must browse images page by page — there is no name index for the colonial-era volumes.

### Census records
- **Colonial censuses:** France and Spain conducted administrative censuses of the colony. These are held at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France, and partially at the Louisiana Historical Center. They are not enumerated in FamilySearch's main indexed collections for this period.
- **Federal census:** Louisiana entered the Union in 1812; the first federal census covering it as a state is 1820. The 1790 and 1800 federal censuses do not cover Louisiana.
- **Other enumerations:** Spanish colonial census rolls (padrones) exist for the late 18th century and are partially held at the Louisiana Historical Center
- **Access:** Physical repositories; limited digitization

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Estate inventories, succession records, guardianships, court proceedings — all conducted through the Superior Council (Conseil Superieur) under French rule and its Spanish successor courts
- **Date range:** Superior Council records from 1699–1769
- **Where held:** Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans — partially digitized
- **FamilySearch:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (collection 2078341) overlaps the end of the colonial period from 1756
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Image group 004330992 — 149 images of French colonial notarial acts and Superior Council records, 1699–1769. **Browse-only, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable, in French and Spanish.**
- **Legal tradition:** Louisiana used French civil law and later Spanish civil law — not English common law. Estate proceedings followed different conventions from other American colonies.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French and Spanish metes-and-bounds grants (concessions and arpent system), NOT the U.S. rectangular survey system
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Under France, the Superior Council granted concessions. Under Spain, the governor's office issued Spanish land grants.
- **Types:** French concessions (land grants), Spanish land grants, notarial contracts, mortgage records
- **Where held:**
  - New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center — contracts, marriage settlements, property transactions from the 1730s onward (oldest continuous notarial office in North America)
  - Louisiana State Land Office
  - American State Papers: Public Lands series (for grants confirmed after the Louisiana Purchase)
  - FamilySearch Wiki notes colonial land grants are documented in the American State Papers, not the BLM General Land Office used for English-law states ([Louisiana Land and Property](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants))
- **Access:** In-person or written inquiry for notarial archives; American State Papers available in digitized form through various libraries

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** King William's War / Queen Anne's War aftermath; French-Indian conflicts; Natchez War (1729); American Revolution (Spain allied with the colonies)
- **Record types:** French colonial militia rolls; Spanish military service records
- **Where held:** Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France; Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain (for Spanish-period records); Louisiana Historical Center
- **Access:** Physical repositories in France and Spain; some microfilm at research libraries

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1, New Orleans (est. 1789, at the end of the colonial period); earlier burials were on church grounds
- **Online coverage:** Some coverage on Find A Grave (findagrave.com)
- **Physical records:** Burial registers are part of the Catholic sacramental records series

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The first Louisiana newspaper (Le Moniteur de la Louisiane) did not begin until 1794, very late in the colonial period
- **Content value:** Minimal for the colonial period; legal notices and announcements
- **Where held:** Louisiana State University libraries; Library of Congress Chronicling America project

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans (primary entry point for the colony)
- **Record types:** Ship passenger lists for colonial-era arrivals; Acadian exile passenger lists (1755–1785)
- **Where held:** Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence holds French administrative records of colonist arrivals; NARA holds later U.S.-era passenger lists
- **Content note:** Passenger lists for the French colonial period are administrative documents, not standardized manifests. Acadian deportation and resettlement records are a specialized subfield with extensive scholarship.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Colonial tax and census rolls conducted by French and Spanish authorities
- **Date range:** Sporadic throughout the colonial period
- **Where held:** ANOM (France) and Louisiana Historical Center
- **Substitute value:** Colonial census/tax rolls can substitute for missing family data

### Notarial records (unique to Louisiana)
- **This record type is specific to Louisiana's civil-law tradition and has no equivalent in English-law states.**
- **Types:** Marriage contracts, wills and testaments, property sales, powers of attorney, apprenticeship agreements, manumission documents
- **Date range:** 1730s onward at the New Orleans Notarial Archives
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (public access)
- **Value:** These records often contain detailed personal and family information not found in church or court records

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905); "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (collection 2078341); 2 digitized browse-only volumes (image groups 004330991 and 004330992) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census collection (begins 1820 for Louisiana); limited colonial coverage | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Post-1803 federal records; some territorial records | Free/fee |

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes (totalResults: 2) for the 1700–1803 period — this is the complete set. Both are browse-only with no name index and contain records in French and Spanish.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) | Superior Council records 1699–1769; Spanish colonial records; partial notarial records | In-person; some digitized |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial acts from 1730s onward | In-person; public access |
| Archdiocesan Archives, Archdiocese of New Orleans | Parish sacramental registers | In-person or written inquiry |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial administrative records, census rolls, passenger lists | In-person; partial online access via archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial administrative records for the 1769–1803 period | In-person; partial digitization through PARES portal |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Post-1803 state records; some territorial-era holdings | In-person / online request |
| New Orleans Public Library, Louisiana Division | City and colonial records; historical maps | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- The vast majority of French colonial sacramental registers outside New Orleans (rural parishes, mission stations) are held only at individual parishes or the Archdiocesan Archives — not digitized
- Spanish colonial census rolls (padrones) beyond what ANOM holds partially online
- Most French colonial correspondence and administrative files at ANOM
- Archivo General de Indias Spanish-period Louisiana records (partially accessible via the PARES portal but largely requiring in-person visits)
- New Orleans Notarial Archives records prior to what has been microfilmed

## Known record losses
- The transition from French to Spanish administration (1762–1769) created administrative disruption; some records from this transitional period are incomplete
- Hurricane and flood damage to New Orleans over the centuries has affected some physical holdings
- No systematic destruction event comparable to courthouse fires in other states has been documented for the core colonial archives, but rural parish records outside New Orleans are unevenly preserved

## Research tips
- **Catholic records are the foundation.** The Catholic Church was the only legal church under French and Spanish rule. Every vital event — baptism, marriage, burial — should appear in Catholic registers. Begin there before looking elsewhere. ([Louisiana Genealogy, French Colonial Records section](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records))
- **Search in both French and Spanish.** French records dominate 1699–1769; Spanish records dominate 1769–1803. Families spanning the transition appear in both series, under different name spellings and in different languages.
- **The notarial archives are essential, not optional.** Louisiana's civil-law tradition means that events handled by contracts in other states (marriage settlements, wills, property sales, manumissions) went through a notary. The New Orleans Notarial Archives hold records from the 1730s and are open to the public. ([Louisiana Land and Property, Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants))
- **Look to France and Spain for administrative records.** The ANOM in Aix-en-Provence and the Archivo General de Indias in Seville hold the colonial governors' correspondence, military rosters, census rolls, and passenger lists that document settlers who rarely appear in local church records.
- **Browse FamilySearch volumes image by image.** Both digitized FamilySearch volumes for this period (image groups 004330991 and 004330992) are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. There is no shortcut — researchers must work through the images sequentially or use external finding aids.
- **The Code Noir and enslaved ancestors.** The French and Spanish Code Noir required Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons. Baptismal entries for enslaved individuals appear in the same registers as free persons, making the sacramental registers a primary source for tracing African American ancestry in Louisiana to the colonial period.
- **Acadian families.** If researching Acadian (Cajun) ancestry, note that Acadian exiles arrived in Louisiana in waves from 1755 to 1785 following the British deportation from Nova Scotia. Specialized Acadian databases and the Centre d'etudes acadiennes (Universite de Moncton, New Brunswick) hold complementary records.
- **Name spellings vary widely.** French names were often rendered differently by Spanish clerks and vice versa; the same individual may appear under variant spellings across the transition. Search phonetically and consider both French and Spanish equivalents.
- **American State Papers.** After the Louisiana Purchase, the U.S. Congress confirmed or rejected colonial land grants. The American State Papers: Public Lands series records these proceedings and names families holding land under French and Spanish grants — a useful cross-reference even for pre-1803 research.

The Spanish colonial period (1769-1803) produced its own notarial and ecclesiastical records in Spanish; researchers must read both French and Spanish to cover the full 1700s.

The Catholic Church was the only legally recognized church under French and Spanish rule; all vital events (baptisms, marriages, burials) are in Catholic sacramental registers — there are no Protestant or civil registration alternatives for this period.

Under the Code Noir, the Catholic Church was required to baptize enslaved persons; those baptismal entries appear in the same sacramental registers as free persons and are a primary source for enslaved ancestor research.
FamilySearch holds 2 digitized volumes covering this period (image groups 004330991 and 004330992); both are browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) and in French and Spanish.
The Archdiocese of New Orleans sacramental registers begin in 1720 at St. Louis Cathedral. Registers for parishes outside New Orleans are held at individual parishes and the Archdiocesan Archives.

The Superior Council (Conseil Superieur) records (1699-1769) are held at the Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) and have been partially digitized. They include land grants, estate inventories, court proceedings, and contracts.

The Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France holds administrative correspondence and colonial census rolls for French Louisiana — essential for families who never appear in local church or notarial records.
Louisiana uses a civil-law (Napoleonic) tradition inherited from France and Spain, not English common law; probate and property records follow different legal conventions from other U.S. states.

The New Orleans Notarial Archives (oldest continuous notarial office in North America) holds contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions from the 1730s onward and provides public access.

French and Spanish land grants in Louisiana are documented in the American State Papers: Public Lands series and at the Louisiana State Land Office — not at the Bureau of Land Management GLO used for English-law states.
Colonial-era records are in French (1699-1769) and Spanish (1769-1803); researchers must be prepared to work in both languages or hire a translator.
added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Louisiana (French Colonial Period, 1699–1803)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1699 (French settlement); New Orleans founded 1718
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New France (France), then the Spanish Crown (1762/1769–1800/1803)
- **Population during period:** Sparse; colonial censuses recorded in the hundreds to low thousands of free settlers; enslaved population grew substantially through the 18th century
- **Economy:** Plantation agriculture (indigo, tobacco, sugar), fur trade, river commerce
- **Ethnic composition:** French colonists, Acadian exiles (arriving 1755–1785 after the Grand Derangement), Spanish administrators and settlers, German Coast settlers, enslaved Africans, and Indigenous peoples
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic exclusively under French and Spanish rule (the Code Noir prohibited other public worship)
- **Key historical events:** Founding of New Orleans (1718); Natchez massacre (1729); cession to Spain (Treaty of Fontainebleau, 1762); Spanish effective control begins (1769); arrival of Acadian exiles (1755–1785); Louisiana Purchase (1803)

## Boundary changes
- **1699–1762:** French Louisiana encompassed the entire Mississippi River basin
- **1762:** France secretly ceded Louisiana west of the Mississippi to Spain (Treaty of Fontainebleau); the eastern portion east of the river went to Britain
- **1769:** Spain takes effective administrative control; French records continue in transitional years 1762–1769
- **1800:** Spain secretly retrocedes Louisiana to France (Treaty of San Ildefonso)
- **1803:** Louisiana Purchase transfers the territory to the United States
- **Critical research implication:** Records from the same territory fall under French record-keeping (pre-1769), Spanish record-keeping (1769–1803), and then U.S. systems (post-1803). Researchers must search all three series for families spanning these transitions.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Civil registration did not exist during the French or Spanish colonial period. The FamilySearch Wiki Louisiana Vital Records page returned only generic content and does not state a specific start date for Louisiana statewide civil registration. The Catholic sacramental registers are the sole vital record series for the 1700s.
- **What exists:** No civil birth, marriage, or death certificates for the colonial period
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) — the primary and essential source for all vital events during this period

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (exclusively; other denominations were legally prohibited under French and Spanish rule)
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including of enslaved persons under the Code Noir), marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Earliest records:** St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans — registers from 1720 (FamilySearch image group 004330991, 264 images, covering 1720–1803)
- **Where held:**
  - Archdiocesan Archives of New Orleans (local parishes and New Orleans registers)
  - FamilySearch has 1 digitized volume of Archdiocese of New Orleans sacramental registers (image group 004330991, 1720–1803): **browse-only, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable, in French and Spanish**
  - FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905) covers the broader period
- **Language:** French (1720–1769); Spanish and French (1769–1803)
- **Critical note:** This is the single most important record type for the colonial period. Every free and enslaved person was expected to have a Catholic baptismal record. Researchers must browse images page by page — there is no name index for the colonial-era volumes.

### Census records
- **Colonial censuses:** France and Spain conducted administrative censuses of the colony. These are held at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France, and partially at the Louisiana Historical Center. They are not enumerated in FamilySearch's main indexed collections for this period.
- **Federal census:** Louisiana entered the Union in 1812; the first federal census covering it as a state is 1820. The 1790 and 1800 federal censuses do not cover Louisiana.
- **Other enumerations:** Spanish colonial census rolls (padrones) exist for the late 18th century and are partially held at the Louisiana Historical Center
- **Access:** Physical repositories; limited digitization

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Estate inventories, succession records, guardianships, court proceedings — all conducted through the Superior Council (Conseil Superieur) under French rule and its Spanish successor courts
- **Date range:** Superior Council records from 1699–1769
- **Where held:** Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans — partially digitized
- **FamilySearch:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (collection 2078341) overlaps the end of the colonial period from 1756
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Image group 004330992 — 149 images of French colonial notarial acts and Superior Council records, 1699–1769. **Browse-only, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable, in French and Spanish.**
- **Legal tradition:** Louisiana used French civil law and later Spanish civil law — not English common law. Estate proceedings followed different conventions from other American colonies.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French and Spanish metes-and-bounds grants (concessions and arpent system), NOT the U.S. rectangular survey system
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Under France, the Superior Council granted concessions. Under Spain, the governor's office issued Spanish land grants.
- **Types:** French concessions (land grants), Spanish land grants, notarial contracts, mortgage records
- **Where held:**
  - New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center — contracts, marriage settlements, property transactions from the 1730s onward (oldest continuous notarial office in North America)
  - Louisiana State Land Office
  - American State Papers: Public Lands series (for grants confirmed after the Louisiana Purchase)
  - FamilySearch Wiki notes colonial land grants are documented in the American State Papers, not the BLM General Land Office used for English-law states ([Louisiana Land and Property](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants))
- **Access:** In-person or written inquiry for notarial archives; American State Papers available in digitized form through various libraries

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** King William's War / Queen Anne's War aftermath; French-Indian conflicts; Natchez War (1729); American Revolution (Spain allied with the colonies)
- **Record types:** French colonial militia rolls; Spanish military service records
- **Where held:** Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France; Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain (for Spanish-period records); Louisiana Historical Center
- **Access:** Physical repositories in France and Spain; some microfilm at research libraries

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1, New Orleans (est. 1789, at the end of the colonial period); earlier burials were on church grounds
- **Online coverage:** Some coverage on Find A Grave (findagrave.com)
- **Physical records:** Burial registers are part of the Catholic sacramental records series

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The first Louisiana newspaper (Le Moniteur de la Louisiane) did not begin until 1794, very late in the colonial period
- **Content value:** Minimal for the colonial period; legal notices and announcements
- **Where held:** Louisiana State University libraries; Library of Congress Chronicling America project

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans (primary entry point for the colony)
- **Record types:** Ship passenger lists for colonial-era arrivals; Acadian exile passenger lists (1755–1785)
- **Where held:** Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence holds French administrative records of colonist arrivals; NARA holds later U.S.-era passenger lists
- **Content note:** Passenger lists for the French colonial period are administrative documents, not standardized manifests. Acadian deportation and resettlement records are a specialized subfield with extensive scholarship.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Colonial tax and census rolls conducted by French and Spanish authorities
- **Date range:** Sporadic throughout the colonial period
- **Where held:** ANOM (France) and Louisiana Historical Center
- **Substitute value:** Colonial census/tax rolls can substitute for missing family data

### Notarial records (unique to Louisiana)
- **This record type is specific to Louisiana's civil-law tradition and has no equivalent in English-law states.**
- **Types:** Marriage contracts, wills and testaments, property sales, powers of attorney, apprenticeship agreements, manumission documents
- **Date range:** 1730s onward at the New Orleans Notarial Archives
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (public access)
- **Value:** These records often contain detailed personal and family information not found in church or court records

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905); "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (collection 2078341); 2 digitized browse-only volumes (image groups 004330991 and 004330992) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census collection (begins 1820 for Louisiana); limited colonial coverage | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Post-1803 federal records; some territorial records | Free/fee |

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes (totalResults: 2) for the 1700–1803 period — this is the complete set. Both are browse-only with no name index and contain records in French and Spanish.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) | Superior Council records 1699–1769; Spanish colonial records; partial notarial records | In-person; some digitized |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial acts from 1730s onward | In-person; public access |
| Archdiocesan Archives, Archdiocese of New Orleans | Parish sacramental registers | In-person or written inquiry |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial administrative records, census rolls, passenger lists | In-person; partial online access via archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial administrative records for the 1769–1803 period | In-person; partial digitization through PARES portal |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Post-1803 state records; some territorial-era holdings | In-person / online request |
| New Orleans Public Library, Louisiana Division | City and colonial records; historical maps | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- The vast majority of French colonial sacramental registers outside New Orleans (rural parishes, mission stations) are held only at individual parishes or the Archdiocesan Archives — not digitized
- Spanish colonial census rolls (padrones) beyond what ANOM holds partially online
- Most French colonial correspondence and administrative files at ANOM
- Archivo General de Indias Spanish-period Louisiana records (partially accessible via the PARES portal but largely requiring in-person visits)
- New Orleans Notarial Archives records prior to what has been microfilmed

## Known record losses
- The transition from French to Spanish administration (1762–1769) created administrative disruption; some records from this transitional period are incomplete
- Hurricane and flood damage to New Orleans over the centuries has affected some physical holdings
- No systematic destruction event comparable to courthouse fires in other states has been documented for the core colonial archives, but rural parish records outside New Orleans are unevenly preserved

## Research tips
- **Catholic records are the foundation.** The Catholic Church was the only legal church under French and Spanish rule. Every vital event — baptism, marriage, burial — should appear in Catholic registers. Begin there before looking elsewhere. ([Louisiana Genealogy, French Colonial Records section](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records))
- **Search in both French and Spanish.** French records dominate 1699–1769; Spanish records dominate 1769–1803. Families spanning the transition appear in both series, under different name spellings and in different languages.
- **The notarial archives are essential, not optional.** Louisiana's civil-law tradition means that events handled by contracts in other states (marriage settlements, wills, property sales, manumissions) went through a notary. The New Orleans Notarial Archives hold records from the 1730s and are open to the public. ([Louisiana Land and Property, Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants))
- **Look to France and Spain for administrative records.** The ANOM in Aix-en-Provence and the Archivo General de Indias in Seville hold the colonial governors' correspondence, military rosters, census rolls, and passenger lists that document settlers who rarely appear in local church records.
- **Browse FamilySearch volumes image by image.** Both digitized FamilySearch volumes for this period (image groups 004330991 and 004330992) are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. There is no shortcut — researchers must work through the images sequentially or use external finding aids.
- **The Code Noir and enslaved ancestors.** The French and Spanish Code Noir required Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons. Baptismal entries for enslaved individuals appear in the same registers as free persons, making the sacramental registers a primary source for tracing African American ancestry in Louisiana to the colonial period.
- **Acadian families.** If researching Acadian (Cajun) ancestry, note that Acadian exiles arrived in Louisiana in waves from 1755 to 1785 following the British deportation from Nova Scotia. Specialized Acadian databases and the Centre d'etudes acadiennes (Universite de Moncton, New Brunswick) hold complementary records.
- **Name spellings vary widely.** French names were often rendered differently by Spanish clerks and vice versa; the same individual may appear under variant spellings across the transition. Search phonetically and consider both French and Spanish equivalents.
- **American State Papers.** After the Louisiana Purchase, the U.S. Congress confirmed or rejected colonial land grants. The American State Papers: Public Lands series records these proceedings and names families holding land under French and Spanish grants — a useful cross-reference even for pre-1803 research.

Here is the locality guide produced for Pennsylvania coal mining town research:

---

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Mining Region (Late 1800s)

## Jurisdiction Overview

**Core counties:** Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna (formed from Luzerne in 1878), Carbon, and Northumberland
**County seats:** Pottsville (Schuylkill), Wilkes-Barre (Luzerne), Scranton (Lackawanna)

**Key boundary change:** Lackawanna County was carved from Luzerne County on **August 13, 1878**. Events in the Scranton area before that date are filed under Luzerne County — deeds, probate, court records, and naturalizations.

**Ethnic composition:** Irish and Welsh miners (1820s–1860s), followed by large waves from Poland, Lithuania, Slovakia, Ukraine, and Italy (1870s–1900s).

---

## The Single Most Important Warning

Pennsylvania did **not** require statewide civil registration of births and deaths until **1906**. For the entire 1850–1905 window, you are almost entirely dependent on **ethnic parish church registers** for birth and death information. Identifying the correct national parish — not just geographic location — is the prerequisite step, since multiple co-located national parishes could serve families on the same street.

---

## Key Record Types

### Vital Records
- **Births & Deaths before 1906:** Church registers only (see Church Records below)
- **Deaths from 1906:** *Pennsylvania Death Certificates* (FamilySearch collection 2255317) — 4.2M records, indexed + images, free
- **Marriages:** Three FamilySearch collections cover Pennsylvania marriages:
  - *PA County Marriages, 1885–1950* (524,189 records, indexed + images, free)
  - *PA Civil Marriages, 1677–1950* (312,045 records, indexed + images, free)
  - *PA Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900* (198,765 records, name index only)

### Church Records — *Essential Substitute for Civil Vital Records*
- Determine ethnic background and denomination **first**, then select the right parish
- **Catholic parishes by ethnicity:** Irish, Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Italian → Diocese of Scranton Archives; Ukrainian/Ruthenian → Byzantine Ruthenian Diocese Archives
- **Protestant:** Welsh Congregational/Methodist records at local chapels or Historical Society of Schuylkill County; Lutheran records at Lutheran Archives Center, Philadelphia; Presbyterian at Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and confirmations (a separate dated event providing an independent age/residence record)
- **FamilySearch:** *Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records* — 1.2M records, 607K images, indexed + images, free (verify holdings at FamilySearch)

### Census Records
- Federal censuses for **1850, 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900, and 1910** are fully indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry
- **1890 census is destroyed** — substitute with 1889–1891 tax lists and city directories
- **1880 mortality schedules** list individuals who died in the prior 12 months, including mine accident victims — the last mortality schedule before civil death registration
- No Pennsylvania state census was conducted during this period

### Mining-Specific Records — *Unique to This Region*
- **Mine Inspector Reports (1870 onward):** Published annually by Pennsylvania; list fatal accident victims by name, age, and nationality. Held at Pennsylvania State Archives; some volumes digitized. Critical for immigrant miners who left few other records
- **Mine Worker Employment Cards (Schuylkill Co., 1870–1900):** FamilySearch vol. 002240015 — 410 images, **95% name-indexed and full-text searchable**
- **Mine Accident Reports (Luzerne Co., 1870–1895):** FamilySearch vol. 002240016 — 287 images, **browse-only** (no name index)
- **Colliery Payroll Ledgers (Lackawanna Co., 1878–1900):** FamilySearch vol. 002240017 — 199 images, **browse-only**
- **Note:** The volume search returned only 3 of 23 digitized volumes for this region; 20 additional volumes were not cataloged in this survey

### Probate & Court Records
- **Probate:** *Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994* (FamilySearch, 3.2M images, **browse-only**) — filed at the county level
- **Naturalizations (pre-1906):** Could be filed in any court of record; Schuylkill County naturalizations at Pennsylvania State Archives. Declarations of Intention ("first papers") often give the precise European village of origin
- **Post-1906 naturalizations:** Federal courts only; NARA Philadelphia (RG 21), increasingly indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch

### Newspapers
- ***Miners' Journal*** (Pottsville, 1825–present): Most important regional paper — obituaries, accident reports, marriage notices, labor news. Well-preserved archive; digitized on Newspapers.com (subscription)
- **Ethnic-language papers** (Polish *Górnik*, Welsh-language sheets): Carry community news and death notices not in English papers; microfilm at Pennsylvania State Library and local societies
- **Obituaries in ethnic parish bulletins** frequently give the European village of origin — information found nowhere else

### Immigration Records
- **Passenger lists:** Ancestry (subscription) and FamilySearch (free) for pre-1892; Ellis Island records (1892–1957) free at libertyellisfoundation.org
- **Tip:** Search the entire manifest page, not just the named individual — chain migrants from the same European village typically traveled together
- **Primary ports:** Philadelphia, New York (Castle Garden/Ellis Island from 1892), and Baltimore

### Cemetery Records
- FindAGrave covers major Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Lackawanna county cemeteries with headstone photos (free)
- Sexton records vary; held at individual cemeteries or associated congregations

### Tax Records
- County property and personal property tax lists survive from the early 19th century
- **Best substitute for the missing 1890 federal census**
- Held at county archives and Pennsylvania State Archives

### Military Records
- **Civil War:** Service records and pension files at NARA (RG 94, RG 15); Pennsylvania State Archives for regimental records; Fold3 (subscription)
- **WWI Draft Registration (1917–1918):** Captures men born 1870s–1890s; fully indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry — useful for confirming birthplace information

---

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Mining Region (1850-1910)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Core counties:** Schuylkill (formed 1811), Luzerne (1786), Lackawanna (1878, formed from Luzerne), Carbon, and Northumberland
- **County seats:** Pottsville (Schuylkill), Wilkes-Barre (Luzerne), Scranton (Lackawanna)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Commonwealth of Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the population tool for this jurisdiction; consult the Pennsylvania State Archives and the decennial U.S. federal censuses (1850, 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900) directly
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated. The region supplied the bulk of the nation's hard coal. Mining companies maintained payrolls, employment cards, and accident logs as routine administrative records
- **Ethnic composition:** Initial waves of Irish and Welsh miners (1820s-1860s), followed by large-scale immigration from Poland, Lithuania, Slovakia, Ukraine, and Italy (1870s-1900s). German settlers also present. Ethnic identity is a primary research key — identifying a family's exact nationality determines which church kept their vital records
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (Irish, Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Italian parishes), Welsh Congregational and Methodist, Presbyterian, Episcopal, Lutheran, Eastern Rite/Greek Catholic (Ukrainian and Ruthenian), Baptist, and various Protestant immigrant congregations
- **Key historical events:** Molly Maguires trials (1875-1877, Schuylkill County); Great Railroad Strike of 1877; formation of United Mine Workers of America (1890); Lattimer Massacre (1897, Luzerne County); Anthracite Coal Strike (1902)

## Boundary changes

- **Critical split:** Lackawanna County was carved from Luzerne County on **August 13, 1878**. Scranton-area families researched before that date must be sought under Luzerne County — court records, deeds, probate, and naturalizations filed before 1878 in the Scranton area are Luzerne County records, not Lackawanna. After 1878, Scranton records fall under Lackawanna County
- **Schuylkill County** has been stable at its 1811 boundaries through the target period
- **Carbon County** was formed from Northampton and Monroe counties in 1843; pre-1843 Carbon County records are in those parent jurisdictions

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Registration levels and start dates:** The FamilySearch wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records did not return jurisdiction-specific content on this survey run. Based on the FamilySearch collections returned: Pennsylvania Death Certificates (collection 2255317) begin **1906**, indicating statewide civil death registration began no earlier than that year. No indexed statewide birth or death collection for the pre-1906 period appeared in tool results. County-level marriage registration is documented in collections beginning **1677/1885** (see Marriage section below)
- **Pre-1906 births and deaths:** Church registers are the primary and often only source for births (baptisms) and deaths (burials) before statewide civil registration. Do not assume a birth or death record exists in a county courthouse for events before 1906
- **Marriages:** FamilySearch holds three collections covering Pennsylvania marriages:
  - *Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950* (collection 1921317): 524,189 records, 312,045 images — indexed + images, free at FamilySearch
  - *Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950* (collection 1571957): 312,045 records, 156,023 images — indexed + images
  - *Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900* (collection 1502909): 198,765 records, no images — name index only, no images online
- **Gaps:** No statewide civil birth or death registration collection for the 1850-1905 period appeared in tool results. This is the single largest gap for this research window

### Church records

Church records are the **essential** substitute for absent civil vital records and often the richest source of family data in this region. Identifying the correct ethnic parish is the prerequisite step.

- **Denominations and record languages:**
  - Irish Catholic parishes: English-language registers; Diocese of Scranton (est. 1868) and Diocese of Allentown archives
  - Welsh Congregational and Methodist: English; local chapel records, often held by the congregation or the Historical Society of Schuylkill County
  - Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak Catholic: Latin registers with Polish/Lithuanian/Slovak marginalia; Diocese of Scranton
  - Ukrainian/Ruthenian Greek Catholic: Church Slavonic or Ukrainian; Byzantine Ruthenian Diocese archives
  - Italian Catholic: Latin/Italian; Diocese of Scranton
  - Lutheran (German): German-language registers for earlier decades, shifting to English; Lutheran Archives Center at Philadelphia
  - Presbyterian and other Protestant: English; Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia

- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and (for Catholic parishes) confirmations — confirmations are a separate dated event and appear years after baptism, providing an independent age and residence record

- **FamilySearch holdings:** The collection *Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records* (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1708-1985) returned in the survey with 1,245,830 records and 607,220 images — **indexed + images**, free at FamilySearch. Note this collection's ID carries a "synthetic test fixture" label; verify actual holdings at familysearch.org/search/collection/SYNTH-PA-CHURCH before relying on this count

- **Where else held:** Diocese of Scranton archives; Lutheran Archives Center at Philadelphia; local parishes (many still hold original registers); Historical Society of Schuylkill County; Anthracite Heritage Museum, Scranton

- **Critical research tip:** Many immigrant parishes organized along ethnic lines, not geography — two families living on the same street in Shenandoah or Hazleton could belong to different national parishes with separate registers. Determine the family's exact ethnic background before selecting a parish to search ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Mining Community Sources](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))

### Census records

- **Federal census:** Decennial enumerations for 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900, and 1910 all cover this region and are fully indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry. The 1890 federal census was almost entirely destroyed by fire — 1889 and 1891 tax lists and city directories are the best substitutes
- **Mortality schedules:** The 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 federal mortality schedules list individuals who died in the twelve months preceding the census — particularly valuable before civil death registration. Mine accident victims frequently appear. The 1880 mortality schedule is the last
- **Occupation column:** From 1880 onward, the census occupation column reliably captures "miner," "mine laborer," "breaker boy," and related roles. Cross-referencing occupation with birthplace and neighbor clusters identifies entire immigrant communities
- **No Pennsylvania state census** was conducted during this period — the federal decennials are the only enumerations available
- **Access:** All surviving federal censuses for this period are indexed + images on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription)

### Occupational and mining-specific records

This is the record class unique to the coal region and should be searched alongside standard genealogical sources.

- **Mine Inspector Reports (Pennsylvania, 1870 onward):** Published annually by the state. List fatal accidents with the victim's name, age, nationality, and cause of death. Held at the Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; some volumes digitized. Invaluable for identifying immigrant miners who died before leaving other records ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Coal Mining Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining))

- **Mine Worker Employment Cards (Schuylkill County, 1870-1900):** FamilySearch volume 002240015 — 410 images, **95% name-indexed and full-text searchable** — the most accessible mining-specific record set in the survey. Search at FamilySearch using the image group number

- **Mine Accident Reports (Luzerne County, 1870-1895):** FamilySearch volume 002240016 — 287 images, **0% indexed, not full-text searchable** — browse-only image by image. No name search possible; must be read sequentially

- **Colliery Payroll Ledgers (Lackawanna County, 1878-1900):** FamilySearch volume 002240017 — 199 images, **0% indexed, not full-text searchable** — browse-only. Records begin 1878, the year Lackawanna County was formed

- **Survey coverage note:** The volume search returned 3 volumes from a total of 23 matches (first page only; a second page exists under token PA_COAL_REGION_PAGE_2). The 20 additional volumes were not examined in this survey. Request a deeper search to see the full set

- **Company records (fragmentary):** Payroll ledgers and employment records of individual mining companies survive unevenly. The Pennsylvania State Archives, the Historical Society of Schuylkill County, and the Anthracite Heritage Museum in Scranton hold the largest collections. No comprehensive online index exists

- **UMWA records:** The United Mine Workers of America (founded 1890) membership rolls and grievance files are a source for the 1890-1910 window. Contact the UMWA archives or the Pennsylvania State Archives

### Probate and court records

- **Probate:** FamilySearch collection *Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994* (1999196) holds 3,200,560 images — **browse-only** (0 indexed records). Images must be browsed by county volume. Wills, administrations, inventories, and guardianships are all included. Filed at the county level: Pottsville (Schuylkill), Wilkes-Barre (Luzerne), Scranton (Lackawanna)
- **Court records:** Naturalizations (pre-1906) were filed in any Pennsylvania court of record — Common Pleas, Orphans' Court, or federal courts. Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s-1906) are at the Pennsylvania State Archives ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Mining Community Sources](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))
- **Post-1906 naturalizations:** After September 27, 1906, naturalizations were centralized in federal courts only. Records are at NARA Philadelphia (RG 21) and increasingly indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch

### Land records

- **Pennsylvania is a state-land state** — land was granted through the Commonwealth, not the federal land office, so there are no BLM General Land Office patents for this region
- **Deeds and mortgages:** Filed at the county Recorder of Deeds. Mining-town workers often rented company housing rather than owning land, so deed records may be sparse for individual families, but company land transfer records can document when families were resident in a patch town
- **Tax records:** County property and personal property tax lists survive from the early 19th century and are held at county archives and the Pennsylvania State Archives. They substitute for missing census years and confirm residence

### Military records

- **Civil War (1861-1865):** Many miners served. Pennsylvania served extensively; records include service records (NARA RG 94), pension files (NARA RG 15), and the Pennsylvania State Archives' regimental records. Irish and Welsh miners formed specific ethnic units
- **Spanish-American War (1898):** Pennsylvania volunteers; records at NARA and Pennsylvania State Archives
- **No draft-era conflict falls squarely in the 1850-1910 window** except for the Civil War; WWI draft registration (1917-1918) falls outside the window but captures men born in the 1870s-1890s and is fully indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry
- **Where held:** NARA (service and pension records), Fold3 (digitized military records, subscription), Pennsylvania State Archives (state-level records)

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Each mining town had Catholic, Protestant, and often ethnic-specific sections or separate cemeteries. Miners' Union cemeteries exist in some patches
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com, free) covers major cemeteries in Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Lackawanna counties with many headstone photographs. BillionGraves offers additional coverage
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers vary by cemetery; many survive at the cemetery or with the associated congregation
- **Mine disaster burials:** Mass graves and memorial sections exist at several county cemeteries following major mine disasters; Historical Society of Schuylkill County holds documentation

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The *Miners' Journal* (Pottsville, 1825-present) is the region's most important paper — contains obituaries, marriage notices, mine accident reports, legal notices, and labor news. The *Scranton Tribune* and *Wilkes-Barre Record* cover their respective counties
- **Ethnic press:** Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Ukrainian, and Welsh-language newspapers circulated in the region and carried community news, death notices, and immigrant correspondence not found in English-language papers. Titles include *Górnik* (Polish miners' paper) and various Welsh-language sheets
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (subscription) holds digitized regional papers; the Pennsylvania State Library and local historical societies hold microfilm. The *Miners' Journal* archive is particularly well preserved
- **Content value:** Obituaries in ethnic parish bulletins and local papers frequently give the European village of origin — information not captured in any official record

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Ports of entry:** Philadelphia and New York (Castle Garden / Ellis Island from 1892) were the primary arrival points for coal-region immigrants. Baltimore was also used by Central and Eastern European arrivals
- **Passenger lists:** Fully indexed on Ancestry and partially on FamilySearch (free) and MyHeritage. Ellis Island records (1892-1957) are free at libertyellisfoundation.org. Pre-1892 New York arrivals are indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch
- **Naturalization records:** Schuylkill County naturalizations (1840s-1906) are at the Pennsylvania State Archives. Post-1906 records are at NARA Philadelphia. Declarations of intention ("first papers") were filed 2+ years before the final petition and often give the European birthplace more precisely than any other document
- **Passport applications:** State Department passport records (NARA) begin providing detailed family data from the 1860s. Miners applying to visit European relatives are documented here
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard including infants traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest page for siblings, traveling companions, and neighbors — chain migrants from the same European village typically traveled together and can be identified in clusters

### Tax records

- **Types:** County property tax, personal property tax, and poll/occupation tax lists
- **Date range:** Survive from early 19th century for established coal counties
- **Where held:** County archives (courthouse) and Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the best substitute for the destroyed 1890 federal census and fill gaps in years between decennial enumerations

### Occupational and organizational records (additional)

- **Molly Maguires trial records (1875-1877):** Schuylkill County courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives. Contain names of accused, witnesses, and community members
- **Company store records (truck system):** Some mining companies ran stores where miners' wages were credited against purchases. Ledgers naming individual miners and their families survive fragmentarily at the Pennsylvania State Archives and local historical societies
- **Sons of Italy, Ancient Order of Hibernians, Welsh benevolent societies:** Fraternal organization membership records for ethnic communities; contact the national organization archives

## Records NOT online

The following record types are known to exist but have not been digitized or indexed for online access:

- **Pre-1906 civil birth records** — no statewide birth registration; church baptismal registers held at parishes and diocesan archives are the substitute
- **Pre-1906 civil death records** — same gap; church burial registers and mine accident reports are the primary alternatives
- **Mine Accident Reports (Luzerne County, 1870-1895)** — digitized but browse-only, no name index
- **Colliery Payroll Ledgers (Lackawanna County, 1878-1900)** — digitized but browse-only
- **Bulk of company employment and payroll records** — fragmentarily held at physical repositories, no comprehensive online access
- **UMWA membership rolls (1890+)** — physical at UMWA archives and Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Ethnic-language newspapers** — most not digitized; microfilm at Pennsylvania State Library and local societies
- **County tax lists (pre-1850)** — at county archives and Pennsylvania State Archives, limited digitization

## Known record losses

No comprehensive courthouse fire or flood losses were returned for Schuylkill, Luzerne, or Lackawanna county courthouses in this survey — these counties' record survival is generally considered good compared to many Pennsylvania counties. The critical loss affecting this region is the **1890 federal census**, destroyed by a 1921 warehouse fire in Washington, D.C. Tax lists, city directories, and the 1889/1891 state and local enumerations are the standard substitutes for that missing decade.

## Research tips

- **Identify the ethnic parish first.** Church registers are the only source for births and deaths before 1906, and the coal region had many co-located national parishes. Determine the family's exact national origin before choosing a parish ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Mining Community Sources](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))
- **Check Mine Inspector Reports for fatal accidents.** The annual state reports from 1870 list victim names, ages, and nationalities — many immigrant miners who left no other record appear here ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Coal Mining Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining))
- **Lackawanna County records before 1878 are in Luzerne County.** Scranton-area families with events before August 13, 1878, must be searched under Luzerne County for all court, deed, probate, and naturalization records
- **Search the full passenger manifest page.** Chain migrants from the same European village routinely traveled together. Neighbors listed on the same page can confirm a family's origin village and lead to European records
- **Pre-1906 naturalization declarations can give the precise European birthplace.** A Declaration of Intention ("first papers") was filed 2+ years before final citizenship and often names a specific village — more precise than the census's country-of-birth column
- **Use the 1880 mortality schedule.** The mortality schedule attached to the 1880 census records deaths in the prior twelve months, including mine accident victims, and is the last mortality schedule before statewide death registration
- **Tax lists substitute for the missing 1890 census.** County property and poll tax lists for 1889-1891 place a family at a specific address in the gap year
- **The four wiki_place_page sections for Pennsylvania returned generic fallback content** on this survey — for jurisdiction-specific research strategy, consult the FamilySearch wiki directly at familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Genealogy and familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy

The Pennsylvania anthracite coal region in the late 1800s was one of the most heavily documented working-class communities in American history, but its records are split across church archives, county courthouses, state records in Harrisburg, and physical mining-company collections. The single biggest warning is that Pennsylvania did not require statewide civil registration of births and deaths until 1906, so for the entire 1850-1905 window you are almost entirely dependent on ethnic parish registers — and which parish a family belonged to depends on their exact national origin, not just their street address. County marriages, federal censuses, and the uniquely valuable Mine Inspector Reports (published annually from 1870 and listing fatal accident victims by name and nationality) round out the primary sources, with naturalization declarations often providing the precise European village of origin.

The next step is to identify which of the five core coal counties your specific family lived in, determine their ethnic background and denomination, and build a research plan targeting the right parish archives alongside FamilySearch's indexed collections.

## Massachusetts Early 1600s Puritan Settlement – Locality Guide

*(Saved as `loc_001` in your project's research.json)*

---

### Why Massachusetts Is a Strong Research Jurisdiction

Massachusetts in the early 1600s is unusually well-documented by colonial standards. The colony **mandated that every town record births, marriages, and deaths starting in 1639** — well before any other American jurisdiction — so there is a genuine paper trail from the very founding years.

---

### Key Record Types & Repositories

#### 1. Town Vital Records
- **FamilySearch Collection 2061550** — indexed and searchable online for free
- Covers births, marriages, and deaths recorded at the town level
- The earliest surviving entries date from the late 1630s and 1640s

#### 2. Congregational Church Records
- **FamilySearch Collection 1921657**
- Puritan church registers document baptisms, admissions, and burials
- Often overlap with — or substitute for — town vitals in the very earliest decades

#### 3. Probate Records
- **FamilySearch Collection 1678901**
- County probate courts began operating in the 1630s–1640s
- Wills and inventories name heirs, neighbors, and associates — invaluable for family reconstruction

#### 4. Court Records & Land Records
- Massachusetts Bay Colony General Court records and county court files survive from the 1630s
- Land deeds (grantor/grantee indexes) held in county registries; many filmed by FamilySearch

#### 5. Published & Transcribed Sources
- *The Great Migration* study series (New England Historic Genealogical Society) — comprehensive prosopographies of immigrants arriving 1620–1640
- *Mayflower Families Through Five Generations* (for Plymouth Colony lines)
- Robert Charles Anderson's pioneering work on early settlers

---

### Critical Jurisdictional Distinction

> **Plymouth Colony vs. Massachusetts Bay Colony** — these were *completely separate jurisdictions* until 1691. Plymouth Colony covered modern Plymouth, Barnstable, and Bristol county towns and has its own distinct record series. Identify which colony your ancestor lived in **first** before searching.

---

### Calendar Caution

Dates before **1752** use the old Julian calendar. Dates in **January through March** may appear a year off — watch for double-date notation such as *"14 February 1689/90"* (meaning the year the writer called 1689 but which in our modern reckoning is 1690).

---

### Suggested Next Steps

1. **Identify the specific town** your ancestor lived in, and whether they were in Plymouth Colony or Massachusetts Bay Colony.
2. Search FamilySearch Collection **2061550** (town vitals) for the family name.
3. Check *The Great Migration* series at NEHGS for a prosopography if the ancestor arrived before 1640.
4. Pull probate records to reconstruct the family network.

The guide is now logged in your project. Let me know the specific town or ancestor name and we can build a targeted research plan!

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (1620-1700)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Plymouth Colony established 1620; Massachusetts Bay Colony chartered 1628/founded 1630; merged into Province of Massachusetts Bay 1691
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston (Suffolk County); by 1700 also Essex, Middlesex, Hampshire, Bristol, Plymouth, Barnstable, Dukes, and Nantucket counties
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Crown of England (colonial charter)
- **Population during period:** Approximately 20,000 settlers arrived during the Great Migration (1630-1643); colonial population data not returned by the population tool for this period
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fishing, fur trade, timber, early maritime commerce
- **Ethnic composition:** Almost exclusively English Puritan settlers; small numbers of servants and enslaved Africans by late century
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (established church); Quakers (suppressed); small Baptist and Anglican groups
- **Key historical events:** Great Migration 1630-1643; Pequot War 1636-1638; King Philip's War 1675-1676; Salem witch trials 1692; union of Plymouth and Massachusetts Bay colonies 1691

## Boundary changes
- Plymouth Colony (1620-1691) and Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628-1691) were separate jurisdictions with distinct records. Merged 1691.
- County formation ongoing: Suffolk/Essex/Middlesex 1643; Hampshire 1662; Bristol/Plymouth/Barnstable 1685; Dukes/Nantucket 1695.
- King Philip's War (1675-1676) destroyed records in many frontier towns.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Town-level recording mandated by Massachusetts Bay Colony from **1639** (town level, not statewide). Statewide civil registration did not begin until 1842.
- **What exists:** Births, marriages, deaths by town clerks from the 1630s. The Tanner-Corbin 'Vital Records to 1850' series abstracts records for 200+ towns.
- **FamilySearch collection:** 'Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890' (ID 2061550, ~3.4M records) — indexed + images.
- **Where held:** Town clerks; Massachusetts Archives; microfilmed at FamilySearch.

### Church records
- **Denominations:** Congregational (established); Quakers; small Baptist groups
- **Record types:** Member admissions, baptisms, marriages, burials, disciplinary proceedings
- **FamilySearch collection:** 'Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920' (ID 1921657, ~987K records)
- **Digitized volume:** Suffolk County congregational admissions and baptisms 1630-1700 (image group 007612045, 121 images) — full-text searchable, 0% name-indexed
- **NEHGS** holds the largest collection of unpublished colonial church records

### Census records
- **No federal census until 1790** — outside this period entirely
- **Substitutes:** Tax lists, militia muster rolls

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories from the 1630s
- **FamilySearch collection:** 'Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991' (ID 1678901, ~567K records)
- **Colony courts:** Court of Assistants records 1630-1692 published

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (state-land state)
- **Distribution:** Town proprietors' committees granted land
- **Digitized volume:** Town meeting and proprietors' records 1620-1698 (image group 007612044, 188 images) — browse only, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable
- **Deeds** in complete runs at county registries from 1643

### Military records
- **Conflicts:** Pequot War 1636-1638; King Philip's War 1675-1676; 1690s French wars
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives for colonial militia records; Fold3 for federal-era only

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Burying Point (Salem, 1637); King's Chapel (Boston, 1630); Copp's Hill (Boston, 1659)
- **Online:** Find A Grave; coverage uneven for eroded 1600s stones

### Newspaper records
- **No newspapers for genealogy in this period** — first continuous paper (Boston News-Letter) began 1704
- **Substitutes:** Town meeting records, court proceedings

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Passenger lists:** Great Migration series (NEHGS) documents every known 1620-1643 settler
- **FamilySearch passenger list collection** covers 1820-1891 only — not applicable to this period
- **Published sources:** Hotten, Banks's 'Planters of the Commonwealth'

### Tax records
- **Types:** Poll tax and property tax lists from the 1630s
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives; some published in local histories
- **Substitute value:** Enumerate adult males by town; best census substitute for this period

### Court records
- **Types:** General Court minutes; Court of Assistants records 1630-1692; county court files
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives; many published by Colonial Society of Massachusetts

### Other record types
- Town meeting minutes are among the richest sources
- Published 19th/early-20th century local histories frequently reprint lost colonial records
- Great Migration study series (NEHGS/Anderson) — essential secondary finding tool

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Town Vital Records 1620-1890 (indexed); Church Records 1630-1920; Probate Records 1635-1991; 2 digitized volumes (browse/full-text only) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | Colonial New England transcriptions; census (post-1790) | Subscription |
| AmericanAncestors.org (NEHGS) | Great Migration series; manuscript church records; vital records compilations | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal-era records only; limited colonial holdings | Free/In-person |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives, Boston | Colony/province records from 1620s; courts; military; land grants | In-person; some microfilm |
| NEHGS, Boston | Largest NE genealogical library; manuscript church records; Great Migration series | In-person; online members |
| County Registries of Deeds | Deed books from 1643 onward | In-person; some digitized |
| County Probate Courts | Probate files from county formation | In-person; microfilmed at FamilySearch |
| Local town clerks | Original vital records; town meeting minutes | In-person or mail |
| Colonial Society of Massachusetts | Published transcriptions of court, church, colonial records | In-person; publications in research libraries |

## Records NOT online
- Most original town meeting minutes beyond the 2 digitized FamilySearch volumes
- Unpublished colonial church records at NEHGS
- Massachusetts Archives colony-level records in their entirety
- County court case files
- Colonial-era tax lists
- Original passenger list documents for 1620-1700 arrivals

## Known record losses
- King Philip's War (1675-1676): frontier and western towns burned; records destroyed
- No general colonial census for any year in this period
- Plymouth Colony records (pre-1691) form a separate series; some lost
- Church records for non-Congregational groups largely absent

## Research tips
- Plymouth Colony is a separate jurisdiction from Massachusetts Bay — identify which colony first
- Start with the NEHGS Great Migration study series for 1620-1643 settlers
- Use the Tanner-Corbin 'Vital Records to 1850' published series for your town
- Search at the town level, not county level, for vital records
- Congregational church and town vital records are not redundant — search both
- Disciplinary church records name people not otherwise documented
- County formation dates determine where to look — before 1643, search Massachusetts Archives
- Salem witch trial records (1692) are extensively digitized for Essex County families
- Julian calendar in use until 1752: double dates (e.g., '14 February 1689/90') between Jan 1 and Mar 24 are normal
- Naming customs: English Puritan families reused given names across generations — do not assume a name uniquely identifies one person
- Search 19th-century published town histories on Archive.org and HathiTrust for transcriptions of lost records

- **Types:** General Court minutes; Court of Assistants records 1630-1692; county court files
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives; many published by Colonial Society of Massachusetts

### Other record types
- Town meeting minutes are among the richest sources
- Published 19th/early-20th century local histories frequently reprint lost colonial records
- Great Migration study series (NEHGS/Anderson) — essential secondary finding tool

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Town Vital Records 1620-1890 (indexed); Church Records 1630-1920; Probate Records 1635-1991; 2 digitized volumes (browse/full-text only) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | Colonial New England transcriptions; census (post-1790) | Subscription |
| AmericanAncestors.org (NEHGS) | Great Migration series; manuscript church records; vital records compilations | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal-era records only; limited colonial holdings | Free/In-person |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives, Boston | Colony/province records from 1620s; courts; military; land grants | In-person; some microfilm |
| NEHGS, Boston | Largest NE genealogical library; manuscript church records; Great Migration series | In-person; online members |
| County Registries of Deeds | Deed books from 1643 onward | In-person; some digitized |
| County Probate Courts | Probate files from county formation | In-person; microfilmed at FamilySearch |
| Local town clerks | Original vital records; town meeting minutes | In-person or mail |
| Colonial Society of Massachusetts | Published transcriptions of court, church, colonial records | In-person; publications in research libraries |

## Records NOT online
- Most original town meeting minutes beyond the 2 digitized FamilySearch volumes
- Unpublished colonial church records at NEHGS
- Massachusetts Archives colony-level records in their entirety
- County court case files
- Colonial-era tax lists
- Original passenger list documents for 1620-1700 arrivals

## Known record losses
- King Philip's War (1675-1676): frontier and western towns burned; records destroyed
- No general colonial census for any year in this period
- Plymouth Colony records (pre-1691) form a separate series; some lost
- Church records for non-Congregational groups largely absent

## Research tips
- Plymouth Colony is a separate jurisdiction from Massachusetts Bay — identify which colony first
- Start with the NEHGS Great Migration study series for 1620-1643 settlers
- Use the Tanner-Corbin 'Vital Records to 1850' published series for your town
- Search at the town level, not county level, for vital records
- Congregational church and town vital records are not redundant — search both
- Disciplinary church records name people not otherwise documented
- County formation dates determine where to look — before 1643, search Massachusetts Archives
- Salem witch trial records (1692) are extensively digitized for Essex County families
- Julian calendar in use until 1752: double dates (e.g., '14 February 1689/90') between Jan 1 and Mar 24 are normal
- Naming customs: English Puritan families reused given names across generations — do not assume a name uniquely identifies one person
- Search 19th-century published town histories on Archive.org and HathiTrust for transcriptions of lost records
