# Locality Guide: Vermont (pre-statehood, c. 1750-1791)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Vermont declared independence from both New York and Great Britain on 15 January 1777, operating as the Republic of Vermont until admitted as the 14th U.S. state on 4 March 1791. Prior to 1777 the territory was claimed by both New Hampshire (which issued Wentworth grants from 1749) and New York (which asserted authority after a 1764 Privy Council ruling).
- **County seat / administrative center:** No single capital during the colonial period; the Republic of Vermont held its legislature in various towns. Windsor and Montpelier were used at different points.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New Hampshire (grant authority, 1749-1764); New York (disputed authority, 1764-1777); self-governing Republic of Vermont (1777-1791).
- **Population during period:** Population figures were not returned by the place_population tool for this place and period. Vermont's 1790 federal census is the earliest enumeration covering the territory.
- **Economy:** Subsistence and small-scale commercial farming; timber; small-scale iron working; potash production.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English-descent settlers from southern New England (Connecticut, Massachusetts, Rhode Island); small numbers of French Canadians along the northern border; indigenous Abenaki people, whose records are largely outside the civil/church documentation system described here.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist (dominant); Baptist; Methodist (arriving later in the period); Quaker settlements in some areas; Anglican/Episcopal in a few towns.
- **Key historical events:** New Hampshire Wentworth land grants (1749-1764); Privy Council ruling awarding territory to New York (1764); Green Mountain Boys resistance to New York (1770s); Battle of Bennington (1777); Vermont Declaration of Independence (1777); Vermont Constitution (1777, first in North America to prohibit adult slavery); Republic of Vermont period (1777-1791); admission to the Union (1791).

## Boundary changes
- **Before 1764:** Territory was subject to New Hampshire grant authority; towns were chartered by Governor Benning Wentworth.
- **1764:** British Privy Council awarded the territory to New York, voiding or disputing New Hampshire grants. This created the central land-title conflict of the era and generated extensive documentation.
- **1777:** Republic of Vermont declared, organizing its own county structure and courts. The Republic established Bennington, Chittenden, Orange, and Windsor counties (among others) progressively from 1778.
- **1791:** Statehood. County structure continued; the existing Republic-era record series continued without interruption.
- **Critical note:** Because the territory was claimed by two competing jurisdictions before 1777, records for the same event or person may appear in both New Hampshire and New York archives. Neither set cancels the other — search both.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths did NOT begin until 1857 (town level). The FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy page states this explicitly: "Statewide civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths began in 1857. Earlier town clerk records (some back to the 1770s) survive unevenly; consult town clerk offices directly." ([Vermont Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))
- **What exists:** Some town clerk offices began recording vital events voluntarily as early as the 1770s. Survival is uneven and town-specific.
- **Where held:** Individual town clerk offices. Each Vermont town is its own civil registration unit — there is no county-level vital records office for this period.
- **Gaps:** Most pre-1791 vital events are not recorded in any civil register. The period c. 1750-1791 is almost entirely dependent on substitute sources (see below).
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptism, marriage, burial); family bibles; cemetery inscriptions; town proprietors' records; 19th-century town histories.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregationalist (dominant in most towns); Baptist (growing rapidly in the 1780s-1790s); Quaker (particularly in Danby, Monkton, and nearby areas); Methodist (present by the late 1780s); Anglican/Episcopal in a few towns.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations, and membership/covenant records. Congregational churches often kept detailed membership lists and covenants that function as a census substitute.
- **Where held:** Some records remain with individual churches or successor congregations. Many have been deposited with the Vermont Historical Society (Barre, VT) or respective denominational archives. FamilySearch has microfilmed some Vermont church records — check the FamilySearch Catalog directly by town name. The FamilySearch Vermont Church Records topic page did not return Vermont-specific content during this survey; it is a gap in the wiki.

- **Digitization:** Varies by collection and congregation. No systematic online digitization is confirmed by tool results.

The FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy page identifies this as "the earliest systematic resident list for the future state." This guide covers Vermont from roughly 1750 through its admission to the Union in 1791. The territory had no civil vital registration during this entire period — births, marriages, and deaths were never required to be filed with any government office, so the records do not simply await discovery in a courthouse. Instead, the key sources are the competing land-grant records held in New Hampshire and New York, church registers surviving at individual congregations and the Vermont Historical Society, town grand lists (the annual tax rolls that can place a man in a specific town year by year), the 1771 Grant Survey Schedule documenting roughly 1,800 early grantees, Revolutionary War pension files rich in family detail, and the 19th-century town histories that reprinted proprietors' records now otherwise inaccessible. The one major warning: because Vermont was simultaneously claimed by two different colonial governments, records for the same ancestor can sit in archives in Concord, New Hampshire and Albany, New York as well as in Vermont — searching only Vermont repositories will miss material.

The guide has been saved to the project (entry `loc_001`). When you are ready, a research plan can be built from this locality survey targeting specific ancestors and research questions.

Records generated under both competing authorities must be searched.

Town clerk offices are the primary civil repository for the pre-statehood period. Some town clerk records survive from the 1770s onward, but survival is uneven — contact individual town clerks directly before assuming a gap.
The first federal census that included Vermont was 1790, taken just before formal statehood was completed. It covers heads of household only, not all individuals by name.

Nineteenth-century Vermont town histories (most published 1860–1900) often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access. These are a critical finding aid for the pre-statehood period.

The Republic of Vermont organized county courts from 1778 onward; probate districts were established at that time. Search the county-level probate and court records from 1778 for events in the Republic period.

Settlers in the Vermont territory in the pre-statehood period often migrated from southern New England (Connecticut, Massachusetts, Rhode Island). Searching records of the origin colony may be necessary to establish parentage and origins.

The FamilySearch Wiki topic-specific pages for Vermont (Vital Records, Church Records, Land and Property, Probate Records, Census, Naming Customs) all resolved to a generic guidance page rather than Vermont-specific content during this survey — those pages are a coverage gap in the FamilySearch Wiki as of the survey date. Use the Vermont Genealogy page directly: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy

# Locality Guide: Vermont (pre-statehood, c. 1750–1791)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Vermont declared independence from both New York and Great Britain on 15 January 1777, operating as the Republic of Vermont until admitted as the 14th U.S. state on 4 March 1791. Prior to 1777 the territory was claimed by both New Hampshire (which issued Wentworth grants from 1749) and New York (which asserted authority after a 1764 Privy Council ruling).
- **County seat / administrative center:** No single capital during the colonial period; the Republic of Vermont held its legislature in various towns. Windsor and Montpelier were used at different points.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New Hampshire (grant authority, 1749–1764); New York (disputed authority, 1764–1777); self-governing Republic of Vermont (1777–1791).
- **Population during period:** No tool-returned population figures for this place and period. The 1790 federal census is the earliest enumeration; Vermont's population at statehood was approximately 85,000 (from general historical knowledge — not from a tool result).
- **Economy:** Subsistence and small-scale commercial farming; timber; small-scale iron working; potash production.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English-descent settlers from southern New England (Connecticut, Massachusetts, Rhode Island); small numbers of French Canadians along the northern border; indigenous Abenaki people, whose records are largely outside the civil/church documentation system described here.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist (dominant); Baptist; Methodist (arriving later in the period); Quaker settlements in some areas; Anglican/Episcopal in a few towns.
- **Key historical events:** New Hampshire Wentworth land grants (1749–1764); Privy Council ruling awarding territory to New York (1764); Green Mountain Boys resistance to New York (1770s); Battle of Bennington (1777, American Revolution); Vermont Declaration of Independence (1777); Vermont Constitution (1777, first in North America to prohibit adult slavery); Republic of Vermont period (1777–1791); admission to the Union (1791).

## Boundary changes
- Before 1764: Territory was subject to New Hampshire grant authority; towns were chartered by Governor Benning Wentworth.
- 1764: British Privy Council awarded the territory to New York, voiding or disputing New Hampshire grants. This created the central land-title conflict of the era and generated extensive documentation.
- 1777: Republic of Vermont declared, organizing its own county structure and courts. The Republic established Bennington, Chittenden, Orange, and Windsor counties (among others) progressively from 1778.
- 1791: Statehood. County structure continued; the existing Republic-era record series continued without interruption.
- Note: Because the territory was claimed by two competing jurisdictions before 1777, records for the same event or person may appear in both New Hampshire and New York archives. Neither set cancels the other.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths did NOT begin until 1857 (town-level registration). The FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy page states this explicitly: "Statewide civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths began in 1857" ([Vermont Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)). No statewide or territorial registration existed in the pre-statehood period.
- **What exists:** Some town clerk offices began recording vital events voluntarily as early as the 1770s. Survival is uneven by town.
- **Where held:** Individual town clerk offices. Each Vermont town is its own civil registration unit — there is no county-level vital records office. Contact town clerks directly.
- **Gaps:** Most pre-1791 vital events are not recorded in any civil register. The period 1750–1791 is almost entirely dependent on substitute sources.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptism, marriage, burial); family bibles; cemetery inscriptions; town proprietors' records; 19th-century town histories.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregationalist (the dominant church; most early towns organized a Congregational society); Baptist (grew rapidly in the 1780s–1790s); Quaker (particularly in Danby and Monkton areas); Methodist (present by the late 1780s); Anglican/Episcopal in some towns.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and membership lists. Congregational churches often kept detailed membership and covenant records.
- **Where held:** Some records remain with individual churches or their successor congregations. Many have been deposited with the Vermont Historical Society (Barre, VT) or the respective denominational archives. FamilySearch has microfilmed some Vermont church records, but the FamilySearch Wiki topic page for Vermont Church Records did not return Vermont-specific content during this survey — check the FamilySearch Catalog directly by place name.
- **Language:** English throughout.
- **Digitization:** Varies by collection. Check FamilySearch Catalog and the Vermont Historical Society's online finding aids.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The 1790 U.S. Federal Census is the first to include Vermont (taken just before formal statehood was complete). It lists heads of household by name with tallies of other household members by age/sex category — not all individuals by name. It is indexed and available free on FamilySearch and on Ancestry.
- **State/provincial census:** No Vermont state census was taken during the pre-statehood period. No tool result returned any state enumeration for this period.
- **Other enumerations:** The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule (prepared under New York colonial authority) enumerates approximately 1,800 grantees of New Hampshire grants and is the earliest systematic resident list for the territory. The FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy page identifies this as "the earliest systematic resident list for the future state" ([Vermont Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)). Tax lists and militia musters served as informal population counts.
- **Access:** The 1790 census is indexed + images online (free, FamilySearch and Ancestry). The 1771 Grant Survey Schedule — check the FamilySearch Catalog and the Vermont State Archives for access.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories, and court minute books.
- **Date range:** Republic of Vermont organized county courts and probate districts from 1778. Records for towns settled before 1778 may have no surviving probate record from that earlier period.
- **Where held:** Vermont county probate courts (records often transferred to the Vermont State Archives, Middlesex, VT). Some records are held at county courthouses.
- **Digitization:** The FamilySearch Wiki topic page for Vermont Probate Records did not return Vermont-specific content during this survey. Check the FamilySearch Catalog by place for what has been microfilmed or digitized.
- **Note on testate vs. intestate:** Search both will books (testate) and administration files (intestate). For the pre-statehood period, estates were sometimes not formally probated at all — watch for land division deeds in the deed books instead.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (New England township system). Towns were granted as whole townships; individual lots within each township were distributed by the town proprietors.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Two competing authorities issued grants: (1) Governor Benning Wentworth of New Hampshire issued township grants (Wentworth grants) beginning 1749; (2) New York colonial government issued competing patents after the 1764 Privy Council ruling. The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule documents the disputed New Hampshire grantees. After 1777, the Republic of Vermont's Governor and Council issued its own grants, voiding New York patents.
- **Types:** Township grants (proprietors' records), individual lot deeds, town land records, tax lists, and the 1771 Grant Survey Schedule.
- **Date range:** Wentworth grants began 1749. Town proprietors' records in some towns go back to the 1760s–1770s.
- **Where held:** (1) New Hampshire State Archives (Concord, NH) holds the original Wentworth grant records. (2) New York State Archives (Albany, NY) holds competing patent records. (3) Individual Vermont town clerk offices hold deeds and proprietors' records from the town's founding. (4) Vermont State Archives holds Republic-era and early state-era grants.
- **Digitization:** The FamilySearch Wiki topic page for Vermont Land and Property did not return Vermont-specific content during this survey. Check the FamilySearch Catalog by place.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (1754–1763, territory not yet heavily settled but some participation); American Revolutionary War (1775–1783), including the Battle of Bennington (1777) and service in the Continental Army and Vermont militia.
- **Record types:** Continental Army service records and pension files at NARA; Vermont militia records (some at the Vermont State Archives); bounty land warrants for Revolutionary War service (NARA); pension application files often contain family information including wives' and children's names and ages.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, DC / St. Louis) for federal records; Vermont State Archives for state militia; Fold3 and Ancestry have digitized much of the Revolutionary War pension and bounty land file series.
- **Digitization:** Revolutionary War pension files and compiled service records are indexed and available as images on Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/). Many are also on Ancestry and FamilySearch.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Every Vermont town established at least one burying ground, typically associated with the Congregational church or the town center. Many of the oldest stones date from the 1770s–1790s.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has coverage for many Vermont cemeteries. The Vermont Old Cemetery Association has conducted systematic surveys.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for this period are sparse; headstone transcriptions are the primary access point. Many early stones have been damaged or lost.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Vermont Gazette (Bennington, founded 1783) is among the earliest Vermont newspapers, falling within the Republic period. The Vermont Journal (Windsor) also dates to the 1780s.
- **Where held:** The Vermont Historical Society and the Vermont State Library hold microfilm holdings. Some early Vermont newspapers are available through Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and the Library of Congress Chronicling America project (https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/).
- **Content value:** Marriage notices, death notices, legal notices (estate settlements, land sales), and community news. Coverage in the 1780s is thin but not zero.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Settlers coming to Vermont in the pre-statehood period were overwhelmingly internal migrants from other New England colonies/states — not trans-Atlantic immigrants. No ocean port arrival records apply to the majority of this population.
- **Record types:** Not passenger lists, but rather: removal certificates (Congregational and Quaker churches issued these when a member moved from one congregation to another); town pauper records (towns were responsible for "warning out" people who might become public charges, generating records of arrivals); settlement examinations.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices and church records hold warning-out records and removal certificates respectively.
- **Internal migration note:** Because settlers largely came from Connecticut, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island, searching those states' records for your ancestor's origins is often the key step when the Vermont record is silent on parentage.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Town grand lists (annual property tax assessments), polls (taxable males).
- **Date range:** Some towns have grand lists from their founding, potentially from the 1760s–1770s.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices; some have been deposited with the Vermont State Archives or Vermont Historical Society.
- **Substitute value:** Grand lists are the primary substitute for the missing census years before 1790 and can place a man in a specific town in a specific year, making them especially valuable for the 1770s–1780s.

### Other record types
- **Town proprietors' records:** Each township's original proprietors met, voted, and kept minutes recording lot divisions, road layouts, and membership. These are often the earliest records naming residents of a Vermont town and are not widely digitized. Some are transcribed in 19th-century town histories.
- **Town histories:** The FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy page specifically notes that 19th-century town histories (most published 1860–1900) "often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access" ([Vermont Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)). These are a primary research tool for the pre-statehood period.
- **Warning-out records:** Towns formally warned out (served notice to) recent arrivals who lacked legal settlement, in order to avoid poor-relief liability. These records name individuals, places of origin, and arrival dates.
- **Republic of Vermont government records:** The Vermont State Archives holds session laws, council records, and other Republic-era documents that may name individuals.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | 1790 federal census (indexed + images); some Vermont church record microfilm in the Catalog; general U.S. Revolutionary War pension and service records | Free |
| Ancestry (ancestry.com) | 1790 federal census; Revolutionary War pension files; some Vermont town records | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Revolutionary War compiled service records and pension application files | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Vermont cemetery transcriptions | Free |
| Newspapers.com (newspapers.com) | Early Vermont newspapers including the Vermont Gazette (1783+) | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Finding aids for federal records | Free finding aids; some digitized |
| Chronicling America (chroniclingamerica.loc.gov) | Some early Vermont newspaper microfilm | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The external_links_search tool returned 6 results for Vermont in this time window, all of which are generic national repositories rather than Vermont-specific curated collections. The FamilySearch-specific collections_search and volume_search tools were not called in this survey batch due to the tools available in this environment — check the FamilySearch Catalog directly by searching for "Vermont" by place to see all microfilmed and digitized collections.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Vermont State Archives and Records Administration (Middlesex, VT) | Republic of Vermont records; state grants; some probate and court transfers; military records | In-person / written request; some online finding aids |
| Vermont Historical Society (Barre, VT) | Town histories; church records; manuscripts; newspaper microfilm; cemetery surveys | In-person; some digitized finding aids |
| Individual town clerk offices | Deed books, proprietors' records, grand lists, vital records from town's founding | In-person / mail; highly variable by town |
| New Hampshire State Archives (Concord, NH) | Original Wentworth grant records; New Hampshire colonial records | In-person / written request |
| New York State Archives (Albany, NY) | New York colonial patent records for the disputed Vermont territory | In-person / written request |
| NARA (Washington, DC) | Revolutionary War service and pension records; 1790 census originals | In-person; many records digitized on Fold3/Ancestry |

## Records NOT online
- Town grand lists (most towns, pre-1791): held at town clerk offices or Vermont State Archives; not systematically digitized.
- Town proprietors' records and meeting minutes: largely physical-only; some transcribed in town histories.
- Vermont county court minute books (1778–1791): some microfilmed; check FamilySearch Catalog by county.
- Church records for many individual congregations: held at churches, denominational archives, or Vermont Historical Society; digitization is incomplete.
- Warning-out records: town clerk offices; not digitized in any systematic way.
- Republic of Vermont council and legislative records: Vermont State Archives; limited online access.
- New Hampshire Wentworth grant records: New Hampshire State Archives; not comprehensively digitized.

## Known record losses
- No major, documented statewide courthouse fire or flood for the pre-statehood period has been confirmed in the tool results for this survey. However, because vital registration did not exist at all before 1857, the primary "gap" is structural rather than due to destruction: the records simply were never required to be created in most instances.
- Individual town records vary in survival. Some towns suffered losses from fires or neglect. Contact the specific town clerk for confirmation of what survives.
- Warning-out records and early church registers are known to be sparse or missing for many towns settled in the 1760s–1780s.

## Research tips
- **Start with the 1771 Grant Survey Schedule.** The FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy page identifies this as the earliest systematic resident list for Vermont, naming approximately 1,800 grantees of the disputed New Hampshire grants. If your ancestor held land in Vermont before statehood, this is your first stop. ([Vermont Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))
- **Search both New Hampshire and New York land records.** The competing grant systems mean your ancestor may appear in both. New Hampshire State Archives (Wentworth grants) and New York State Archives (colonial patents) both have relevant holdings.
- **Use the 1790 federal census as your anchor.** It is the earliest indexed, images-online enumeration and establishes where a family was located at the moment of statehood. Work backward from it.
- **Town grand lists are the substitute census for the 1770s–1780s.** Annual property tax lists can place a man in a specific town year by year. Check the Vermont State Archives and individual town clerk offices.
- **Read the 19th-century town history for every town of interest.** The FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy page specifically flags these (published 1860–1900) as reprinting colonial-era proprietors' records not otherwise accessible. ([Vermont Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))
- **Search the origin colonies first if Vermont is silent.** The vast majority of Vermont settlers came from Connecticut, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island. If your ancestor's parentage or birth is not documented in Vermont, the Connecticut Barbour Collection of vital records and Massachusetts vital records are the logical next step.
- **Church records stand in for civil vital records.** No civil vital registration existed in this period. Congregational church records — baptisms, marriages, burials, and membership covenants — are the closest equivalent. Seek out the records of every church in the ancestor's town.
- **Revolutionary War pension files are rich sources.** Many Vermont men served in the Revolution; their pension applications (on Fold3 and Ancestry) often contain depositions naming wives, children, and sometimes parents, providing family relationship evidence not found elsewhere.
- **The Republic of Vermont operated its own government.** From 1777, Vermont had its own courts, land office, and legislature. These Republic-era records (at the Vermont State Archives) are separate from both the pre-1777 colonial records and the post-1791 state records.
- **FamilySearch Wiki topic-specific pages for Vermont** (Vermont Vital Records, Vermont Church Records, Vermont Land and Property, Vermont Probate Records, Vermont Census, Vermont Naming Customs) all returned a generic page rather than Vermont-specific content during this survey — a coverage gap. Use the Vermont Genealogy overview page directly for what FamilySearch has documented: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy
